lessons.title: Insertion sort
lessons.description: Build a sorted prefix, one carefully placed element at a time.

transcript.text: How does insertion sort work? We will sort these six numbers, derive the time complexity, and finish with the details you should remember. Do keep up.
Keep a sorted prefix on the left. The first element, one, is already sorted. Take the next element and move it left across larger neighbours, one adjacent swap at a time.
Start with four. Compare it with one. One is smaller, so four stays put. The sorted prefix now contains one and four.
Next, take three. Four is larger, so swap the adjacent four and three.
Compare three with one. One is smaller, so stop. The prefix is now one, three, four.
Take six. Four is smaller, so no swap is needed. Extend the sorted prefix to include six.
Take five. Six is larger, so swap six and five.
Four is smaller than five, so stop. The first five elements are sorted.
Now take two. It must travel left through the sorted prefix. Watch each comparison and swap.
Six is larger than two. Swap them, moving two one position left.
Five is larger than two. Swap again.
Four is larger than two. Swap again.
Three is larger than two. Swap once more.
One is smaller than two, so stop. All six numbers are sorted. That took eleven key comparisons and six adjacent swaps. They are different counts, darling.

Why is stopping safe? The prefix was already sorted, so everything before that smaller neighbour is also no larger than the inserted element. Each insertion preserves every record and enlarges the sorted prefix.
To derive the worst case, reverse the six numbers. Each new element is smaller than the entire prefix. Successive insertions need one, two, three, four, then five swaps.
For n elements, add one through n minus one. The sum is n times n minus one, divided by two. That grows quadratically, giving theta of n squared worst-case time.
For already sorted input, each insertion makes one key comparison and stops. There are n minus one such comparisons and zero swaps. The best-case time is theta of n.
For a uniformly random ordering of distinct keys, each pair is inverted with probability one half. The expected swap count is n times n minus one, divided by four. Average time is still quadratic.

More precisely, an inversion is an earlier element larger than a later one. Every adjacent swap removes exactly one inversion. With I inversions, runtime is theta of n plus I. Few inversions explain why nearly sorted data can be fast.

Things to take note of. Swap only when the left key is strictly greater. On equal keys, stop. Two A must stay before two B, so this version is stable. Greater than or equal would break that guarantee.
This iterative version is in-place. Its indices and one temporary swap value use constant extra space. An empty array or a singleton needs no insertion. The outer loop starts at index one.
Binary search can find the insertion position with fewer comparisons. But elements in an array still have to move. Binary insertion therefore still has quadratic worst-case movement and time.

When tracing, show every insertion and mark the growing sorted prefix. Count key comparisons separately from swaps. Remember: linear best case, quadratic average and worst cases, constant extra space, and stable with the strict comparison. Hmph. Your turn to explain it.

lessons.title: Merge sort
lessons.description: Split the problem. Merge the answers. Understand every level.

transcript.text: How does merge sort work? Watch these eight numbers. We will split them, merge them in order, and derive the running time. Do try to keep up.
First, split the array into two halves, with four elements in each.
Split each half again. Now we have four groups of two.
Keep splitting until every group has one element. A single element is already sorted. That is our base case.
Now work back upward. To merge two sorted groups, compare their front elements and move the smaller one into the next output position.
Eight versus three: three moves first, then eight. Our first sorted pair is three, eight.
The other pairs merge the same way: one, five; two, seven; and four, six.
Merge the first two sorted pairs. One moves first, then three, then five. The right group is empty, so copy the remaining eight.
Merge the other two pairs. Two, four, six, then the remaining seven. Both halves are now sorted.
For the final merge, compare only the two front elements. You do not search the entire groups, obviously.
One beats two. Move one into the output, and advance the left pointer.
Three versus two. Move two, and advance the right pointer.
Three beats four. Move three from the left.
Five versus four. Move four from the right.
Five beats six. Move five from the left.
Eight versus six. Move six from the right.
Eight versus seven. Move seven. The right group is now empty.
Copy the remaining eight. There. All eight numbers are sorted.

Why is merging linear? Each element enters the output once. Across one merge level, all groups together contain eight elements, so that level makes eight output placements. In general, that is theta of n work.
For eight elements, we merge pairs, then groups of four, then all eight: three merge levels. For n elements, repeated halving gives about log base two of n levels.
Multiply linear work per level by logarithmic levels: theta of n log n time. Equivalently, two half-sized recursive sorts plus a linear merge give this recurrence.
Things to take note of for merge sort. First, the standard version takes theta of n log n time in the best, average, and worst cases.
Use half-open ranges: start is included; end is excluded. Stop when end minus start is at most one, including an empty range. Odd lengths split into unequal halves.
Temporary arrays require linear auxiliary space. Recursion adds a logarithmic stack. Total extra space stays linear, so this version is not in-place.
On equal keys, take the left element first. Here, two A came before two B, so the merged output keeps A before B. Stability depends on this tie rule.
The slides also list order n log n swaps. In this implementation, these are element copies and writes, rather than pairwise swaps. Hmph. Remember the details.

lessons.title: Quicksort
lessons.description: Follow the pivot, the partition, and the recursive calls.

transcript.text: How does quicksort work? Choose a pivot, partition around it, then recursively sort the two sides. The partition itself does not sort either side, so do try to resist celebrating early.
Use a half-open range: start is included and end is excluded. Stop when its size is zero or one, and place the chosen pivot at end minus one.
Here are six keys: four, two, six, one, five, three. Keep three at the end as pivot, and start both the scan and the boundary at index zero.
Four is not smaller than three, so leave it where it is. Two is smaller, so swap two with four at the boundary, then advance the boundary.
Six is not smaller than three, so scan past it. One is smaller, so swap one with four at the boundary, then advance the boundary again.
Five stays on the large side, and the scan is finished. Swap the pivot with six at the boundary: three now has its final index, two.
The left part is two, one, which still needs sorting. Recurse on the left and right ranges while excluding the settled pivot, producing one through six.
Before each scan, everything before the boundary is smaller than the pivot. Between the boundary and scan are processed keys at least as large; everything beyond the scan is still unknown.
Now derive the cost. A partition scans a range once, so its work is linear. Balanced splits give about log base two of n levels, with at most linear total work on each level.
If every pivot leaves one empty side, the work becomes n minus one, plus n minus two, down to one. That triangular sum is quadratic, and sorted input with a last pivot can trigger it.

For distinct keys, uniform random pivots give expected n log n time, but quadratic worst-case time remains possible. Expected means averaged over the random choices; it is not a promise about every run.
Things to take note of. Ordinary recursion uses logarithmic stack space when balanced and linear space in the worst case, so this is not constant-space under our course definition.
Recursing only on the smaller side and looping on the larger bounds the stack by log n. Quicksort is unstable, and many duplicate keys favour three-way partitioning, which skips the equal region.

Keep the pivot convention and recursive bounds consistent. A middle array position is not necessarily a median value, and random pivots improve expectation without removing the worst case. There, now your partition actually means something.

lessons.title: Counting sort
lessons.description: Turn key frequencies into stable output positions.

transcript.text: How does counting sort work? Use small integer keys as array indices, count their frequencies, and turn those counts into output positions. The labels travel with their records, naturally.
Our six records have keys from zero through three, so the range size is four. The letters distinguish equal-key records; they are not extra sorting keys.
Scan the input once and increment the counter for each key. We get frequencies one, one, two, two: one zero, one one, two twos, and two threes.
Add each frequency to the cumulative total before it. The cumulative counts become one, two, four, six; each says how many records have a key at most that value.
These are counts, not zero-based output indices. For a key v, decrement its cumulative count first, then use the new count as its output position.
Scan the input from right to left. Three b goes to index five, then one goes to index one, and two b goes to index three.
Continue backwards: the earlier three goes to index four, zero goes to index zero, and two a goes to index two. Both pairs of equal keys retain their input order.
Why is that stable? A later equal record is processed first and receives the later available position. Earlier equals fill earlier positions, preserving their relative order.
Derive the time by counting the loops. Initialising and prefixing the k counters costs order k; scanning n inputs and placing n records costs order n. Together that is theta of n plus k.
The output buffer holds n records, and the count array holds k counters. Auxiliary space is order n plus k, so this stable implementation is not in-place under the course definition.
Things to take note of. Linear time in n requires the range k to be at most proportional to n. Six records spread across a billion possible keys would be a rather wasteful choice.

A known bounded negative range can be shifted to start at zero, but its width still determines storage. Empty input needs no placements; singleton input must still respect the chosen range convention.

Preserve whole records, choose one count convention, and scan backwards for this placement rule. Counting sort avoids the comparison-only lower bound by using integer indexing, not by magically doing fewer comparisons.

lessons.title: Radix sort
lessons.description: See why one stable digit pass builds on the last.

transcript.text: How does radix sort work? Stably sort by the least significant digit first, then move one digit left at a time. Stability is doing the clever work here, so do pay attention.
Use eight three-digit decimal numbers, matching the course example. Units come first, then tens, then hundreds; a shorter number would be treated as having leading zeros.
Sort by units while preserving the order of equal digits. Four thirty moves first, the three numbers ending in one follow in their current order, then two, three, and the two fours.
The result is four thirty, one forty-one, three forty-one, one twenty-one, two oh two, three thirteen, two twenty-four, three oh four. Only the last digit is sorted so far.
Now stably sort that result by tens. The zeros come first, followed by one, the twenties, thirty, and the forties; equal tens retain the units ordering established before.

We now have two oh two, three oh four, three thirteen, one twenty-one, two twenty-four, four thirty, one forty-one, three forty-one. The last two digits are sorted, although the whole numbers are not.
Finally, stably sort by hundreds. One twenty-one and one forty-one remain in that order, followed by the two hundreds, the three hundreds, and four thirty.

After t passes, the sequence is sorted by its t least significant digits. The next stable pass orders the new digit while preserving the previous suffix order inside ties. Induction gives the final sorted sequence.
Suppose there are d digits in base b. Counting sort takes theta of n plus b per digit, so d passes take theta of d times n plus b. The buffers can be reused between passes.
For keys below k, choose enough digits that b to the power d is at least k. If b equals n and k is at most n to a fixed constant power, only constantly many passes are needed.
Things to take note of. Each digit sort must be stable: reversing equal tens can destroy the units order. This implementation uses extra buffers and is not constant-space.

State the base and digit count instead of simply claiming linear time. Empty input needs no passes, all-zero input needs a clear digit convention, and very long keys increase the work. Hmph, digits do not sort themselves.

lessons.title: Heapify
lessons.description: Read the heap, then repair it from the inside out.

transcript.text: How does heapify work? Repair one misplaced root by moving it down a heap, choosing the smaller child in a min-heap. The child subtrees must already be valid heaps.
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array. In zero-based storage, the children of index i are two i plus one and two i plus two, if those indices exist.
Here the root is nine, with children two and three. Below them, four, five, six, and seven already satisfy their own parent relationships, so only the root needs repair.
Compare the two children and choose two, the smaller one. Since nine is larger, swap nine with two; the root is now correct, but nine may still violate order farther down.
Nine now has children four and five. Choose four and swap again; nine reaches a leaf, so the repair stops.
The resulting array is two, four, three, nine, five, six, seven. It is a valid min-heap, although it is not a sorted array: siblings and separate branches need no relative order.

Why choose the smaller child? Moving it up makes it no larger than either child at the repaired position. Choosing the larger child could leave the smaller child below a parent that is still too large.
At each step, stop if the parent is already no larger than both valid children. Otherwise descend one level; the only remaining possible violation follows the item moving down.
A node of subtree height h can descend at most h levels. Each level uses a constant number of comparisons and one possible swap, giving order h time and logarithmic worst-case time at the root.

An iterative repair needs only an index and a few temporary words, so auxiliary space is constant. A recursive repair instead keeps up to logarithmically many active calls; those frames count as space.
Things to take note of. Check child bounds against the active heap size before reading them, and never invent a missing right child. A single root heapify cannot repair an arbitrary unordered tree.

Empty heaps have no root to repair, and a singleton is already a heap. Reverse the comparisons and choose the larger child for a max-heap. Follow the violation down one branch, and the whole repair becomes quite civilised.

lessons.title: Build a heap
lessons.description: Start at the last parent and discover why building is linear.

transcript.text: How does build-heap work? Repair internal nodes from the bottom upwards, so every heapify call starts with valid child subtrees. This builds a heap in linear time, which is more subtle than it looks.
Start with seven, six, five, four, three, two, one in zero-based array order. The last internal index is floor of n over two, minus one; here that is index two.
Indices three through six are leaves, and each leaf is already a valid heap. Process internal indices two, one, then zero, which puts every child before its parent in the repair schedule.
At index two, five has children two and one. Swap five with the smaller child, one, and that subtree is repaired.
At index one, six has children four and three. Swap six with three, so the second child subtree is also a min-heap.
Now repair the root seven: choose child one, and swap. Continue down with seven, choose child two, and swap again; now the entire array satisfies min-heap order.
The array is one, three, two, four, six, seven, five. Every parent is no larger than its children, but the array is not fully sorted. A heap exposes the minimum without ordering every pair.
Multiplying n heapify calls by the root cost log n gives an upper bound, but it is loose. Most nodes are near the bottom, so most cannot travel down logarithmically many levels.
At height h, there are at most order n over two to the power h plus one nodes. Charge each order h work; the weighted geometric sum is a constant times n.

The loop processes linearly many internal nodes, supplying a matching linear lower bound for this implementation. Bottom-up build-heap therefore takes theta n time, while repeated insertion has an n log n worst-case bound.

Things to take note of. Use iterative heapify for constant auxiliary space, and include recursive frames if you implement repair recursively. Empty and singleton arrays have no internal node to process.

Do not scan internal nodes from the root down: the required child heaps may not exist yet. Linear heap construction does not imply linear comparison sorting, because the resulting heap is only partially ordered. Quite a useful distinction.

lessons.title: Priority queues
lessons.description: Insert, extract, and follow every change in the heap.

transcript.text: How do heap priority queues work? A min-priority queue returns the smallest key first, using a min-heap to make that key easy to find. Arrival order does not determine priority.
Our heap starts as one, three, two, seven, five, four. Peeking reads the root, one, without removing it; this takes constant time because heap order guarantees that root is a minimum.
To insert zero, append it at the next array position, preserving the complete-tree shape. The new leaf may be smaller than its parent, so repair upwards along its ancestor chain.
Zero is below two, so swap zero above two. It is still below one, so swap again; zero is now the root, and insertion is complete.
To extract the minimum, first save the old root zero as the return value. Replace it with the last key, two, then shrink the active array; returning the replacement would be rather embarrassing.
The replacement two is larger than its smaller child one. Swap them and stop, giving one, three, two, seven, five, four again; the extracted record remains zero.
Decrease-key lowers a known record, so its possible violation is upwards. Lower seven to zero, swap it above three, then above one; an indexed heap must update record locations after every swap.

A complete binary tree has logarithmic height. Sift-up and sift-down cross at most that many parent-child edges, doing constant work per edge, so insertion repair, extraction, and known-position decrease-key each take order log n.

The heap stores n records, and an indexed version also stores their locations. A single iterative repair needs constant temporary space; a recursive repair can add a logarithmic stack. Building from an array takes linear time.

Things to take note of. Searching the whole heap for a record can cost linear time, so decrease-key assumes its position is already known. Heap repair bounds also separate from occasional array resizing costs.
Define what extraction and peek do on an empty queue. A singleton extraction simply returns its only record and leaves an empty heap, with no sift-down needed.
Insertions rise, root replacements sink, and decrease-key rises from its known position. Keep whole records together and save the extracted root before overwriting it. There, a queue with standards.

lessons.title: Heapsort
lessons.description: Shrink the active heap. Grow the sorted suffix.

transcript.text: How does heapsort work? Build a heap, repeatedly remove its root, and repair the remaining heap. Let me show the tree and output together, then connect this to the in-place version.
With a min-heap, the root is the smallest remaining key. The lecture first copies each extracted minimum into a separate output array, from left to right. That output buffer uses order n extra space.
Remove one into output position zero, and move the last leaf, six, to the root. Swap six with the smaller child two, then with three; the heap is valid again.
Remove two next and replace it with the last leaf, six. Swap six with the smaller child three, then with five; three is now the next minimum at the root.
Remove three into the next output slot and put the last leaf, six, at the root. Swap six with the smaller child four to restore the min-heap.
Remove four into output and replace it with six. Swap six with its only child, five; the root is the next smallest key again.
Remove five next, leaving just six in the heap, so no repair is needed. Finally remove six; the heap is empty and the separate output array is sorted.
For the in-place version, use a max-heap and put removed maxima at the right end of the original array. The tree and array are two views of the same data; the green suffix reuses array storage.

Now build a max-heap from three, one, six, five, two, four. Work from the last internal node upwards: six already beats its child four; swap one with five; then swap three with six and finally with four. The root six is now the largest remaining value.
Swap the root six with the last active key, three, and shrink the active prefix to five keys. Six belongs to the sorted suffix, but the replacement three still needs repair.
Compare three with children five and four, then swap with the larger child five. The active heap becomes five, three, four, one, two; never pull the settled six back into heapify.
Swap five with the last active key two, and shrink again. Sift two down below four, leaving four, three, two, one as the active heap and five, six as the sorted suffix.
Swap four with one and shorten the heap to three keys. Repair by swapping one below three; the remaining max-heap is three, one, two.
Move three to the end of that prefix, leaving two and one. Move two to its final position, and the singleton one needs no repair; the array is now one through six.
After each completed repair, the active prefix is a max-heap and the suffix is sorted ascending. Every suffix key is at least as large as every remaining heap key; the prefix need not be sorted.
Building costs theta n. The remaining n minus one extractions each cost at most order log n, giving an n log n total upper bound and a matching worst-case bound.
Do not infer that every best case for every implementation is theta n log n. With an early-stopping repair, equal keys can stop immediately; the safe general guarantee is the n log n upper bound.
Things to take note of. Iterative heapify makes auxiliary space constant, while recursive repair adds a logarithmic stack. Heapsort is unstable because distant swaps can reverse equal-key records.

Use a max-heap for this ascending end-placement procedure, and repair only inside the active prefix. Empty and singleton inputs need no extraction loop. The sorted suffix is finished work, so kindly leave it alone.

lessons.title: Breadth-first search
lessons.description: Explore layer by layer, with a queue to keep your place.

transcript.text: How does breadth-first search work? Use a first-in, first-out queue to explore a graph one distance layer at a time. With unweighted edges, the first discovery gives a shortest edge-count distance.
Our directed graph has arrows from A to B and C, from B and C to D, then from D to E. We scan neighbours alphabetically, initialise all other distances to infinity, and enqueue A at distance zero.
Remove A from the front and inspect its neighbours. Discover B and C, give each distance one and parent A, and enqueue them in that order.
Remove B next, leaving C waiting. Discover D at distance two, set its parent to B, and add it behind C; the queue now contains C followed by D.
Remove C and inspect its arrow to D. D was marked when it was enqueued, so skip it rather than adding a duplicate; the queue now contains only D.
Remove D and discover E at distance three, with parent D. Then remove E, which has no undiscovered neighbours, and the queue becomes empty.
To recover a route to E, follow parents backwards: E, D, B, A, then reverse that list. The route A, B, D, E uses three edges, matching the distance label.

Why is first discovery optimal? The queue processes all vertices at distance d before vertices at distance d plus one. Any shorter route to a newly discovered vertex would have offered it from an earlier layer already.

Let n count vertices and m count edges. Initialisation costs order n, each vertex enters the queue at most once, and adjacency lists scan each directed edge once; undirected lists scan each edge twice.

Distances, parents, and the queue together need order n auxiliary space, separate from the graph representation. An adjacency matrix instead scans n entries per expanded vertex, giving an n squared worst-case time bound.

Things to take note of. Mark vertices at enqueue time, and distinguish discovery from expansion. Another neighbour order may change parents while preserving distances; unreachable vertices remain at infinity.

Repeat from unvisited starts if you need all undirected components. Ordinary BFS does not solve arbitrary weighted shortest paths, because fewer edges need not mean less weight. Keep the queue honest, and the layers take care of themselves.

lessons.title: Depth-first search
lessons.description: Follow the call stack, classify edges, and find cycles.

transcript.text: How does depth-first search work? Follow one branch as far as possible, then backtrack to the last vertex with an unexplored neighbour. The call stack remembers the active path, so you need not.
Use the same directed graph: A reaches B and C, each can reach D, and D reaches E. Choose neighbours alphabetically and mark a vertex immediately when its call begins.
From A, discover B and leave A waiting on the stack. From B, discover D, then from D discover E; each recursive call suspends the previous one.
E has no outgoing neighbour to explore, so finish E and return to D. D is then finished, followed by B, and the stack returns to the suspended call for A.
A still has its neighbour C, so discover C now. C points to D, but D is already visited and finished; skip it, finish C, then finish A.
The discovery order was A, B, D, E, C. The finishing order was E, D, B, C, A; writing the discovery order when asked for postorder would produce a completely different answer.
A search from one source only visits reachable vertices. For the whole graph, loop over every vertex and start another call at each unvisited one; the result is a DFS forest.

For directed cycle detection, distinguish undiscovered, active, and finished vertices. An edge to an active ancestor gives a back edge and a cycle; an edge to an already finished vertex alone does not.

Each vertex is first discovered once and each adjacency entry is examined once. Initialisation contributes order n and edge scanning contributes order m, so the full forest takes order n plus m with adjacency lists.

Visited and parent arrays use order n space, and a long chain can create n active recursive calls. An explicit stack avoids a language recursion limit, but reproducing the exact recursive order requires tracking where each call resumes.

Things to take note of. DFS does not generally find shortest paths, and neighbour order can change its tree and orders. In undirected simple graphs, scanning the reverse parent edge is not evidence of a cycle.

With parallel edges, track the parent edge identity rather than skipping every edge to that vertex. Discover on entry, finish on return, and backtrack only after a branch is exhausted. There, wandering with a proper memory.

lessons.title: Topological sorting
lessons.description: Put dependencies in order with source removal and DFS.

transcript.text: How does topological sorting work? List every vertex so each directed prerequisite arrow points forwards in the list. Such an ordering exists exactly when the graph has no directed cycle.
Use arrows A to C, B to C, and C to D. Both A and B can start, but C must wait for both, and D must wait for C.
For source removal, count each vertex’s incoming edges. The indegrees are zero, zero, two, one; add A and B to a ready queue because they have no remaining prerequisites.
Remove A from the ready queue and append it to the output. Decrement C from two to one; C is not ready yet, so the remaining queue contains B.
Remove B and append it next. Decrement C from one to zero, then enqueue C; reaching zero is the event that makes a vertex ready.
Remove C, append it, and decrement D to zero. Enqueue and remove D, producing A, B, C, D; every arrow now points forwards.
Choosing B before A would instead give B, A, C, D, which is also valid. Multiple ready vertices allow different topological orders; if exactly one is ready at every step, the order is forced.

If the ready worklist empties before all n vertices are output, the remaining graph contains a directed cycle. Its vertices keep waiting on one another, so a partial list is not a complete topological order.
The other taught method uses a full DFS forest and rejects back edges. On this graph, alphabetical DFS finishes D, C, A, then B; reverse that sequence to obtain B, A, C, D.

In a DAG, an edge goes to a vertex that finishes before its source, whether reached recursively or already finished. Reversing the finishes therefore puts the source before the destination; plain finishing order points the wrong way.

Computing indegrees scans n vertices and m edges once. Each vertex enters the worklist once and each outgoing edge causes one decrement, so source removal takes order n plus m time and order n auxiliary space.

Things to take note of. A constant-time queue or stack keeps the source-removal bound linear; repeatedly rescanning all vertices for zero counters can be slower. Use adjacency lists for that n plus m analysis.

For an empty graph, the empty order is valid, and an isolated vertex is ready immediately. Check every edge against the final order, and reverse DFS finishes when using that method. Prerequisites first; dramatic entrances later.

lessons.title: Bellman-Ford
lessons.description: Relax every edge and see what each pass guarantees.

transcript.text: How does Bellman-Ford work? Relax every directed edge repeatedly, allowing negative weights and checking for reachable negative cycles. It is deliberately systematic, which is occasionally more useful than trying to be clever.

Start with distance zero at S and infinity elsewhere. Relaxing u to v tests whether distance u plus the edge weight is smaller than distance v; on improvement, update both the distance and its parent.
Our chain is S to A with weight two, A to B with negative one, then B to T with five. Scan edges backwards each pass: B to T, A to B, S to A.
In pass one, B and A still have infinite distances when their outgoing edges are checked. Only the last edge, S to A, improves a label, setting A to two.
In pass two, B to T still cannot improve anything. A to B now offers two minus one, so B becomes one; S to A leaves its label unchanged.
In pass three, B to T offers one plus five, giving T distance six. We now know the route S, A, B, T, and its parent pointers reconstruct that route backwards.

After k full passes, every vertex with a finite shortest path using at most k edges has its correct distance. An in-place scan may propagate farther within one pass, so k is a guarantee, not an exact limit.

Without a reachable negative cycle, a finite shortest route can be chosen simple, using at most n minus one edges. That explains the n minus one complete passes; a whole unchanged pass permits early stopping.

After those passes, an additional scan checks for any improvement from a finite-distance tail. An improvement certifies a negative cycle reachable from S; the improving edge itself may merely be downstream of that cycle.

With n vertices and m edges, there are at most n minus one full scans of m edges, plus initialisation and the detection scan. This gives order n plus n m time and order n auxiliary labels and parents.

Things to take note of. Negative edges are allowed, but a reachable negative cycle can make distances unbounded below for targets it can reach. A disconnected negative cycle does not affect this source’s distances.

Skip numeric relaxation from infinity and respect the specified edge order when tracing. A singleton needs no ordinary pass but still needs the cycle check for a negative self-loop. Repeated relaxation needs a stopping argument, and now you have one.

lessons.title: Dijkstra’s algorithm
lessons.description: Track tentative distances until the next minimum is certain.

transcript.text: How does Dijkstra’s algorithm work? Repeatedly settle the smallest tentative distance, then relax its outgoing edges. The guarantee requires nonnegative edge weights, including zero; a negative edge is enough to break it.

Set the source S to zero, other distances to infinity, and keep an indexed min-heap keyed by tentative distance. A parent records the route responsible for each improvement; discovering a route does not yet settle its destination.
Settle S first. Its edges offer A distance four and B distance one, so update those queue keys and parents; B is now the smallest unsettled candidate.
Settle B at one. Via B, A improves from four to three, and T receives a tentative nine; decrease A’s queue key instead of leaving the old priority behind.
Next settle A at three. Its edge to T offers three plus two, improving nine to five; update T’s parent to A and lower its queue key.
Finally settle T at five. Following parents backwards gives T, A, B, S, so the route S, B, A, T costs one plus two plus two, which is five.

Every settled label is optimal. If a cheaper route to the extracted minimum existed, its first unsettled vertex would already have been offered a no-larger prefix cost by its settled predecessor; nonnegative remaining edges preserve that comparison.
See why negative edges matter: S to A costs one, S to B costs two, and B to A costs negative three. A could settle at one before B reveals the true distance negative one, even without any cycle.

An indexed binary heap extracts each vertex at most once and performs at most one successful decrease-key per scanned edge. With logarithmic heap operations, the total is order n plus m, times log n, using adjacency lists.

Labels, parents, membership flags, and an indexed heap use order n auxiliary space. A lazy duplicate-entry queue needs separate accounting and must skip stale entries; it is not the same queue implementation.

Things to take note of. Stop once the target is settled for a single-target query, or once the smallest remaining label is infinite. Equal-distance routes may choose different parents; strict improvement keeps unnecessary parent changes out.

For a one-vertex graph, the source distance is zero; an empty graph has no valid chosen source. Keep tentative labels separate from settled facts, and never smuggle a negative edge into the assumptions. Hmph, even greed needs a proof.

lessons.title: DAG shortest paths
lessons.description: Use a topological order to handle even negative edges.

transcript.text: How do DAG shortest paths work? Process vertices in a topological order and relax each outgoing edge once. Unlike Dijkstra, this schedule can handle negative edge weights because a DAG has no directed cycles.

The shortest-path recording mentions this linear-time DAG tutorial problem. We can derive the procedure by combining the course’s topological ordering with its relaxation rule, rather than inventing a different kind of distance.
Use the topological order S, A, B, T. Set distance S to zero and the rest to infinity; although A to B has weight negative four, every arrow still points forwards in the order.
Process S first and relax both outgoing edges. A receives two and B receives five, with parent S; these are the best routes seen so far, not a finalisation by smallest distance.
Next process A, even though a different graph might give another later vertex a smaller label. A to B offers two minus four, improving B to negative two, while A to T offers nine.
Process B next and relax its edge to T. Negative two plus three equals one, improving T from nine to one and changing its parent to B.
T has no outgoing edges, so the pass is complete. The final route S, A, B, T costs two minus four plus three, which is one; following the parents recovers it.
Why can one pass suffice? Every predecessor of a vertex appears earlier in topological order, so every possible final incoming edge has already offered its candidate before that vertex is processed.

Topological sorting takes order n plus m time with adjacency lists. Initialisation costs order n, and the subsequent pass scans every vertex and edge at most once, so total time remains order n plus m.
Distances, parents, and the topological order need order n auxiliary storage. A DFS-based topological sort may also use a linear stack; source removal can use an indegree array and worklist instead.

Things to take note of. Verify acyclicity before relying on this schedule, skip arithmetic from unreachable infinity labels, and process all vertices in a valid topological order. Sorting vertices by tentative distance is a different algorithm.

Negative edges are allowed because there is no cycle to revisit, not because negative weights are harmless everywhere. A singleton source stays at zero, and unreachable vertices stay infinite. Use the graph’s dependency order, and repeated passes disappear.

lessons.title: Prim’s algorithm
lessons.description: Grow one tree by choosing its cheapest outward edge.

transcript.text: How does Prim's algorithm work? Imagine eight places that need to be connected by cables. The numbers are cable costs; we want to connect every place for the smallest total cost, without making a loop.
A minimum spanning tree connects all eight places using seven edges. It minimises their total cost, not the distance from one starting place. Green will show the tree we have already built.
Start at any place; we will start at A. Blue edges are possible next steps: one endpoint is green and the other is outside. Choose the cheapest blue edge, add its outside endpoint, and repeat.
From A, the choices cost two, three, and three. Add the edge from A to B, costing two. The edge from C to E costs only one, but neither endpoint is in our tree yet, so we cannot use it now.
Now look outwards from both A and B, not just from B. Three possible edges tie at cost three; choose the edge from A to C. This adds C while keeping one connected tree.
Adding C exposes the edge from C to E, costing one. Add that edge now. A new choice can be cheaper than the previous choice; Prim does not take all graph edges in sorted order.
The edge from B to E costs three, but both endpoints are already green. Adding it would close the highlighted loop through B, A, C, and E. Ignore it: the next edge must bring in a new place.
The cheapest eligible edge now connects A to D for three. Add D to the tree. We compare all blue edges again after every addition.

To leave our current tree, the costs are four, six, seven, and eight. Choose the edge from E to H, costing four. The cheaper edge from G to H was not eligible before this step, because both places were outside.
Now H is inside, so the edge from H to G becomes a valid choice. Add G for two, which is cheaper than the other crossing edges. The blue boundary changes whenever the green tree grows.
Only F is still outside. Its possible connections cost five, six, seven, eight, and nine. Choose the edge from H to F for five; now all eight places are connected.

Our selected costs are two, three, one, three, four, two, and five, adding up to twenty. Seven edges connect eight vertices with no cycle. Different tie choices may give different trees with the same minimum cost.

Why is the greedy choice safe? Split the graph into the green tree and everything outside. The cheapest edge across that boundary can extend our tree towards a minimum spanning tree; this is the cut property.

In code, each outside vertex remembers its cheapest edge into the tree and who offered it. For example, after we added C, E could join through C for one instead of through B for three. These are single edge costs, not full route distances.

Now let us derive the running time instead of memorising a formula. Write n for the number of vertices and m for the number of undirected edges. Our graph has eight vertices and fourteen edges; runtime counts operations as these sizes grow.

Two choices affect different jobs. An adjacency list or matrix tells us how to find a vertex's neighbours. An array or priority queue tells us how to select the cheapest outside vertex; an adjacency list and a binary heap are commonly used together.

Consider the eager version, with one key per vertex. It removes each of the n vertices once, including the starting vertex with key zero. As each vertex enters the tree, it inspects that vertex's neighbours and improves keys when a cheaper joining edge is found.

With an unsorted array, inspect every remaining key to find the smallest. Here the scans inspect eight entries, then seven, down to one, which makes thirty-six key inspections. In general, n plus n minus one down to one equals n times n plus one over two, so all selections together cost order n squared.

With adjacency lists, A lists just B, C, and D. Over the whole run, every vertex's list is scanned once; each undirected edge appears at both endpoints. There are twenty-eight neighbour entries here, or twice m in general, so the total neighbour checking costs order n plus m, not n times m.

Combine the two independent costs: quadratic time to select vertices, plus linear graph scanning. That gives order n squared plus m with adjacency lists and an unsorted key array. A list saves neighbour work, but it does not remove the repeated minimum scans.

A matrix stores a possible connection for every pair of vertices, even where no edge exists. Scan eight cells in each of eight rows here; in general, n rows times n cells costs order n squared. With array selection, add the two quadratic costs to get order n squared, not n to the fourth.

A binary heap roughly doubles its capacity at each new level, so its height grows like log n. Removing the minimum can sift down, while lowering a key can sift up, crossing at most that many levels. Keep an index from each vertex to its heap position, so locating a key does not require another linear search.

Now multiply counts by heap costs. There are n removals at order log n each. Each edge can improve an outside key only when its first endpoint enters; when the second enters, both endpoints are already inside. Therefore there are at most m decreases, each costing order log n. Our trace has eight removals and nine improvements; fourteen is an upper bound, not the observed update count.

Initialising keys and building the heap costs order n. Add graph scanning, removals, and decreases to get order n plus m, times log n. For a connected graph, m is at least n minus one, so this is commonly simplified to order m log n.

A heap speeds up selection; it does not change how a matrix finds neighbours. Keep the n squared scanning term, then add the heap term: the quantity n plus m, multiplied by log n. On a dense simple graph, a list with a binary heap has an n squared log n upper bound, while the matrix and array version remains quadratic.

A Fibonacci heap changes the price of a decrease: constant amortised time instead of logarithmic time. Removals still cost log n amortised, so adjacency lists give m plus n log n time. Ordinary binary heaps do not have that cheaper decrease operation.

For space, adjacency lists store order n plus m entries, while a matrix stores order n squared cells. Eager Prim adds order n keys, parent values, membership flags, and heap positions. A lazy edge-heap version is different: it can queue order m edge records and has an order m log m time bound with adjacency lists.

Things to take note of. Use an undirected weighted graph; negative costs are allowed, and equal costs need a consistent tie rule. If the graph is disconnected, restart from another component to get a minimum spanning forest.

Prim grows one tree. Look at every edge leaving that tree, choose the cheapest, and bring in one new vertex. Keep doing that until everybody is connected; there, much easier when you can actually see the boundary.

lessons.title: Union-find
lessons.description: Watch sets merge, paths compress, and ranks change.

transcript.text: How does union-find work? It keeps track of groups that do not overlap, such as which people are on the same team. We will use eight letters, starting with eight separate groups.

Union means merge the groups containing two elements. It first locates their roots, then makes one root point to the other. Let us see the merge first; afterwards, we will learn how find locates a root.
Call union on A and B. Link root A under root B, so A now belongs to B's group. The parent table changes from A to B in A's column; B still points to itself.

We use a score called rank to keep the trees shallow. Put a lower-rank root below a higher-rank root; on a tie, this course puts the first root below the second and increases the second root's rank. These choices change the shape, not which elements share a group.
Now merge C with D. Put root C below root D, and raise D's rank to one. Every arrow points towards the root that represents the group.
Now merge E with F. Put root E below root F, and raise F's rank to one. Every arrow points towards the root that represents the group.
Now merge G with H. Put root G below root H, and raise H's rank to one. Every arrow points towards the root that represents the group.
We now have four pairs: A with B, C with D, E with F, and G with H. Each coloured tree is one group. Union only changes a root's parent pointer; every descendant comes along.
Next merge the groups containing B and D. Link root B below root D, and increase D's rank to two. A still points to B, so A comes along automatically; we do not detach it.
Merge the groups containing F and H in the same way. Link F below H, making H's rank two. E stays below F, and G stays below H; these four elements now share one group.
Finally merge the two four-element groups. Link D below H and raise H's rank to three. All eight elements now share one root, even though several arrows still form longer paths.

Find means tell me which group this element belongs to. Start at that element and follow its parent arrows until a vertex points to itself. That vertex is the representative; it need not be the smallest letter.
Let us find the representative of A. Start at A and follow its parent to B. B is not a root because B points to D, so follow that arrow too.
From D, follow the arrow to H. H is its own parent, so find stops and returns H. This only identifies A's group; it does not merge any groups.

Path compression makes later finds faster. Change A's parent directly to H, and change B's parent directly to H; D already points there. We shortened the path, but all eight elements are still in the same group.
Find A again. It now takes just one arrow to H instead of three. H's rank stays three after compression: rank is a historical upper bound on height, not the current height.
Now let us combine both operations in a fresh example. We have reset to two groups: A, B, C, D under root D, and E, F, G, H under root H. Suppose we call union on A and E; neither argument is a root.
First, find A by following A to B, then B to D. D is the root of the first group. Record D as the answer; a compressing find can also shorten A's parent pointer.
Next, find E by following E to F, then F to H. H is the root of the second group. The roots are different, so union must merge these two groups.
Both finds can also compress their paths. Point A directly to D, and E directly to H. The groups are still separate until union links their roots.
After finding both roots, link D under H and increase H's rank to three. We link the roots, not A directly to E. This brings every element of the first group into the second group.
If we now call union on B and G, both finds return H. Because the representatives match, do nothing: they already share a group. Never link a root back into its own tree.

Why do these optimisations help? A rank increase requires merging two equally ranked groups, so rank r needs at least two to the power r elements. That limits rank to log n, giving logarithmic worst-case single operations; compression also makes repeated operations much faster.

Across many operations, union by rank together with path compression gives inverse Ackermann n amortised time per operation. This function grows extremely slowly, but is not literally constant. Initialising n singletons and performing q more operations costs order n plus q times inverse Ackermann n.

Things to take note of. Find may shorten parent paths, but it never merges groups; union merges only when roots differ. In Kruskal, different roots mean accept the graph edge and union the groups, while equal roots mean the edge would make a cycle.

Union joins groups by linking their roots. Find follows parent arrows to report a root, and compression remembers a shorter route. Watch the parent table beside the trees: each changed arrow is one precise update, not a mysterious whole-tree operation.

lessons.title: Kruskal’s algorithm
lessons.description: Sort edges, reject cycles, and bring the forest together.

transcript.text: How does Kruskal's algorithm work? We will connect these eight places as cheaply as possible. Unlike Prim, we can build several separate trees and join them later.
Begin with no chosen edges, so each vertex is a tiny tree by itself. Sort every edge by cost, from smallest to largest. We will accept an edge only when it joins two different trees.

Union-find keeps track of which tree each vertex belongs to. Find returns that tree's representative, which is its parent-pointer root. If two endpoints have different roots, union merges their groups; equal roots mean we must reject the edge.
First consider the edge from C to E, costing one. C and E are in separate trees, so accept the edge. Union links root C under root E; one of our eight trees has now merged with another.
The coloured edges are the connections we have actually selected. Grey possibilities are hidden here so the separate trees are easy to see.
Next take the edge from A to B, costing two. Its endpoints are still separate, so accept it and link root A under root B. Notice that our A and B tree is separate from the C and E tree.
These groups do not need to touch yet. Kruskal always checks the next cheapest edge anywhere in the graph.
The edge from G to H also costs two. Accept it and link root G under root H. We now have three little two-vertex trees, plus the single vertices D and F.
Five separate trees remain, even though three edges have been accepted. The next accepted edge will reduce that count by one.
At cost three, we will try A to C before the other tied edges. A belongs to the A and B tree; C belongs to the C and E tree. They are different trees, so this edge can join them.
Watch the parent-pointer view. From A, follow the arrow to B; B is its own parent, so find returns B. From C, follow the arrow to E; find returns E.
Accept the graph edge from A to C. Union links root B under root E, merging both whole groups. The chosen cable is A to C, while the new parent arrow is B to E; those are different jobs.

The graph now contains one four-vertex tree with A, B, C, and E. D is still alone, and G and H still form another tree. Parent arrows are bookkeeping; they do not have to match the selected graph edges.
The edge from A to D also costs three. Find A returns E, while find D returns D, so accept it. Union puts the lower-rank root D under E, bringing D into the larger group.

Next is the edge from B to E, again costing three. Find B and find E both return E, so the endpoints are already connected. The orange path runs from B through A and C to E; adding the red edge would close a cycle, so reject it.
The edge from B to C costs four, but these vertices are also already in the same tree. The existing path through A already connects them. Reject this edge too; neither rejection changes the groups.
Now consider E to H, costing four. E represents the large tree; H represents the G and H tree. Accept this edge because it joins those two trees without creating a cycle.
Union links the lower-rank root H under E. G still points to H, so the whole G and H group comes along. We changed just one parent pointer to merge two sets.
At cost five, try C to D first. Both endpoints already lead to root E, and the selected path through A connects them. Reject this edge because it would create a cycle.
The edge from F to H also costs five. F is alone, but H leads to root E, so accept the edge and link root F under E. We have accepted seven edges; all eight vertices now belong to one tree.

The accepted costs are one, two, two, three, three, four, and five, totalling twenty. We can stop now, without checking the more expensive edges. A connected graph with eight vertices needs seven accepted edges.

Why process edges from cheapest to most expensive? The cheapest available edge joining different trees is safe by the cut property. Union-find only answers whether its endpoints are already connected; the sorted order supplies the greedy cost choice.

Now let us count Kruskal's work step by step. Let n be the number of vertices and m the number of undirected edges: eight and fourteen in this example. Separate preparing the edge list, ordering it, and checking whether each candidate joins different groups.

Adjacency lists are neighbour lists. To collect unique edges for Kruskal, scan one list per vertex and two entries per edge. This costs the vertex count plus the edge count, shown as order n plus m; the collected edges still need sorting.

If the input is an adjacency matrix, inspect one triangular half to avoid duplicate undirected edges. There are n times n minus one over two possible pairs, so preparation costs order n squared even if few edges exist. This input cost does not disappear when we speed up sorting or union-find.

Comparison sorting orders m edge records, not n vertices. With merge sort, each level processes at most order m records, and there are about log m levels. Multiply the work per level by the number of levels to get order m log m; this is a growth bound, not an exact comparison count.

Our final tree has seven edges, but we considered ten candidates: seven accepted and three rejected. Every rejected candidate still needs a connectivity test. In general we may examine all m edges, so use m for the testing bound, not n minus one.

Each candidate needs two endpoint finds. Reuse those returned roots for union: our trace then has twenty finds and seven successful root links. A union routine that repeats the finds adds only a constant factor; the total number of union-find operations is still order m.

The cost of each find depends on the group data structure. Unbalanced parent chains can take linear time per find, giving an order m n bound for connectivity work. Union by rank limits depth to log n, so rank alone gives order m log n for the same work.

With both union by rank and path compression, each operation costs inverse Ackermann n amortised across a sequence. Write this as alpha n; it grows extremely slowly, but is not literally constant. Order m operations therefore give order m times alpha n work, plus order n to create the singleton sets.

For an edge-list input, now add initialisation, comparison sorting, and connectivity work. The full bound is order n plus m log m plus m times alpha n. On a connected nontrivial graph, sorting usually dominates this expression, giving the familiar m log m bound; the earlier terms have not magically vanished.

If the edge list is already sorted by weight, remove only the sorting bill. Initialisation and the candidate tests remain, giving order n plus m times alpha n. If the graph arrives as a matrix, add its quadratic preparation bill as well; presorted candidates do not erase matrix scanning.

A binary heap is an alternative way to order Kruskal's edge candidates. Build a heap of m edges in linear time, then remove the next cheapest edge at log m cost, up to m times. The worst-case ordering cost is still m log m, and you still need union-find to test cycles.

For space, union-find stores a parent and rank per vertex, using order n memory. The edge list or edge heap stores order m records, and merge sort can need another order m buffer. A matrix input itself still occupies order n squared storage; always distinguish the input from the extra workspace.

Things to take note of. Tied edges can be processed in either order, which may change the chosen tree but preserves the minimum cost. A disconnected graph produces several minimum trees, called a minimum spanning forest.

Kruskal merges a forest. In cost order, find both endpoints: different roots means accept and union; the same root means skip the cycle. Keep the cable drawing and the parent-pointer drawing separate, and the decisions become much easier to follow.

lessons.title: What does an operating system actually do?

transcript.text: What does an operating system actually do? It manages the hardware and gives programs useful services, so every application does not have to control the machine itself. Calling it the thing that opens your apps is a little vague, darling.

Start with the layers: hardware supplies the processor, memory, and input-output devices. The operating system controls and coordinates those resources, while applications use its services to solve your tasks. The kernel is the core part of that operating system.

Think of the operating system as both a resource allocator and a control program. It decides who gets resources, and controls how programs use the machine. User convenience and efficient hardware use are two goals, and they can pull in different directions.

Let us make that concrete with two jobs, A and B, both available at time zero. Job A needs two units on the processor, then four units of input-output, then two more processor units. B needs four processor units, and our example ignores switching overhead.
In a simple one-job-at-a-time system, A runs on the processor from zero to two. Then A waits for input-output from two to six, so the processor sits idle. A finally runs again from six to eight.

Only then does B use the processor, from eight to twelve. That gives eight units of useful processor work across twelve elapsed units. Processor utilization is eight divided by twelve, or about sixty-seven percent.

Multiprogramming keeps multiple jobs in main memory so the processor has another ready job to choose. A can remain in memory while it waits for input-output. Waiting does not mean A is ready to execute processor instructions.
Now replay the same workload on one processor. A runs from zero to two, then starts its four-unit input-output operation. The operating system switches the processor to B, which runs from two to six.

At time six, A's input-output completes and B has finished. A becomes ready, is selected, and runs its last two units from six to eight. Watch the separate lanes: A's device operation overlaps B's processor work.

The useful processor work is still eight units, but now the elapsed time is eight units too. Eight divided by eight gives one hundred percent utilization in this ideal example. We improved the schedule; we did not add another processor.

That is the opportunity multiprogramming creates, not a promise that the processor never idles. If every job is waiting for a device, there may be nothing ready to run. Switching between jobs also takes time, unlike the zero-overhead model we just used.

Time sharing emphasizes responsiveness by giving ready jobs frequent turns on the processor. Here are two processor-only jobs alternating in short time slices on one core. They make concurrent progress, but only one executes on that core at a time.

Multiprocessing adds hardware execution capacity: multiple processors or processor cores. Put two independent four-unit processor jobs on two cores, and both can run from zero to four at the same time. On one core, those same eight units of processor work take eight units of elapsed time.

These ideas can work together. A multicore operating system can keep many jobs in memory and schedule them across its cores. More jobs is a statement about the workload; more cores is a statement about the hardware.

Things to take note of. Multiprogramming helps use a processor while another job waits; multiprocessing allows work to execute on multiple cores at once. Time sharing emphasizes responsive turns, and concurrency alone does not prove physical parallelism.

Quick check: A waits for a device while B runs on the only processor core. Is that multiprocessing? No: it is the overlap that multiprogramming enables, with one job using the device and another using the processor.

For your examination, name the resources, show the execution order, and explain the motivation. Distinguish processor work from total time before calculating utilization. There, a proper explanation, instead of three impressive words thrown into one sentence.

lessons.title: How do polling, interrupts and DMA differ?

transcript.text: How do polling, interrupts and direct memory access differ? They answer two related questions: how does the processor learn that a device needs attention, and who moves the data? Keep those questions separate, or your explanation will become rather untidy.

A device controller manages its device and usually has a local buffer. The processor can execute instructions while the device performs its operation. In our authored example, the device prepares eight data items, and we ignore setup details until the comparison.

With polling, the processor repeatedly reads the device status. If the device is not ready, it checks again, consuming processor time on those checks. Watch three unsuccessful checks, followed by a ready result; the chosen polling frequency controls how quickly readiness is noticed.

The important distinction is that checking status does not itself transfer the entire buffer. Once ready, a programmed transfer may still require the processor to read each item and write it to memory. The operating system must decide when polling is worth that overhead.

Interrupt-driven input-output replaces repeated readiness checks with a notification. The controller raises an interrupt, the processor preserves the required execution state, and the interrupt vector identifies the appropriate handler. The handler services the event before execution resumes.

An interrupt does not automatically mean a different process must run. The interrupted process may resume after the handler finishes. Likewise, notification and copying remain separate: an interrupt-driven programmed transfer can still involve processor work for the data.

Direct memory access delegates block movement to a suitable controller. The operating system sets up the memory destination, transfer length and direction; the controller moves the block without the processor copying every item. A completion interrupt can report that the block is finished.

In the simplified byte-notification model, eight items could require eight processor service events. With one DMA block containing all eight, there is one completion notification instead. That is an illustrative count, not a claim that every real controller interrupts once per byte.

DMA still has setup, completion handling and possible contention for memory or the bus. It reduces processor involvement in bulk movement rather than creating free bandwidth. Polling can make sense for short predictable waits, while interrupts let the processor do other useful work between events.

Things to take note of. Distinguish polling from interrupt notification, and distinguish both from who copies the data. Explain controller buffers, state preservation and DMA setup; do not promise that every interrupt changes processes or that DMA removes all processor work.

lessons.title: How does the OS protect itself from your program?

transcript.text: How does the operating system protect itself from your program? Hardware distinguishes ordinary application execution from privileged kernel execution. Without that distinction, a badly behaved application could rewrite the very rules meant to contain it.

The course calls these user mode and monitor mode, also called kernel or supervisor mode. Its mode-bit convention is one for user mode and zero for monitor mode. Treat those numbers as the course convention rather than a universal encoding for every processor.

A privileged instruction is permitted only in the privileged mode. For example, loading protection registers must not be available to arbitrary user code. Otherwise an application could enlarge its own permitted memory region and defeat the checks.

When a controlled trap or interrupt enters the kernel, hardware provides the required privileged transition. Returning to user execution restores the appropriate less-privileged state. A user program does not simply assign a value to the mode bit and crown itself ruler of the machine.

Root or administrator is an operating-system account privilege. Kernel mode is a hardware execution mode, so they are not the same thing. A program launched by an administrator still executes ordinary instructions in user mode and requests protected services through the operating system.

Now consider the tutorial memory example. The base register is hexadecimal one thousand, and the limit register is also hexadecimal one thousand, meaning a region of that size. For an absolute physical address, the legal interval starts at the base and stops just before base plus limit.

Adding the base and size gives hexadecimal two thousand as the exclusive upper boundary. Therefore the last legal address is hexadecimal one F F F. Check it against both inequalities: at least the base, and strictly less than the upper boundary.

An access to hexadecimal two thousand fails the strict upper-bound check and traps. Do not mistake a limit expressed as a size for an inclusive final address. Later, execution-time relocation will check a logical offset against the size before adding the base; that is a different address convention.

The slides also classify hardware input-output instructions as privileged. An application requests input-output through operating-system services, which can check validity and permission. A request to open a file is not permission to issue arbitrary device-control instructions.

Things to take note of. Keep account privileges separate from processor mode, and keep a region size separate from its exclusive upper boundary. The tutorial address one F F F is legal in this example; two thousand is the first address outside it.

lessons.title: What happens when a program makes a system call?

transcript.text: What happens when a program makes a system call? A system call is a controlled request from a user program to a protected operating-system service. It connects application needs to privileged work without giving the application unrestricted control of the hardware.

Start with the course example: an application calls the C library function F open. That library function can perform user-space work and eventually invoke the open system call. The library interface and the kernel entry are related layers, not two names for one identical instruction.

The application supplies arguments such as a pathname and access mode. A user-space stub follows the operating system calling convention to identify the requested service and arrange its arguments. The exact registers and instruction depend on the architecture and operating system.

In the supplied xv6 lab, the stub uses a system-call number and an ecall instruction to enter the kernel. That creates a trap rather than an ordinary function call across the protection boundary. Kernel trap handling then reaches the numbered system-call dispatcher.

The dispatcher selects the matching kernel handler. That handler checks the request and performs the permitted service, potentially using file-system or device layers. User-provided values cannot simply be trusted because they arrived through a legitimate entry instruction.

After the service, a result is placed according to the calling convention and execution returns to user mode. The result might be a file descriptor or an error indication. The application continues after the call, unless the requested operation blocks or changes that control flow.

A blocking request can make the caller wait while another process runs. Later the event makes the caller ready, and the scheduler may select it again. That is why a system call can involve scheduling, while a fast successful call may return without switching to another process.

Compare a device interrupt with the system call. A device interrupt reports an asynchronous hardware event; a system call is a deliberate service request by the running program. Both may enter kernel handling, but their origins and purposes differ.

Not every library function invokes a system call every time it runs. A calculation may remain entirely in user space, and buffered input-output can defer kernel requests. In the course model, a system call uses a controlled trap, but an ordinary API invocation is not proof that a trap occurred.

Things to take note of. Trace application, library, stub, trap, dispatcher, handler and return in order. Explain which stage changes privilege, distinguish asynchronous interrupts, and never claim that a file descriptor is the file contents themselves.

lessons.title: How does a process change state?
lessons.description: SC2005 · Processes and threads · Through Week 7

transcript.text: How does a process change state? A process is a program in execution, including its current execution state and resources. The same stored program can have several separate process instances, so the file on disk and a running instance are different concepts.

The process image includes code, data, a heap and a stack. Its process control block records information such as the process identifier, state, program counter, registers and resource information. These records allow the operating system to manage and later resume the process.

Use five conceptual states: new, ready, running, waiting and terminated. Ready means eligible for a processor but not currently executing. Waiting means the process needs an event, such as input-output completion, before it can make that kind of execution progress.
After admission, process A joins the ready queue. Dispatch moves A onto the processor and changes ready to running. Process B can remain ready behind it without being blocked on a device.

Suppose a timer causes A to be preempted. A moves from running back to ready, and the scheduler can dispatch B instead. This is different from A requesting input-output: preemption does not itself create an input-output dependency.

Now suppose process A runs again and requests a device operation that has not finished. It changes from running to waiting, joining the relevant device or event wait list. The processor can execute another ready process while process A is blocked.
When the device completes, A moves from waiting to ready. It does not leap directly onto the processor merely because the event happened. Dispatch is the separate step that turns ready into running.

On a process switch, the required context of the outgoing process is saved and the incoming context restored. For an authored example, preserve A at program counter one hundred before executing B, then restore that saved point when A resumes. The exact saved structures depend on the system.

Long-term scheduling controls admission, short-term scheduling selects ready execution, and medium-term scheduling can suspend and later resume resident workload through swapping. A process that finishes changes to terminated in the conceptual model. The xv6 lab adds implementation states such as zombie until reaping.

Things to take note of. Distinguish ready from waiting, preemption from blocking, and event completion from dispatch. If an xv6 listing says runnable, it means eligible for selection, not already executing; show the state-changing event before writing your answer.

lessons.title: What do fork, exit and wait actually do?
lessons.description: SC2005 · Processes and threads · Through Week 7

transcript.text: What do fork, exit and wait actually do? Fork creates a child process, exit ends execution, and wait allows a parent to collect a child result. The trick is to follow two execution histories instead of pretending that one line of code still means only one process.

Imagine a parent with process identifier ten reaching a successful fork. The operating system creates a child, which we label eleven in this authored example. Parent and child then have distinct process identities, even though they continue from corresponding points in the program.

The successful return value distinguishes the two paths. The parent receives the child identifier, eleven here, while the child receives zero. Failure is a separate case, so do not invent a successful child when fork reports an error.

Both processes can now make progress under the scheduler. The child may run first or the parent may run first unless some explicit synchronization orders them. A neat parent-before-child printout from one run is an observation, not a scheduling guarantee.

Their ordinary private memory is logically separate. If each changes its own private counter, that is not a shared-memory race on a single counter. File-descriptor references can still refer to shared underlying kernel objects, which is why resource ownership needs a more careful diagram.

Suppose the child finishes and calls exit before the parent calls wait. In the xv6 lab, the child becomes a zombie: it is no longer executing, but enough process-table information remains for the parent to collect its status. Zombie does not mean a process secretly keeps using the processor.

When the parent waits and the child has exited, the kernel can return that child result and reclaim its remaining process-table slot. If no suitable child has finished yet, wait can block the parent until the required event. Waiting changes which process is ready to execute.

The lab makes this visible by delaying the parent, then using the process dump to observe a zombie. After reaping, the retained entry disappears or becomes reusable. In that lab branch, sleep arguments are clock ticks, so do not read an arbitrary sleep value as seconds.

A parent can also wait before the child completes, producing the opposite order of events. The dependency is still that wait collects an exited child, not that the child must run immediately after fork. Trace the actual return, block, exit and wakeup events.

Things to take note of. Separate process identity, fork return values, private memory and shared kernel references. Explain the zombie interval and the later reaping event; neither an exit nor a sampled print order proves that every piece of process bookkeeping has already vanished.

lessons.title: How do processes communicate?
lessons.description: SC2005 · Processes and threads · Through Week 7

transcript.text: How do processes communicate? They can exchange messages or share a memory region, but both approaches need a clear agreement about who produces data and when it can be consumed. Concurrent execution alone does not magically create a safe communication protocol.

With shared memory, both processes map an agreed region and exchange data there. Ordinary private memory after fork is not automatically that shared region. Once shared access exists, conflicting updates need synchronization so the consumer sees a consistent result.

Message passing provides send and receive operations rather than requiring direct access to shared variables. Direct communication names the other process. Indirect communication sends to a mailbox or port, so the communicating parties agree on that intermediary.

A bounded mailbox has finite capacity. A send may have to wait when there is no free slot, and a receive may have to wait when there is no message. Whether an individual operation blocks is part of its specified semantics, not something you can guess from the word send.

The lab uses pipes, which are unidirectional byte streams. Pipe endpoint zero is for reading, and endpoint one is for writing. To send a request one way and a reply back, draw two pipes rather than quietly using a single one as if it were bidirectional.

After fork, parent and child descriptor tables can contain references to the same underlying pipe endpoints. Closing one descriptor removes that reference, not every reference in every process. The endpoint can remain open while another descriptor still refers to it.

For ping and pong, the parent keeps the request writer and reply reader. The child keeps the request reader and reply writer; each closes its unused ends. Animate ping from parent to child first, then pong back to the parent through the other pipe.

A read reaches end of file only when no buffered data remains and all write-end references are closed. If the reader itself accidentally keeps an unused writer open, waiting for end of file may never finish. Merely closing the writer in the other process does not repair that extra reference.

Check read and write return values and distinguish byte counts from safe text strings. A received sequence is not necessarily terminated as a C string, and a failed operation is not a successful empty message. The lab also requires closing descriptors and collecting the child appropriately.

Things to take note of. Classify shared memory versus messages, direct versus mailbox naming, and bounded capacity versus operation blocking. For pipes, draw every descriptor reference after fork and close unused ends before reasoning about end of file.
