lessons.title: What does a thread share with its process?
lessons.description: SC2005 · Processes and threads · Through Week 7

transcript.text: What does a thread share with its process? A thread is an execution path with its own program counter, registers and stack. Threads inside one process share that process address space and resources, so two stacks do not mean two isolated worlds.

Picture a server with two threads, T one and T two. Both can execute the same program code and access shared process data. Open files belong among the process resources they can share rather than being copied into a completely private file system for each thread.

Each thread still needs a private current instruction position and saved registers. Its stack holds its own active calls and local execution state. If one thread pauses inside a function, resuming another thread must restore that other thread context, including the correct stack.
Watch T one call a function and push a frame onto its stack. T two can call the same function but use a different frame on its own stack. Their code is shared; their active call frames are distinct.

Now both update a shared counter initially five. If they both read five and each later writes six, one increment is lost. Their private registers and stacks did not protect that shared data; a synchronization mechanism must coordinate the conflicting accesses.

Threads can improve responsiveness when one execution path waits and another remains able to run. With appropriate kernel execution contexts, one thread can block on input-output while another uses a processor. The mapping matters: a blocking kernel call can stall all user threads sharing only one kernel thread.

On one processor core, ready threads alternate; they are not executing instructions simultaneously on that same core. With multiple cores and enough independently schedulable kernel contexts, threads can actually run in parallel. Creating extra logical threads alone does not add hardware cores.

Compared with separate processes, sharing an address space can make cooperation convenient and reduce some management costs. It also means a mistaken shared-memory access can affect peer threads. The benefit is not a guarantee that every threaded program becomes faster.

For the examination, classify code, shared data and open resources on the process side. Classify thread identifier, program counter, registers and stack on the thread side. If the question asks about an actual implementation, use its stated mapping rather than silently assuming one thread per core.

Things to take note of. Separate shared resources from private execution state, concurrency from parallelism, and possible responsiveness from guaranteed speedup. When a trace contains a shared variable, ask who can reach the same storage before claiming that private stacks make it safe.

source.summary: S2 printed2.29–2.33; study guide§2; Lab2 Part3 conceptual connection. Authored two-thread example.

lessons.title: How are user threads mapped to kernel threads?
lessons.description: SC2005 · Processes and threads · Through Week 7

transcript.text: How are user threads mapped to kernel threads? The user-level threading abstraction and the kernel scheduling abstraction need not be one to one. Follow four user threads through the three mappings, and keep the number of physical processor cores visible.

In many to one, several user threads share one kernel thread. A user-level library selects which logical thread uses that kernel execution context. Since there is only one such context for these threads, they cannot run simultaneously on two cores through that mapping.

Suppose one of those user threads makes a blocking kernel call. If its sole kernel thread blocks, the kernel has no other runnable execution context for the remaining user threads in that group. They may all lose progress even though another user thread has work to do.

Do not confuse that case with a library-level wait. A cooperative library can park one logical thread and switch to another without asking the kernel to block the sole kernel thread. Which layer performs the wait determines whether the whole group is stopped.

In one to one, each user thread has a corresponding kernel thread. The operating system can schedule those kernel threads independently, including on separate cores. One blocked kernel thread therefore does not inherently block every peer thread in the process.

The cost is that creating many logical threads also creates many kernel-managed execution contexts. Their stacks and management data consume resources, and creation or switching can cost more than a lightweight library-only operation. Greater scheduling freedom comes with implementation costs.

Many to many maps a larger set of logical threads onto a pool of kernel threads. Here four user threads share two kernel contexts, allowing at most two of these threads to execute at once when two cores are available. The runtime chooses the user-to-kernel assignments over time.

If one kernel context blocks, another may continue to run logical work; the exact result depends on the runtime design and available contexts. The mapping itself does not guarantee ideal load balance. A language feature such as a coroutine also does not, by itself, specify one universal kernel-thread mapping.

The slides ask why not map one sequential user thread to many simultaneous kernel executions. One instruction stream cannot simply be executed twice as independent progress without changing its semantics. Extra execution contexts are useful when there are multiple schedulable logical activities to run.

Things to take note of. Count logical threads, kernel contexts and physical cores separately. For every blocking question, state whether the library parks a logical thread or the kernel blocks an execution context, then show which remaining path can actually run.

lessons.title: How do you calculate scheduling performance?

transcript.text: How do you calculate scheduling performance? Begin with a timeline, not a memorized formula with unexplained letters. We will track arrival, first execution, completion, processor work and blocked time separately, because different metrics answer different questions.

Our authored process arrives at time zero and waits ready until time two. It runs from two to four, waits in a device queue from four to five, and receives device service from five to eight. It then waits ready until nine, runs until eleven, and finishes.

Response time measures the delay to the first execution. First run is two and arrival is zero, so response is two minus zero, equal to two. Later preemptions or device operations do not reset that first response measurement.

Turnaround measures the entire time from arrival to completion. Completion is eleven and arrival is zero, giving eleven units. That interval includes processor execution, ready-queue waiting, device-queue waiting and actual device service in this example.

Total processor execution is two plus two, equal to four units. Ready-queue waiting is the initial two units plus the unit from eight to nine, giving three. The remaining blocked interval from four to eight has one unit queued for the device and three units of service.

Under the ready-only definition, subtract total processor work and all blocked time from turnaround. Eleven minus four minus four gives three units waiting for the processor. That calculation agrees with adding the two ready intervals directly.

The photographed course exercise includes time in the ready queue and time queued for a device, while excluding actual device service. Under that convention, eleven minus four minus three gives four. State which waiting definition you are using before calculating, because the two definitions count different intervals.

Throughput counts completed processes per unit of time, not the number currently waiting. If two processes complete across ten time units, throughput is two divided by ten. Do not confuse this system-wide rate with the turnaround of one process.

For two cores observed over ten time units, suppose the useful busy times total fifteen core-time units. Utilization is fifteen divided by two times ten, or seventy-five percent. Dividing by ten alone would incorrectly exceed one hundred percent for a multicore aggregate.

Things to take note of. Calculate each process metric before averaging, keep units consistent, and distinguish first execution from completion. If the question has one processor burst and no blocking, waiting simplifies to completion minus arrival minus burst; do not carry that shortcut unchanged into an input-output trace.

source.summary: S3 printed3.3–3.10; IMG_2065–2066 waiting convention. Authored process timeline separates ready delay, device queue and I/O service.

lessons.title: How does FCFS scheduling work?

transcript.text: How does first come, first served scheduling work? Select the first ready process and let it keep the processor until it blocks or finishes. This is nonpreemptive scheduling, so a later short job cannot simply take the processor away.

Use the lecture example: P one needs twenty-four processor units, and P two and P three each need three. All arrive at zero, with the stated queue order P one, P two, P three. Ignore input-output and context-switch costs for this trace.

P one begins immediately and runs from zero to twenty-four. During that long interval, P two and P three remain ready but cannot preempt it. Watch their remaining execution stay unchanged while their waiting time grows.

At twenty-four, P one completes and P two runs for its three units, finishing at twenty-seven. P three then runs from twenty-seven to thirty. The schedule follows the original queue order, not a fresh comparison of burst lengths.

For this single-burst example, waiting equals completion minus arrival minus burst. P one waits zero, P two waits twenty-four, and P three waits twenty-seven. Their total waiting is fifty-one, divided by three processes, giving an average of seventeen.

Now replay the same three burst lengths with the short jobs first: P two, P three, then P one. The short jobs run from zero to three and three to six; the long job finishes at thirty. We changed order, not the total processor work.

In that reordered trace, the original long job waits six, the first short job waits zero, and the second waits three. Six plus zero plus three, divided by three, gives an average waiting time of three. The last completion is still thirty, but individual delays differ greatly.

This illustrates the convoy effect: short ready jobs wait behind an earlier long job. First come, first served is simple and respects its queue rule, but it does not minimize every response or waiting objective. A scheduling policy has consequences even when no work is lost.

With different arrival times, do not schedule a process before it exists in the ready set. If no process is ready, show idle time rather than moving a future arrival backwards. Simultaneous arrivals also need a stated queue tie rule.

Things to take note of. First come, first served is nonpreemptive, its outcome depends on queue order, and completion time is not waiting time. Reconstruct the Gantt chart first, then calculate per-process delays and their average.

source.summary: S3 printed3.11–3.13. Lecture bursts24,3,3 and two all-at-zero arrival orders.

lessons.title: How do SJF and SRTF choose a process?

transcript.text: How do shortest job first and shortest remaining time first choose a process? Both favor short work, but their preemption rules differ. Shortest job first lets a selected burst continue; shortest remaining time first can reconsider when shorter remaining work becomes ready.

Use the lecture processes with arrivals zero, two, four and five, and bursts seven, four, one and four. At zero only P one is ready. A policy cannot select a future one-unit job before that job has arrived.

Under nonpreemptive shortest job first, P one starts at zero and continues until seven. P two arrives at two, P three at four and P four at five, but none interrupts that selected burst. Only after P one finishes do we choose among the waiting jobs.

P three is now the shortest and runs from seven to eight. P two and P four both need four, so the stated earlier-arrival tie rule selects P two next, then P four. Their completion times are seven, twelve, eight and sixteen by process identifier.

Subtract arrival and burst from each completion to obtain waits zero, six, three and seven. The sum is sixteen, and sixteen divided by four gives mean waiting four. The one-unit job still waited three because the running burst was nonpreemptive.

Now change to shortest remaining time first. P one runs until time two, when P two arrives needing four and P one still needs five. Four is shorter than five, so P two preempts and runs until the next relevant arrival.

At time four, P three arrives needing one while P two still needs two, so P three runs until five. P two then has the shortest remaining time and finishes at seven. P four runs from seven to eleven, before P one finally finishes at sixteen.

The resulting waits are nine, one, zero and two. Twelve total waiting units divided by four gives mean three, lower than four in the nonpreemptive trace. This result follows from the event choices; it is not a reason to compare original bursts after a process has already partly executed.

Shortest-work policies assume a burst estimate or known execution requirement in the model. Long work can be postponed by repeated shorter arrivals, so fairness is a separate issue. If two remaining times tie, apply the question tie rule rather than inventing an extra preemption.

Things to take note of. Choose only ready processes, distinguish nonpreemptive selection from preemptive reconsideration, and update remaining work after every interval. Use completion minus arrival minus burst only under the stated no-blocking model, then average the individual waits.

source.summary: S3 printed3.14–3.16. Lecture arrivals0,2,4,5; bursts7,4,1,4. Ties keep incumbent, then earlier arrival.

lessons.title: Can priority scheduling starve a process?

transcript.text: Can priority scheduling starve a process? Yes: a ready process can wait indefinitely if more highly ranked work always wins selection. Priority decides whom to choose, while preemption decides whether the current execution can be interrupted; they are separate policy choices.

A priority number is meaningful only with its direction specified. The slides commonly use a smaller integer for higher priority. A system using the opposite convention would choose differently, so write the convention before tracing anything.

Imagine low-priority process L is ready at zero and needs two processor units. A high-priority process H is also ready and can remain runnable forever. If selection always favors H, every new scheduling decision selects H again.

Watch timer ticks repeatedly preempt the current execution and create new choices. Nothing in strict priority requires those choices to alternate between classes. If H stays eligible, L can remain ready without ever receiving its first processor unit.

That is exactly the conceptual risk in the lab strict even-identifier policy on one processor. An eligible even-identifier process must win over odd-identifier work. An odd process can therefore starve if the favored class never stops providing runnable work.

Finite high-priority work produces postponement, but not necessarily indefinite starvation. If H eventually blocks or finishes and no other high-priority process is eligible, L can run. A short observation of no output does not prove an infinite execution history by itself.

Aging changes the selection rule by improving the effective priority of a waiting ready process. In this authored illustration, L is promoted to outrank H after six waiting units, so the next selection can give L the processor. A real guarantee depends on bounded priority levels and the complete tie and selection rules.

Distinguish this from a deadlocked process waiting for an event it cannot cause. A ready starving process is eligible but repeatedly unselected; a blocked process may not be a scheduling candidate at all. Raising the priority of a blocked process does not necessarily release the lock it needs.

On multiple processors, one favored process cannot execute simultaneously on every core in a sequential-process model. Therefore a one-core starvation example must not be copied unchanged as a proof for several cores. Check whether enough favored runnable work exists at each selection.

Things to take note of. State priority direction, preemptive behavior, ties and the workload that keeps preferred work eligible. Use aging to explain a changed fairness rule, and never claim that a timer interrupt by itself guarantees that every ready process gets a turn.

source.summary: S3 printed3.17; Lab2 Part2 strict even-PID selection; IMG_2346–2347. Authored repeating high-priority workload.

lessons.title: How does round robin work?

transcript.text: How does round robin work? Give the head ready process at most one time quantum, then move unfinished work to the tail. Unlike shortest job first, the queue rotates according to time slices rather than sorting all processes by burst length.

The lecture uses bursts fifty-three, seventeen, sixty-eight and twenty-four, with quantum twenty. All arrive at zero in process-identifier order, and switching costs are ignored. Track the ready queue and remaining work as well as the completed timeline.

P one runs from zero to twenty and still needs thirty-three, so it joins the queue tail. P two needs only seventeen and finishes at time thirty-seven, before using a full quantum. A completion does not pad the slice with imaginary extra execution.

P three runs from thirty-seven to fifty-seven, leaving forty-eight. P four runs until seventy-seven, leaving four. The queue now returns to P one, which runs until ninety-seven and still needs thirteen.

P three next uses twenty units and has twenty-eight left at one hundred seventeen. P four needs only four, so it finishes at one hundred twenty-one. P one then completes its remaining thirteen at one hundred thirty-four.

Only P three remains, so it runs for twenty and then its last eight units, finishing at one hundred sixty-two. Separate slice boundaries still exist, but a lone ready process can immediately receive the processor again. A queue rotation need not imply another process actually executes.

Completion times are one hundred thirty-four, thirty-seven, one hundred sixty-two and one hundred twenty-one. Subtracting each burst gives waiting times eighty-one, twenty, ninety-four and ninety-seven. Their sum is two hundred ninety-two, divided by four, giving mean waiting seventy-three.

Response is based on first execution, so the response times here are zero, twenty, thirty-seven and fifty-seven. They are different from total waits because later queue visits add waiting without changing the first response. Derive the metric you were actually asked for.

A very large quantum approaches first come, first served for these bursts. A very small quantum creates frequent switching overhead if switches have a nonzero cost. The familiar bound of at most n minus one quanta between turns assumes a fixed ready population and ignores that overhead.

Things to take note of. Requeue only unfinished work, stop early on completion, and keep the remaining burst up to date. For simultaneous arrivals and quantum expiry, follow the stated queue ordering; the finished chart is just a record of those decisions.

lessons.title: How does scheduling change with multiple queues or cores?

transcript.text: How does scheduling change with multiple queues or cores? Several queues can represent different service needs, while several cores supply simultaneous execution capacity. Do not confuse a logical queue partition with a physical extra processor.

A multilevel queue can use round robin for interactive foreground work and first come, first served for background work. The operating system still needs an interqueue policy. Fixed foreground priority can starve the background queue even if the policy inside each queue is reasonable.

A time-allocation policy might reserve eighty milliseconds for the foreground and twenty for the background in each hundred-millisecond cycle. That gives eighty percent and twenty percent of the ideal cycle budget. It is an illustrative allocation rule, not a guarantee about the completion time of every process.

With partitioned multicore scheduling, each process is assigned to a core and that core schedules its own work. This permits different local policies, but a poor assignment can leave one core idle while another has ready processes. Placement and load balance become separate problems.

Global scheduling selects from system-wide eligible work when a core becomes available. A process can run on one core now and another later, but one sequential process must not execute on both at once. Migration can introduce synchronization and cache costs.

Use the lecture shortest-remaining-time example with two cores: arrivals zero, two, four and five, and bursts seven, four, one and four. P one begins first, then P two can run concurrently when it arrives at two. At four, the new one-unit process changes which two remaining jobs are shortest.

The global choice serves P three briefly while P one is paused, then resumes P one when the short process completes. P four waits until a core becomes available at six and finishes at ten. P one completes at eight, P two at six, and P three at five.

The waits are one, zero, zero and one by identifier, so mean waiting is two divided by four, or one half. This uses total processor work per process, not the time occupied on one particular core. A migrated process still has a single execution requirement.

A trace showing migration proves that execution moved between cores; it does not alone prove there is exactly one global ready queue. The slides pair partitioned with asymmetric and global with symmetric scheduling as course shorthand. Those labels are not universal synonyms for every implementation.

Things to take note of. Explain policy within queues, selection between queues, and assignment across cores separately. Keep arrival eligibility, remaining execution and one-process-at-a-time constraints visible when reconstructing a multicore schedule.

source.summary: S3 printed3.22–3.30; IMG_2056–2057. Lecture four-process dual-core SRTF input; course AMP/SMP shorthand qualified.

lessons.title: Why is counter++ unsafe?

transcript.text: Why is counter increment unsafe when processes share it? A statement that looks like one operation in source code can require several machine-level steps. If another execution accesses the same storage between those steps, the final value can depend on the interleaving.

Start with shared counter five, a producer that increments once and a consumer that decrements once. Serial execution in either order should return the counter to five. That gives us an independently expected result before inspecting the faulty trace.

An increment can load the counter into a register, add one to the register, then store the register back. A decrement has its own load, arithmetic and store. The registers belong to the executing contexts; the counter is the shared memory location.

The producer loads five and computes six, but has not yet stored it. A context switch preserves that register value while the consumer runs. The shared counter still holds five, so the consumer can load the old value too.
The consumer subtracts one and obtains four in its own register. Both arithmetic results now exist privately: six and four. Neither result represents both updates applied in sequence.

The producer resumes and stores six into the shared counter. Then the consumer resumes and stores four, overwriting that first result. The final counter is four rather than the expected five, which is the lost-update problem shown in the lecture.

Reverse the final two stores and the result can instead be six. That different outcome is not a different arithmetic rule; it is another legal unsynchronized interleaving. A race concerns conflicting shared access, including at least one modification.

Mutual exclusion can protect the whole update sequence so one process completes its read, modify and write before the other enters. Merely preserving each process registers during a switch does not provide this exclusion. Correct context switching can coexist with an incorrect shared-data protocol.

Two processes with only separate private counters do not share this same memory location. Threads in one address space, explicit shared memory, or shared kernel data can create the shared access instead. Identify the actual storage and access path before labeling every concurrent example a race.

Things to take note of. Expand source statements into reads, arithmetic and writes, track private registers separately, and name the interleaving that loses an update. The expected answer follows from the required combined effect, not from whichever final store happens to run last.

source.summary: S4 printed4.3–4.9; A4 race sequence; IMG_2113–2115. Lecture counter5 increment/decrement interleaving.

lessons.title: What makes a critical-section solution correct?

transcript.text: What makes a critical-section solution correct? We need more than a sign saying only one process may enter. The protocol must address mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting as distinct requirements, each supported by its own argument.

The critical section accesses shared data whose conflicting use must be coordinated. Entry code asks permission, exit code releases it, and the remainder is outside that protected work. A correct protocol must be judged under its stated assumptions about execution and atomic access.

Mutual exclusion says that when one process is in its critical section, another cannot be there simultaneously. This is a safety claim about forbidden overlap. Show the variable or ownership rule that makes two simultaneous entries impossible.

Progress asks whether contenders can select a next entrant when the critical section is empty. A process not trying to enter must not indefinitely prevent another from entering. This is not the same as checking that two processes never overlap.

In strict alternation, turn zero allows P zero to enter and turn one allows P one. Exclusion holds because only the selected turn can pass the guard. But if turn stays zero while P zero remains in its remainder section, P one can be stuck despite an empty critical section.

The course separately considers a bound on overtaking under alternation, but that does not repair its progress failure. A bound on how often another process enters is not evidence that an uninterested owner will ever change turn. Explain the failing scenario rather than presenting three unexplained ticks.

The flags-only attempt lets each process announce interest before waiting on the other flag. If P zero sets its flag and P one sets its flag before either checks, both see the other interested. They can then spin forever while nobody is inside.

Bounded waiting limits how many times other processes may enter after a particular request and before it is granted. A solution can allow some progress while repeatedly favoring one contender, so progress alone does not imply bounded waiting. Queue discipline and tie resolution can matter.

A useful proof style is to separate the properties. Give an exclusion invariant, explain how an empty section admits some interested process, then bound overtaking for a particular requester. If the memory model or atomic-access assumptions change, revisit the proof.

Things to take note of. Strict alternation can fail progress, and flags alone can make both contenders wait. Neither a safe-looking lock variable nor a fair processor schedule is a complete proof of all three critical-section requirements.

source.summary: S4 printed4.10–4.19; IMG_2109–2110,2119–2121. Course bounded-overtaking convention distinguished from progress.

lessons.title: How does Peterson’s algorithm resolve a tie?

transcript.text: How does Peterson’s algorithm resolve a tie? It combines two interest flags with a turn variable, so each process announces its wish to enter while allowing the other to win simultaneous contention. We use the course two-process model with atomic reads and writes and the stated ordering assumptions.

For process i, set its own flag true, set turn to the other process k, then wait while the other flag is true and turn favors that other process. On exit, clear the process own flag. The conjunction in the waiting condition is essential.

Start a simultaneous attempt by letting P zero set flag zero true and turn one. P one then sets flag one true and turn zero. Both flags now express interest, but the last turn value resolves who must defer.

P zero checks flag one and whether turn equals one. Flag one is true but turn is zero, so the conjunction is false and P zero enters. P one sees flag zero true and turn zero, so its guard remains true and it waits.

When P zero leaves, it clears flag zero. P one now sees the other flag false, so it may enter regardless of the retained turn value. The exit action releases the waiting competitor without requiring both flags to be reset together.

If only P zero wants entry, P one keeps its flag false. Even though P zero gives turn to P one, the false interest flag makes the waiting conjunction false. This avoids the strict-alternation failure where an uninterested process could hold the turn forever.

For exclusion, suppose a process is already inside with its flag true. A competitor announces itself and gives turn to the current process, making the competitor guard wait. Under the course ordering assumptions, the flag and turn argument prevents both from passing into their critical sections together.

Progress follows because an absent competitor has a false flag, while simultaneous interested processes use turn to select one. Bounded overtaking follows from that reciprocal turn behavior under the assumed execution model. It is a logical protocol proof, not a promise that arbitrary compiled code obeys the model.

Do not reorder the announcement and guard merely because the lines look interchangeable. The photographed exercises deliberately change ordering or scheduling to test the reasoning. On modern processors, compiler and memory reordering also require proper language-level synchronization; ordinary variables are not automatically a portable production lock.

Things to take note of. Write the waiting condition with both the other flag and the turn comparison, clear your own flag on exit, and trace simultaneous interest explicitly. Separate the course proof from claims about an unqualified modern implementation.

lessons.title: How does TestAndSet acquire a lock?

transcript.text: How does test and set acquire a lock? It atomically returns the old lock value and sets that lock true. Both parts form one indivisible shared-memory operation, so two contenders cannot each observe the same free lock as their successful acquisition.

Initially the lock is false, meaning available. P zero executes test and set and receives false while the shared lock becomes true. The false return is the evidence that this process acquired the lock, not a signal that the operation failed.

Now P one attempts the same atomic operation. It receives true because the lock was already held, and the lock remains true. In the basic spin loop, a true return means retry rather than enter the critical section.

When P zero exits, it releases the lock by setting it false according to the lock protocol. A later test and set can then return false to one contender. Watch P one become the next holder only after that successful free-to-held transition.

Mutual exclusion follows from the atomic old-value transition: at most one acquisition can return false before a release. Progress holds for a free lock when an executing contender can acquire it. Basic test and set does not by itself provide a bound on which contender wins next.

P zero might release and repeatedly reacquire before P one succeeds. Each individual acquisition is valid, yet P one can be overtaken without a fixed bound. A fair-looking processor schedule is not the same as a fair lock acquisition policy.

Atomicity must hold against competing accesses on other cores too. Disabling interrupts on one core does not stop another core from touching shared memory. The slide drawings about noninterruption are a simplified model, not a general replacement for a multicore atomic instruction.

Spinning can avoid the overhead of sleeping when the holder runs elsewhere and will release very soon. If the holder cannot run while a waiter monopolizes the only core, spinning does not make it release sooner. Compare the expected hold time with scheduling and switching costs under the stated assumptions.

A blocking semaphore can still use a short internal atomic lock to protect its own counter and wait list. Blocking for the resource and briefly spinning on internal metadata are different operations. The course excludes the more complex bounded-waiting test-and-set algorithm, so do not substitute it for this basic trace.

Things to take note of. False old value acquires, true old value retries, and release permits a later winner. Derive exclusion from the atomic transition, but do not infer bounded waiting or multicore protection from an unrelated timer or local interrupt rule.

source.summary: S4 printed4.24–4.27; A4 TAS sequence; IMG_2207–2209 multicore/short-spin clarification. Excludes advanced bounded-waiting algorithm.

lessons.title: How do semaphores block and wake processes?

transcript.text: How do semaphores block and wake processes? A semaphore coordinates access through wait and signal, with atomic state changes and a defined waiting discipline. The blocking implementation in these slides stores both an integer value and a list of sleepers.

Wait first decrements the value. If the new value is negative, the caller joins the wait list and blocks; otherwise it has acquired a permit. Starting from one, P zero waits and changes the value to zero, acquiring the single available permit.

P one now waits, taking the value from zero to minus one. Because the new value is negative, it is enqueued and becomes waiting rather than consuming processor time in a spin loop. P zero remains the permit holder.

If P two also waits, the value becomes minus two and the wait list contains two sleepers. In this signed-value representation, the negative magnitude describes queued waiters. It is not the same representation as an always-nonnegative count of free resources.

Signal increments the value and wakes one waiter when the new value is less than or equal to zero. P zero signaling from minus two produces minus one, so P one can leave the wait list and become ready. Waking a process does not mean it instantly runs on the processor.

With the direct handoff rule illustrated in the photos, the awakened waiter has a reserved permit. A newcomer cannot steal that permit merely by reaching the processor first. Dispatch determines when a process runs, while the protected counter and waiting-list rules determine ownership.

All counter checks and queue coordination must be synchronized. If one process decrements, another decrements again, and both later test the changed shared value, the first can block incorrectly. Making only one arithmetic instruction atomic is not enough to protect the complete protocol.

The photographed quiz intentionally changes signal to wake only when the new value is less than zero. Starting at minus one, signal increments to zero but then wakes nobody, stranding the remaining waiter. The correct test is less than or equal to zero after incrementing.

A priority queue or last-in-first-out list can still starve a waiter even after that bug is fixed. Correct wakeup accounting and fairness are separate properties. A signal that happens before a wait can leave a permit stored in the value, rather than vanishing like an unremembered event.

Things to take note of. Decrement before the negative test, increment before the nonpositive wakeup test, and track the wait list with the value. Preserve the exact buggy code when tracing a question, then explain the correction; do not silently fix it before computing the requested states.

source.summary: S4 printed4.28–4.36; IMG_2193–2196,2201–2205. Blocking signed-value convention; wrong<=-1 wakeup check traced then repaired.

lessons.title: How do you design a semaphore protocol?

transcript.text: How do you design a semaphore protocol? First separate shared data, resource capacity and ordering dependencies. Those are different responsibilities, so initializing every semaphore to one is not a design method, however tidy the code may look.

For shared mutable data, identify the critical section and protect it with a binary semaphore initially one. Wait before the protected update and signal after it. Keep the protected region focused on the data that must remain consistent.

For a resource pool, initialize a counting semaphore to the number of available instances. Three identical printers begin with three permits, even if only two jobs currently exist. The initial count describes capacity, not the current number of customers.

A job waits for a printer permit before using a printer and signals when that printer is returned. Three successful waits can allocate the three instances; a fourth requester blocks. No single permit should represent two simultaneous users of one printer.

The shared job list needs its own mutex while entries are removed or updated. Using only printers equal to three would allow three concurrent list mutations and could race. Using one mutex around the entire print would protect the list but unnecessarily serialize the printer pool.

For ordering, suppose statement B must occur only after statement A in another process. Initialize an ordering semaphore to zero, signal after A, and wait before B. If the signal arrives first, the permit remembers that A has occurred.

That one-way dependency is not mutual exclusion around an arbitrary shared object. Its zero initialization intentionally prevents B from starting before A. A mutex normally starts with one permit so the first contender can enter an otherwise free critical section.

Incorrect acquisition order can deadlock: P zero takes lock S and waits for Q, while P one takes Q and waits for S. Both waits are individually legitimate, but the combined resource dependencies form a cycle. Consistent ordering or another justified protocol is needed.

Queue discipline matters too. A priority queue may keep favoring new high-priority arrivals, while a last-in-first-out list can bury an old waiter. Preserving a resource count does not by itself prove bounded waiting for each process.

Things to take note of. State what every semaphore means, derive its initial value from that meaning, and pair each acquisition with the appropriate release. Protect the data, count the instances and enforce the dependency; do not interchange those jobs without an argument.

lessons.title: How do producers and consumers share a bounded buffer?

transcript.text: How do producers and consumers share a bounded buffer? We need to coordinate the available slots, the available items and safe access to the buffer structure. A single lock does not express all three of those requirements.

Use three slots, with empty initially three, full initially zero and mutex initially one. Empty permits producers to reserve capacity, full permits consumers to reserve items, and mutex protects shared insertion or removal data. The values have different meanings.

A producer prepares an item, waits on empty, and then waits on mutex. Its capacity reservation changes empty from three to two before the item is physically inserted. Reserving a slot and filling that slot are separate steps in the trace.

Inside the protected region, insert item A and update the shared buffer metadata. Release mutex, then signal full so an item becomes available for consumption. At the completed operation boundary, the buffer has one item, empty is two and full is one.

A consumer first waits on full and then on mutex. It reserves an available item before removing it under mutual exclusion. After removal it releases mutex and signals empty, returning capacity to the producer side.

Fill the remaining example with three produced items A, B and C. When every slot is occupied and there is no free capacity, an additional producer must wait for a consumer to release space. It must not hold the buffer mutex while waiting for that capacity.

The consumer has the dual rule: if no item is available, wait on full before taking mutex. If it instead takes mutex first and then blocks on an empty buffer, the producer cannot acquire mutex to insert an item. The two processes can then wait on each other.

The same mistake on a full buffer can leave a producer holding mutex while waiting for empty. A consumer needs that mutex to remove an item and create capacity. This ordering defect is not repaired merely by adding another processor.

Track physical items and outstanding reservations separately. Empty plus full equals capacity at simple quiescent boundaries, but not necessarily between a wait and its matching completion signal, especially in the signed blocking representation. An invariant must account for in-flight operations rather than pretending each instruction is a completed transaction.

Things to take note of. Producers wait for capacity before mutex; consumers wait for an item before mutex. Update buffer data inside the protected region, signal the opposite resource after completing the change, and explain the specific deadlock caused by swapping those waits.

lessons.title: Why do dining philosophers deadlock?

transcript.text: Why do dining philosophers deadlock? Each philosopher needs two neighboring chopsticks, but each chopstick can be held by only one philosopher at a time. A locally sensible first acquisition can create a circular dependency when everyone follows it together.

There are five philosophers and five chopsticks around the table. Model each chopstick with a binary semaphore initially one. Philosopher i waits for chopstick i and then chopstick i plus one modulo five, eats, and eventually releases both.

Let P zero acquire its first chopstick and then be paused. P one acquires its first, followed by P two and P three. None yet has the second resource needed to eat, but each successful acquisition consumes an available chopstick.

Finally P four acquires the last remaining first chopstick. Now all five resources are held, one by each philosopher. Every next request targets a stick already held by a neighbor, completing the circular wait.

All five block on their second acquisition, and none reaches the release code. A processor scheduler cannot dispatch a blocked philosopher into releasing a resource it has not finished using. Fairness about who runs does not repair the acquisition cycle.

One remedy limits simultaneous contenders to four using another counting semaphore. With at most four philosophers attempting to acquire, the five-person circular hold pattern cannot form in the same way. A permitted philosopher can obtain the missing second stick and make progress.

Another remedy takes both required chopsticks together as an indivisible allocation decision, or waits without holding either. That removes hold and wait, but the implementation must protect the both-or-none decision correctly. Two unrelated successful-looking tests do not make it atomic.

A global resource ordering is also effective: always acquire the lower-numbered chopstick before the higher-numbered one. The philosopher between zero and four must request zero first, breaking the circular direction. An odd-even asymmetric ordering can similarly prevent the all-same-direction cycle.

Proving the absence of deadlock does not automatically prove that every philosopher receives a turn within a fixed bound. A poorly chosen permission or queue rule may still starve a particular philosopher. Keep resource safety, deadlock freedom and fairness as separate claims.

Things to take note of. Show the five first acquisitions, identify the cycle, and explain which deadlock condition your remedy breaks. More hardware or a different quantum does not itself change the order in which this broken protocol requests chopsticks.

source.summary: S4 printed4.47–4.50; S5 printed5.19–5.22; IMG_2210–2211. Five philosophers; one chopstick resource per edge.

lessons.title: How can readers share while writers stay exclusive?

transcript.text: How can readers share while writers stay exclusive? Multiple readers can safely inspect the protected data together, but a writer needs exclusive access against both readers and other writers. The reader-preference semaphore solution separates data access from protection of the reader count.

The mutex protects the shared readcount variable, not the entire duration of reading. The semaphore called write protects admission to the database. A writer waits on that semaphore, writes alone, then signals it when finished.

Now start with no writer. Reader R one takes mutex, increments readcount from zero to one, and as the first reader waits on write. It then releases mutex and performs its reading while holding the group database exclusion against writers.

Reader R two takes mutex and increments readcount to two. Because it is not the first reader, it does not acquire write again. It releases mutex and joins R one in the database, so the two reading activities can overlap.

A writer arriving now waits on write and blocks. That does not stop the current readers from finishing their reads. The data remains protected because the reader group still controls the database semaphore.

When R one leaves, it takes mutex and decrements readcount from two to one. It is not the last reader, so it leaves write unavailable to the writer. Releasing the reader-count mutex does not imply that the database is empty.

R two eventually decrements readcount to zero and signals write because it is the last reader. Under the blocking handoff model, the writer can become ready with the database permit reserved. Dispatch is still a scheduling decision, not an instantaneous consequence of the signal.

The writer then executes exclusively and signals when done. Notice the two different protections: short mutex sections serialize updates to readcount, while write controls the reader group versus a writer. Holding mutex during every whole read would unnecessarily serialize readers.

In this reader-preference version, an ongoing stream of new readers may keep readcount above zero and postpone a writer indefinitely. Exclusion can remain correct while writer fairness fails. Writer preference or a fair arrival policy needs a different admission design.

Things to take note of. The first reader acquires write, the last reader releases it, and every readcount change is protected by mutex. State that this is reader preference and explain its starvation caveat rather than claiming that correct exclusion guarantees fairness.

lessons.title: How do resource graphs reveal deadlock?

transcript.text: How do resource graphs reveal deadlock? A deadlock is a set of blocked processes whose required resources or events can only be supplied by members of that same blocked set. Draw the ownership and requests separately before deciding what can progress.

A resource type may have several instances. A process requests an instance, uses it after allocation, and eventually releases it. A resource-allocation graph records those relationships rather than merely drawing processes that happen to be slow.

A request edge points from a process to a resource type. An assignment edge points from a resource instance to the owning process. Reversing either arrow changes the meaning, so label the relationship as you draw it.
Consider two single-instance locks, A and B. P zero owns A, while P one owns B. So far neither process is necessarily blocked; ownership alone is not a deadlock.
Now P zero requests B and blocks while retaining A. P one requests A and blocks while retaining B. Follow the cycle: P zero needs B, held by P one, which needs A, held by P zero.

If neither process can release its first lock until its second request succeeds, the cycle cannot resolve within this model. Every participant waits for another participant. A scheduler cannot fix it simply by giving these blocked processes more turns.

With one instance of every resource type, a cycle implies deadlock. With multiple instances, a cycle indicates a possibility rather than a sufficient conclusion. An extra available instance or a process outside the cycle that can finish may still break the wait.

No cycle means no deadlock in this resource-allocation model. Do not apply the single-instance conclusion to a drawing with several dots per resource. Count the actual instances and examine which holders can complete.

Starvation differs because other processes may continue completing work while one unfortunate contender is continually denied service. A deadlocked set cannot make the required internal progress. The two problems can share symptoms without sharing the same proof.

Things to take note of. Draw request arrows from process to resource and assignment arrows back to the owner. Use the instance count when interpreting a cycle, and describe the blocked dependency rather than guessing from an idle processor.

source.summary: S5 printed5.4–5.15; guide§5; S4 dining-philosopher example. Authored two-lock graph.

lessons.title: How can deadlock be prevented?

transcript.text: How can deadlock be prevented? Prevention arranges the resource protocol so at least one necessary deadlock condition cannot hold. Identify the condition your rule breaks and the practical cost of that rule.

Mutual exclusion means some resource cannot be shared simultaneously by all contenders. A read-only object may be shareable, but an exclusive device operation or mutable critical section can require an owner. Making every resource freely shareable is therefore not a universal remedy.

Hold and wait means retaining an acquired resource while requesting another. Requesting the whole required set atomically before starting can remove this condition. It may reduce utilization because a process reserves resources before it needs them.

Alternatively, a process that cannot acquire its next resource can release what it holds and retry later. That strategy depends on being able to undo or restart the work safely. Retrying also requires a fairness argument if you want to rule out starvation.

No preemption means resources cannot simply be taken back from their holders. Some resources can be saved and restored, while others cannot be safely revoked halfway through an operation. A prevention answer must name the resource model instead of assuming arbitrary forced release.

Circular wait is prevented by assigning a total order to resource types and requiring every process to acquire them in increasing order. For locks A before B, both processes must acquire A before requesting B. A cycle would require the ordered resource ranks to increase and return to their starting point, which is impossible.
Replay the two-lock example with that order. P zero acquires A and B while P one waits for A without holding B. P zero can finish and release both, allowing P one to continue.

Dining philosophers offers several different prevention rules. Limit simultaneous contenders, acquire a pair atomically, or impose a consistent stick order. Explain the particular wait cycle each rule prevents rather than treating the names as magic.

Avoidance takes another approach: examine a proposed allocation and preserve a safe completion possibility under declared claims. That is different from permanently forbidding hold and wait. A prevention rule and an avoidance test can both be conservative for different reasons.

Things to take note of. Name all four necessary conditions, then break at least one with a concrete resource protocol. Deadlock freedom alone does not guarantee fairness, good utilization, or the absence of starvation.

source.summary: S5 printed5.16–5.25; S4 printed4.40–4.46; guide§5. Authored two-lock resource ordering.

lessons.title: How does Banker’s safety algorithm work?

transcript.text: How does Banker’s safety algorithm work? It asks whether at least one order lets every process obtain its remaining declared need and eventually finish. A safe state has such an order; an unsafe state lacks this guarantee but is not automatically already deadlocked.

The snapshot contains Allocation, Max and Available. Compute Need by subtracting Allocation from Max for each resource component. Keep the three resource columns separate; adding them into one total loses the information needed for feasibility.

Use the lecture example with five processes and initial Available three, three, two. Initialize Work to that vector and mark every process unfinished. Work is the hypothetical resource pool used during the safety test, rather than a permanent allocation to a real running process.

Search for an unfinished row whose Need is less than or equal to Work in every component. P one needs one, two, two and is feasible against three, three, two. Equality is allowed, so a row requiring exactly the available count must not be rejected.

Pretend P one completes, then add its current Allocation two, zero, zero back to Work. Work becomes five, three, two. Release Allocation, not Max or Need, because the temporary resources used to finish are already accounted for within the hypothetical pool.

Next P three can finish and release two, one, one, giving Work seven, four, three. P four can then finish and release zero, zero, two, giving seven, four, five. Mark each completed process so its allocation is not released twice.

P two now fits and releases three, zero, two, producing ten, four, seven. P zero finally releases zero, one, zero, producing ten, five, seven. Every row finished, so P one, P three, P four, P two, P zero is a valid safe sequence.

A different valid sequence can also prove safety. But finding one infeasible candidate does not prove the state unsafe; search the other unfinished rows. Only when no unfinished row fits and some remain unfinished has this repeated-search safety test become stuck.

For an added implementation analysis, at most n successful passes can finish n processes, and each pass can inspect n rows of m resource components. A straightforward repeated-search implementation therefore takes order n squared times m work. This is a derived bound, not an additional claim about examination scope.

Things to take note of. Need equals Max minus Allocation, feasibility is componentwise less than or equal, and completion releases Allocation. Keep Work, Finish and the proposed sequence visible so every update can be checked.

source.summary: S5 printed5.26–5.33; guide§5. Exact lecture five-process matrix; independent completion trace.

lessons.title: When does Banker’s algorithm grant a request?

transcript.text: When does Banker’s algorithm grant a request? Availability is only one gate: the request must also respect the process remaining claim and leave a safe state. The safety check uses a provisional snapshot that must be restored if the request is refused.

First compare Request with Need component by component. A request beyond the declared remaining maximum is an invalid claim under this model. Do not merely wait for extra resources and silently increase the maximum.

Next compare Request with Available. If a requested component exceeds the free amount, the process must wait without making a provisional grant. Passing this gate establishes immediate availability, not safety.
For the lecture snapshot, P one requests one, zero, two. Its original Need is one, two, two, and Available is three, three, two. The request fits both, so proceed to the provisional state.

Subtract the request from Available to obtain two, three, zero. Add it to P one Allocation to obtain three, zero, two, and subtract it from Need to obtain zero, two, zero. All three changes describe the same provisional transfer.

Run the safety test from that new state. P one can finish first, and a full completion sequence still exists, so the request can commit. A safety simulation is evidence of possible future completion, not a command to execute those processes immediately in that order.

Now start from the committed state, not the original slide snapshot. As an added illustration, let P zero request zero, two, zero. This request fits both its remaining Need and the currently free vector, yet its provisional allocation leaves Available two, one, zero.

No unfinished process can meet its remaining Need from two, one, zero in that provisional state. The request is available but unsafe, so it must wait. Restore Available, Allocation and Need together; a partial rollback corrupts the resource snapshot.

Keep three outcomes distinct: an invalid claim, an unavailable request, and an available but unsafe request. Only the last requires a trial allocation followed by a failed safety test. An unsafe decision is about preserving a completion guarantee, not proving a present deadlock.

Things to take note of. Check the claim, check availability, update all three structures provisionally, then commit only if safe. Later requests begin from the latest committed state, and a refused trial leaves that state unchanged.

source.summary: S5 printed5.34–5.37; guide§5. Lecture P1 request(1,0,2); added subsequent unsafe P0 request(0,2,0).

lessons.title: What makes an operating system real time?

transcript.text: What makes an operating system real time? Correctness depends on producing the right result within its timing requirement. A low average response time alone cannot establish that every important deadline will be met.

A hard real-time requirement treats a missed deadline as unacceptable for the specified task. A soft requirement allows degraded value or service when a result arrives late. Apply the distinction to the stated application instead of assuming that any fast computer is real time.

The course job notation contains release R, execution demand C, and relative deadline D. Its absolute deadline is R plus D. A release says when the job becomes eligible, while execution demand says how much processor service it needs.

For an authored job released at time five with execution demand two and relative deadline seven, the absolute deadline is twelve. If it starts at nine and runs continuously for two units, it finishes at eleven. It has waited four units and still meets its deadline.

For a periodic task, the first parameter is period T rather than one release time. Instances arrive at zero, T, twice T, and so on, each carrying its own execution demand and absolute deadline. A fresh release does not erase an unfinished previous instance.

Consider a task with period ten, execution demand six, and relative deadline ten. Its first instance is released at zero with deadline ten, then another arrives at ten with deadline twenty. Keep the instance identities separate when drawing preemption and remaining execution.

Rate monotonic uses a fixed task priority determined by period: shorter period means higher priority. Deadline monotonic uses shorter relative deadline instead. They coincide only when the relevant ordering keys happen to produce the same order.

Earliest deadline first compares the absolute deadlines of ready job instances. The ranking can change as instances arrive, so it is a dynamic-priority policy. It does not mean shortest execution demand or smallest relative deadline considered without release time.

Mark releases, completion times and absolute deadlines before calculating any average. A job still requiring execution when its deadline arrives has missed it. Finishing exactly at a deadline counts as meeting it in the interval model used here.

Things to take note of. Separate release, execution demand, period and relative deadline, then compute each instance absolute deadline. Use the scheduling policy actual comparison key and test the deadline of each job, not just the average completion time.

source.summary: S6a printed1.3–1.13; guide§6; IMG_2313/2319 DM taxonomy. Authored jobR5 C2 D7.

lessons.title: How does rate-monotonic scheduling work?

transcript.text: How does rate-monotonic scheduling work? Assign higher fixed priority to a task with a shorter period, then run the highest-priority ready instance. Preemption changes remaining execution, but it does not change a task period or its instance deadline.

Use the lecture tasks: P one has period ten and execution six, P two period nineteen and execution four, and P three period twenty and execution two. Initially their relative deadlines equal their periods. All first instances arrive at time zero.

P one has the shortest period and runs from zero to six. P two then runs from six to ten, finishing its first four units exactly when the next P one instance arrives. P three is ready throughout this interval but has the lowest priority.

The second P one instance runs from ten to sixteen. P three finally runs from sixteen to eighteen and completes its first instance before deadline twenty. With all released work complete, the processor is idle from eighteen to nineteen.

P two releases its second instance at nineteen and runs for one unit. At twenty, P one releases again and preempts it, running until twenty-six. P two then resumes with three units remaining and finishes at twenty-nine.

P three second instance begins at twenty-nine but is preempted at thirty by another P one release. Label the job identity and the remaining one unit rather than restarting its full execution demand. Each instance keeps its own deadline.

The next slide changes P three relative deadline to fourteen while keeping its period twenty. Its first instance still has not run at time fourteen under the same rate-monotonic priority order. It therefore misses deadline fourteen even though it later finishes at eighteen.

That deadline change does not alter rate-monotonic task priorities because this policy reads period. A deadline-monotonic policy would read the changed relative deadline instead. Keep the comparison key separate from the property you measure afterward.

A finite successful trace proves only what was checked within that interval and task model. Do not add a universal schedulability conclusion from one neat utilization percentage. The supplied material emphasizes tracing releases, preemption and deadlines explicitly.

Things to take note of. Shorter period wins, every periodic release creates a distinct job, and preemption preserves remaining execution. In the changed-deadline example, identify the missed P three instance and the exact time fourteen.

source.summary: S6a printed1.14–1.17; guide§6. Original three-task set then explicitly changed P3 deadline14.

lessons.title: How does earliest-deadline-first scheduling work?

transcript.text: How does earliest-deadline-first scheduling work? Among ready jobs, run the instance with the earliest absolute deadline. Recompute that comparison when jobs arrive or complete, and preserve the deadline through preemption.

Use the changed comparison set: P one has period ten, execution six and relative deadline ten. P two has period nineteen, execution four and relative deadline seventeen, while P three has period twenty, execution two and relative deadline fourteen. These changed deadlines must be retained for a fair policy comparison.

At time zero the deadlines are ten, seventeen and fourteen. P one runs first from zero to six, followed by P three from six to eight because fourteen precedes seventeen. P two then begins its four units at time eight.

At time ten a new P one instance arrives with absolute deadline twenty. P two is still running with deadline seventeen, so it remains ahead and completes at twelve. A new release does not automatically force preemption if its deadline is later.

P one second instance runs from twelve to eighteen, before deadline twenty. The processor is idle until P two next release at nineteen, whose absolute deadline is thirty-six. Watch the absolute deadline change by release time even though the task relative deadline stays seventeen.

At twenty, P one new deadline thirty outranks both P three new deadline thirty-four and P two deadline thirty-six. P one runs until twenty-six, P three then runs until twenty-eight, and P two resumes afterward. Track the residual demand rather than copying a fixed task order.

When P one releases at thirty with deadline forty, P two still has the earlier deadline thirty-six. P two therefore completes at thirty-one before P one runs again. This is exactly why relative deadlines alone are insufficient for the dispatch comparison.

Rate monotonic on this same changed task set keeps P three behind P two and misses its first deadline fourteen. Earliest deadline first instead completes P three at eight. Attribute the improvement to the policy applied to the same parameters, not to silently swapping task sets.

Deadline monotonic is another fixed policy based on relative deadlines, while earliest deadline first ranks individual absolute deadlines. Under overload, a dynamic policy also needs an explicit handling strategy. A priority rule does not manufacture extra processor capacity.

Things to take note of. Compute release plus relative deadline for every instance, compare only ready jobs, and check remaining execution at each deadline. Do not reset deadlines on preemption or claim a whole infinite schedule from a short successful window.

lessons.title: What does virtualization actually change?

transcript.text: What does virtualization actually change? It places an abstraction between the resource a program sees and the resource that implements it. Indirection lets the system control names, allocation and isolation while presenting a useful interface.

Multiplexing shares one physical resource among several virtual entities. A physical processor can supply execution turns to several virtual processors. The virtual identities persist even when they are temporarily waiting for physical service.

Imagine eight virtual machines with two virtual processors each, hosted on four physical cores. There are sixteen virtual processors but at most four can execute simultaneously in this simplified core model. Scheduling chooses which four receive service at a given time.

Overcommitment relies on virtual demand not always reaching its maximum at the same instant. If all sixteen virtual processors are busy, they contend for the four physical execution slots. More virtual names do not multiply the host available processor time.

Aggregation goes the other direction: several underlying resources appear as one larger resource. Combining disk capacity into a logical volume is an example. The abstraction can simplify naming while the layout still determines usable capacity and failure behavior.

For an added illustration with equal disks, striping uses all n disks of size S for different data, giving n times S capacity. Two-disk mirroring stores each item twice, giving S usable capacity. If one disk-equivalent stores parity information, the remaining data capacity is n minus one, multiplied by S.

These are layout-derived capacity formulas under the stated equal-size assumptions. They are not a full theory of recovery, performance or failure independence. Match the capacity to what the layout stores rather than memorizing every combination as simple addition.

Emulation presents a resource whose interface or behavior differs from the underlying implementation. A RAM disk exposes storage operations implemented in memory, while cross-architecture translation presents another instruction environment. One system can combine emulation, aggregation and multiplexing.

For each exam example, identify the exported abstraction and the implementing resources first. Then explain whether the key operation shares one resource, combines several, or presents a different interface. A familiar product name alone is not the mechanism.

Things to take note of. Multiplexing shares, aggregation combines, and emulation supplies a different apparent resource. Count physical capacity separately from virtual identities, and state assumptions before deriving any capacity formula.

lessons.title: How do guests, hosts and hypervisors fit together?

transcript.text: How do guests, hosts and hypervisors fit together? A virtual machine presents a machine-like environment in which a guest operating system runs applications. A hypervisor, also called a virtual machine monitor, controls the relationship between that environment and the physical host.

Inside a guest, its scheduler chooses a guest process to run on a virtual processor. The host scheduling layer chooses when that virtual processor receives a physical execution slot. Both scheduling decisions can affect when the application actually progresses.

Return to sixteen virtual processors backed by four physical cores. A guest may regard its process as selected for a virtual processor while that virtual processor waits for host service. Distinguish a guest-ready process from a virtual processor that is actually executing on hardware.

The conventional Type one diagram places the hypervisor directly above hardware and the guest machines above it. The conventional Type two diagram places a host operating system between the virtualization application and hardware. Trace the layers shown instead of inferring classification from an icon.

The course slide labels KVM with Linux using its Type two diagram convention. That example needs instructor clarification if a question expects a universal product classification. For this course, preserve the displayed convention while understanding the actual layers being discussed.

A process abstraction supplies an execution context and address space within an operating system. A whole virtual machine additionally hosts an operating system and a virtualized machine interface. The two abstractions operate at different layers even though both can involve isolation and scheduling.

The monitor aims to retain control over the underlying machine while supporting useful efficiency and isolation. A guest kernel can administer its own environment without having unrestricted authority over other guests or the physical host. Guest privilege is subordinate to the virtualization control layer.

Isolation is a design goal with mechanisms and assumptions, not an automatic consequence of drawing separate boxes. The monitor must mediate sensitive operations and shared physical resources. Performance likewise depends on workload, scheduling and implementation.

When drawing an answer, label guest applications, guest operating systems, virtual processors, the monitor and the physical hardware. Add a host operating system where the chosen architecture requires one. Then point to the layer responsible for each dispatch or privileged operation.

Things to take note of. Guest processes run on guest virtual processors, and virtual processors need physical service from the host. Learn the Type one and Type two layer diagrams, and keep the slide KVM example qualified as a course convention.

lessons.title: How can a guest run directly while the monitor stays in control?

transcript.text: How can a guest run directly while the monitor stays in control? Limited direct execution lets ordinary guest instructions use the processor while sensitive operations remain subject to virtualization control. Virtualization does not require interpreting every instruction one by one.

Ordinary computation such as arithmetic can often proceed directly under the chosen execution environment. Operations that would change protected machine state require a controlled path. The important distinction is whether the operation can affect resources beyond the guest permitted authority.

In the conceptual trap path, a sensitive guest operation causes control to pass to the monitor. The monitor validates or emulates the permitted effect and resumes guest execution. Hardware virtualization support helps enforce that separation in suitable implementations.

The guest kernel remains a kernel relative to its guest applications, yet it is still controlled relative to the host. Calling a guest privileged therefore needs a layer reference. Do not draw it as freely rewriting physical host ownership merely because it runs operating-system code.

Full virtualization aims to support an unmodified guest using the presented machine interface. Paravirtualization instead exposes a cooperative interface that requires guest awareness or modification. The distinction is about the interface contract, not a claim that one label always guarantees better performance.

Memory names also have layers. A guest virtual address belongs to a guest process, a guest physical address describes the guest machine view, and a host physical address names actual host storage. Keep these conceptual names separate without importing the later chapter page-table algorithms.

A guest may believe a resource occupies a particular location while the monitor maps that identity onto a different physical implementation. That indirection enables controlled allocation and isolation. A virtual name is not proof of a dedicated physical device or a one-to-one capacity reservation.

Direct execution supports efficiency, while controlled transitions preserve the monitor authority. A system can combine that mechanism with device emulation and multiplexed virtual processors. Explain each operation at its own layer rather than choosing one word for the whole machine.

For an exam trace, start at the guest instruction, identify whether it is ordinary or sensitive, then show the appropriate execution or control-transfer path. State which layer validates the requested effect. Keep architectural assumptions visible because implementations need not use identical paths.

Things to take note of. Direct execution and monitor control can coexist through enforced privilege boundaries. Separate full virtualization from cooperative paravirtualization, and distinguish guest virtual, guest physical and host physical names.

lessons.title: How do you trace scheduling events without losing the queue?

transcript.text: How do you trace scheduling events without losing the queue? Build an event ledger before calculating averages. Record arrivals, completion, quantum expiry and wakeups separately, using the tie convention stated by the particular question.

For a CPU-only example, P one through P four arrive at zero, one, two and four. Their bursts are six, six, six and four, with quantum two and zero switch overhead. Existing waiters precede new arrivals, which precede an unfinished process rejoining after its expired slice.

P one runs from zero to two. At two, P two is already waiting and P three has just arrived, so P one rejoins behind them. The next turns are P two from two to four, P three from four to six, then P one from six to eight.

P four arrived at four and now runs from eight to ten. Continue the queue mechanically: P two, P three, P one, P four, P two, then P three. The completion times are sixteen, twenty, twenty-two and eighteen in process order.

Subtract arrivals to get turnaround sixteen, nineteen, twenty and fourteen, averaging seventeen point two five. Response is zero, one, two and four, averaging one point seven five. With no blocking, waiting is turnaround minus burst, averaging eleven point seven five.

For the fork and message worksheet, each executed line costs one unit and the quantum is two. The parent assigns at zero and forks during one to two, so the child enters at two. That child then attempts receive and blocks at three.

The parent sends during three to four and continues to a receive that blocks at five. The child runs its add from five to six and its send from six to seven. Under the worksheet explicit wakeup-before-requeue rule, the parent runs its exit from seven to eight, then the child exits from eight to nine.

The child turnaround is nine minus its arrival two, giving seven; the parent turnaround is eight. Do not charge the child for time before it existed. A nonblocking send does not automatically yield, while an empty receive can create an immediate scheduling event.

Some photo exercises include the running process at the head of the displayed ready queue. That notation differs from an implementation queue containing only waiting runnable processes. Write the convention beside your ledger and do not mix the two halfway through.

Things to take note of. Define simultaneous-event order, update the queue at every event, and calculate metrics from the completed ledger. More I/O devices can alter the execution order, so do not assume every scheduling average must improve monotonically.
