lessons.title: How do you solve a reverse Banker’s question?

transcript.text: How do you solve a reverse Banker’s question? When Available contains unknowns, derive constraints from the safety test rather than guessing a large resource total. Every component must support a complete feasible sequence after the proposed request.

The photographed four-process problem starts with Available x, y, two and asks about P one requesting one, zero, two. After provisionally granting it, Work is x minus one, y, zero. The third component is now zero, restricting which row can finish first.

P one, P two and P four still need a positive amount of the third resource. Only P three has zero remaining need in that column. Its first-resource need is six, so x minus one must be at least six and x must be at least seven.

P three releases three units of resource A, zero of B, and two of C. P four then releases two of A, one of B, and one of C. P two releases two of A and nothing from B or C, so Work grows through returned allocations rather than extra external resources.

P one remaining second-resource need is four. Before its final completion, the other relevant releases add only one unit to the initial second-resource amount y. Therefore y plus one must reach four, forcing y to be at least three.

At the minimum pair seven, three, the provisional Work is six, three, zero. The safe order P three, P four, P two, P one grows Work through nine, three, two; eleven, four, three; thirteen, four, three; and fourteen, five, five. The complete sequence proves sufficiency as well as the earlier necessary bounds.

A second photographed matrix starts at Available one, zero, one. Its unique safe order is P zero, P three, P one, P two. Uniqueness here follows because only one unfinished row fits at each step, not because Banker always has a unique answer.

Let P three request one, zero, zero in that second matrix. The request respects its claim and immediate availability, but the provisional Work becomes zero, zero, one. No unfinished Need row fits, so refuse the unsafe request and restore the original snapshot.

In a reverse problem, a partial inequality such as y at least one may permit an intermediate step without permitting the final process. Continue until every row is finished. To prove a minimum, give both lower-bound reasoning and a full safe witness at that bound.

Things to take note of. Derive the forced first row, propagate allocation releases, and keep the unknown resource components separate. An available request can still fail safety, and a minimum needs a complete completion sequence.

lessons.title: How do you identify a scheduling policy from a trace?

transcript.text: How do you identify a scheduling policy from a trace? Treat each dispatch, preemption and idle interval as evidence. One matching choice can fit several policies, so seek a decision that distinguishes their comparison keys.

In the photographed two-core example, core one handles P zero, P three and P four. P zero arrives at zero with burst three, P three at one with burst two, and P four at four with burst two. The displayed SRTF convention gives a new arrival precedence on equal remaining demand.

At one, P zero has two units left and the arriving P three also needs two. That arrival-first tie makes P three run from one to three, then P zero resumes from three to five. P four runs afterward from five to seven.

At time four, P zero has one unit left but deadline ten, while P four has two units and deadline seven. Keeping P zero matches shortest remaining demand and contradicts earliest deadline first at that decision. Use the distinguishing event, not a vague resemblance.

Core two handles P one, P two, P five and P six. P one runs from two to five, P five from five to six, P two from six to eight, and P six from eight to nine. At five, the new P five has absolute deadline six and overtakes the older P two with deadline nine.

That event rules out first come first served and supports earliest deadline first. At three, P one and the arriving P two have equal remaining demand, yet P one continues, contradicting the worksheet arrival-first SRTF tie. Check all event choices against the stated convention.

Core two is idle before time two while work exists in the core-one set. Under a work-conserving global-ready-queue assumption, that idle slot would accept an eligible waiting job. The displayed behavior therefore supports partitioning into the two specified sets.

The separate EDF quiz has arrivals zero, one, three and six, bursts five, three, six and four, and absolute deadlines thirteen, five, nineteen and eleven. Its order is P zero, P one, P zero, P three, P zero, then P two. Completion by eighteen meets all four deadlines.

The priority-inversion photo appendix is optional: a high-priority job can block on a lock held by a low-priority job while medium-priority work delays that holder. Priority inheritance temporarily raises the holder so it can release sooner. Keep that optional mechanism separate from the confirmed core trace requirements.

Things to take note of. Test comparison keys at discriminating events, preserve explicit ties, and state the queue architecture assumption behind an idle-core argument. A plausible policy name is weaker than a complete explanation of the observed choices.

lessons.title: How does an xv6 user command reach the kernel?

transcript.text: How does an xv6 user command reach the kernel? Follow two connected routes: building the command into the file-system image, then crossing from user execution to a registered kernel service. This companion explains the manual mechanisms without claiming unverified branch-specific line numbers.

A user source file alone does not install a command in xv6. The program must compile, link with the user library, and enter the image through the Makefile UPROGS list. If the binary is absent from the image, the shell cannot execute it just because its source exists on the host.

The user declaration lets compiled code call the interface, while the generated assembly stub performs the machine-level transition. The system-call number identifies the requested service. Keep the user function name and the dispatcher number consistent across registration.

In the RISC-V route used by this lab, the stub places the system-call number in register a seven and executes ecall. Trap handling enters the protected kernel path and selects the registered handler. The returned value is delivered through a zero in the saved user register state.

Tracing the existing process-identifier call provides a registration example before adding the process-count service. The new service needs its user declaration, generated stub, number, kernel dispatch entry and handler connected. A missing link can cause a build error, an unrecognized request, or an incorrect result.

The manual defines getproccount as counting table entries whose state is not UNUSED at the instant each entry is inspected. Zombies are therefore counted while their table entries remain allocated. That definition differs from counting only processes currently executing on a processor.

A table scan with per-entry inspection is not a globally atomic process snapshot. Processes may change state while the scan proceeds, depending on its synchronization. The count can differ from another listing sampled through a different observation path or time.

Things to take note of. UPROGS concerns installation, ecall concerns the privilege crossing, and registration connects the number to the service. Explain the precise count semantics and use your actual lab branch before citing exact source locations.

lessons.title: How do fork, pipes and zombie cleanup connect?

transcript.text: How do fork, pipes and zombie cleanup connect? Fork creates a child execution context and duplicates descriptor references, while pipes supply communication endpoints. Exit and wait govern process completion bookkeeping rather than automatically erasing every shared reference.

After a successful fork, the parent receives the child identifier and the child receives zero. Each process continues after the call with its own user execution state. The scheduler decides which runs next; the return values do not guarantee a parent-first order.

For two-way request and reply, use two directional pipes. The parent writes the request pipe and reads the reply pipe; the child reads the request and writes the reply. Label both directions before deciding which descriptor ends each process should close.

Fork duplicates references to the open endpoints rather than creating unrelated empty copies of the pipe contents. Close the parent unused request read and reply write ends, and the child unused request write and reply read ends. Retaining a spare writer can prevent a reader from observing end of file.

A read on an empty pipe waits if a writer reference still exists under the stated blocking semantics. End of file requires the stream to be drained and all write references to close. Closing one descriptor is insufficient if another process still holds a reference to the same write endpoint.

When the child exits, it stops executing but can retain zombie bookkeeping until the parent reaps it with wait. The process-table slot is not yet equivalent to UNUSED. Distinguish stopped execution, retained status, and eventual resource reclamation.

If the parent calls wait first, it can block until a child exits. If the child exits first, the parent can reap the recorded status later. Both orders should be explainable from the same lifecycle, so one observed run is not proof of a fixed scheduling order.

Things to take note of. Track descriptor references per process, close every unused pipe end, and distinguish an empty stream from end of file. A zombie retains completion metadata until reaping; its existence does not mean it is still executing.

lessons.title: What does xv6 save during a context switch?

transcript.text: What does xv6 save during a context switch? Separate the saved kernel context from the user trapframe, the per-CPU scheduler context, and the process address space. These objects serve related transitions but are not interchangeable storage for one giant switch.

A timer-triggered preemption can lead through yield, sched and swtch to the per-CPU scheduler. Yield marks the current process runnable again under the required synchronization. The scheduler can later choose a runnable process and switch into its saved kernel context.

At the process-to-scheduler call, swtch saves the outgoing process kernel context and restores the CPU scheduler context. At the scheduler-to-process call, the directions reverse. Name both source and destination objects when explaining the two call sites.

The saved RISC-V context includes the return address, stack pointer, and s zero through s eleven. The callee-saved registers must survive the function-call boundary, while the stack pointer selects the suspended kernel stack. The return address supplies the resumption path even though it is not itself a callee-saved general register.

A newly allocated child does not have an ordinary previous kernel call to resume. Its initial saved context is arranged to enter forkret on its first selection. Consult the supplied branch context initialization before asserting exact offsets or a particular source line.

The strict-priority lab selects an eligible runnable even-PID process whenever one exists, then considers odd PIDs only if none qualifies. Preserve state, locking and per-CPU current-process invariants while changing selection. Timer preemption still produces selection points without making that selection fair.

On one CPU, an even child that remains runnable forever can starve an odd child that also remains runnable. A finite workload only demonstrates postponement until the preferred work ends. With spare physical cores, one busy even process does not establish starvation across the whole machine.

Things to take note of. Identify the saved context in both switch directions, justify the register set using the call convention, and preserve scheduler invariants. The strict-PID experiment is a policy argument under a stated workload, while optional GDB work remains outside this companion.

lessons.title: How do user threads switch stacks?

transcript.text: How do user threads switch stacks? A user-thread library can save one thread execution context and restore another while the kernel still schedules their containing process. In the lab many-to-one model, these threads share one kernel scheduling context.

Each user thread needs its own stack and saved register context. Threads share process code and ordinary global data, so switching stacks does not isolate shared memory. Keep the selected thread identity, its state and its stack pointer consistent.

For a suspended thread, saving the stack pointer preserves where its call frames live, while the return address and callee-saved registers preserve the resumption path. Restore those values before returning into that thread. Merely changing a current-thread pointer does not move execution onto its stack.

A new thread has no suspended call frame to resume. Initialize its return path to an appropriate entry or startup routine and its stack pointer to the usable top of its own stack. The startup path must handle the thread function finishing rather than returning into an undefined caller.

The manual uses the standard sixteen-byte stack-alignment requirement for the RISC-V call boundary. Align the initial stack top accordingly and preserve that requirement through the startup layout. Extra bytes of storage alone do not establish correct alignment.

A cooperative thread calls thread yield or exits to let the library select another runnable thread. If it never yields or blocks through a supported library path, its peers may not progress. A blocking kernel call can suspend the whole containing process in this many-to-one model.

Trace one round with A yielding to B and B yielding back to A. Each resumes at its own saved return path with its own stack contents. Check thread states and shared counters as well as printed output, because a plausible print sequence alone does not prove a correct context implementation.

Things to take note of. Private stacks and saved contexts enable resumption, while shared data still needs coordination. Initialize new threads differently from suspended ones, respect sixteen-byte alignment, and distinguish cooperative user scheduling from kernel preemption.

lessons.title: What do O, Omega and Theta actually mean?

transcript.text: What do big O, big Omega, and big Theta actually mean? We will build their definitions around one running-cost function, prove its bounds, and finish with the mistakes that make an otherwise sensible answer wrong.
First say what n measures and what operation you count. For a sorting problem, n might be the number of records, while the cost counts key comparisons; copies and swaps would be different counters.
Suppose our chosen cost is three n squared plus seven n plus four. The whole expression matters for exact work, but its quadratic term will control its asymptotic growth.

Big O gives an eventual upper bound, allowing a positive constant multiplier. There must be one constant c and one threshold n zero such that every input size beyond that threshold satisfies f of n at most c times g of n.

For every n at least one, seven n is at most seven n squared, and four is at most four n squared. Adding these inequalities puts our whole function at most fourteen n squared, so c equals fourteen is a valid upper-bound witness.

Big Omega reverses the inequality and supplies an eventual lower bound. Here the positive extra terms cannot reduce the quadratic term, so our function is at least three n squared for every positive n.
Big Theta requires both sides with positive constants. We have already trapped the function between three n squared and fourteen n squared, which proves a tight quadratic bound.

A tight asymptotic bound does not mean exact equality: the function need not equal n squared, and the two bounding constants may differ. Theta groups functions whose growth differs by at most constant factors after a suitable threshold.
Our function is also big O of n cubed, because n squared is at most n cubed once n reaches one. That upper bound is true but loose, so use Theta when you have actually established a tight order.
A ratio limit can provide a convenient shortcut when it exists. Dividing our function by n squared gives three plus seven over n plus four over n squared, whose limit is the positive constant three.

A ratio approaching zero supplies an upper bound, while a ratio growing without limit supplies a lower bound. These are sufficient tests under the usual positivity assumptions; an oscillating ratio can lack a limit even when asymptotic bounds exist.

Now separate the notation from the input case being analysed. Big O does not mean worst case, and big Omega does not mean best case; either can describe a best-case, worst-case, or suitably defined expected-cost function.

For example, a worst-case function may have both a quadratic upper bound and a quadratic lower bound. An average-case statement additionally needs a distribution on inputs, so do not hide that assumption behind a symbol.

Things to take note of: name the input size and counted operation, keep the constants fixed, and make the inequality hold eventually for every size. Prove both sides for Theta, distinguish a tight bound from a merely valid one, and stop making the letters do the job of a case definition, hmph.

source.summary: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How do we compare growth rates?

transcript.text: How do we compare growth rates? We will simplify a collection of functions, put equivalent growth rates together, and connect logarithms to a loop that repeatedly divides by two.
Begin with a constant function such as one thousand. Its value can be large, but it does not increase with input size, so its growth class is constant.
Next put logarithmic functions together, regardless of their fixed base. The change-of-base formula turns one logarithm into a fixed constant times another, so their Theta class is the same.
The logarithm of n squared belongs in that same group, because it equals twice the logarithm of n. Do not confuse squaring inside the logarithm with squaring the logarithm itself.

Now compare logarithmic growth with the square root of n and with n itself. Every fixed positive power of n eventually outgrows a logarithm, even if a small numerical example initially makes the difference look modest.
Multiplying n by log n places it above linear growth but below a quadratic. Larger fixed polynomial exponents follow, giving n squared before n to the fifth.
Fixed-base exponentials eventually outgrow every fixed-degree polynomial. Changing an exponential base generally matters: two to the n, three to the n, and four to the n form different growth rates.
Two to the power two n simplifies to four to the n. It is not the double exponential two raised to two to the n, so read the parentheses before rearranging your function cards.

Factorial eventually exceeds any fixed-base exponential, while n to the n grows faster still. Our full ordering therefore runs from constants through logarithms, powers and exponentials, then factorial, then n to the n.
Let us now derive a logarithm instead of merely recognising its name. Starting from sixty-four, repeatedly divide by two to get thirty-two, sixteen, eight, four, two, then one, using six divisions.

For an exact power of two, solving n divided by two to the x equals one gives x equals log base two of n. Starting at one and repeatedly doubling until reaching at least n instead requires the ceiling of that logarithm.

For other input sizes, floor division and the stopping condition determine the exact integer count. A loop that keeps dividing while its value exceeds one differs in detail from a real-number loop that stops once it falls below one, although both have logarithmic order.

Things to take note of: simplify first, group Theta ties, and distinguish logarithm bases from exponential bases. Derive loop counts from their updates and stopping conditions, and remember that a finite graph illustrates growth but does not prove the eventual order, how charming.

source.summary: Analysis Techniques p13; Review Week 8 pp4–8; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1,1.3. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How do we build and expand a recurrence?

transcript.text: How do we build and expand a recurrence? We will count subproblems, track the work at every level, and include the leaves before deriving a tight running-time bound.

A recurrence must describe what the algorithm actually does. Count the number of recursive calls, the input size of each call, and the local work outside those calls, instead of guessing from the height alone.

Our course example makes three recursive calls on quarter-size inputs and performs n units of local work. With constant base cost one, this becomes T of n equals three T of n over four plus n, with T of one equal to one. For this expansion, take n to be a power of four.
Start at input size sixty-four and draw the first three children, each of size sixteen. The root performs sixty-four units locally, while those three children together perform forty-eight units.
Each size-sixteen child creates three size-four children, giving nine nodes on the next level. Their local work totals thirty-six, which is another factor of three quarters smaller.
One more expansion creates twenty-seven size-one leaves. Each costs one by the base condition, so their total cost is twenty-seven rather than thirty-six or sixty-four.

At a general level i, there are three to the i subproblems, each with size n over four to the i. Multiplying those quantities gives n times three quarters to the i as the total non-leaf work on that level.
Stop when n divided by four to the L reaches one. The depth L is therefore log base four of n, and the number of leaves is three to the L, equivalently n to the log base four of three.
Now add every internal level and the leaf cost, without counting the leaf level twice. The internal sum is n times a geometric series with ratio three quarters, ending just before depth L.
The infinite version of that geometric series sums to four, so our finite internal sum is at most four n. The leaf exponent is less than one, so the leaves do not raise the order above linear.
The root alone already performs n units, supplying a matching linear lower bound. Combining the lower and upper bounds proves Theta of n, not merely big O of n.

Compare this with merge sort, where two half-size calls make total work per level stay linear. There the linear work repeats for logarithmically many levels, giving Theta of n log n; binary search instead follows one branch with constant local work.

Things to take note of: state the base case, count branches and shrinkage separately, and find the stopping depth before simplifying the sum. Include the leaf work, justify both sides of a tight bound, and never mistake tree depth for total work, hmph.

source.summary: Analysis Techniques pp14–19,21–22,24–27; study notes 01-analysis §§1.4–1.5. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How do we apply the full Master Theorem?

transcript.text: How do we apply the full Master Theorem? We will identify its parameters, check the conditions in each case, and work through examples including the logarithmic extension required by this course.
The theorem applies to a fixed number a of equal-shrink recursive subproblems, each of size n over b. The function f counts local work, and the comparison exponent p equals log base b of a.
Why compare against n to the p? The recursion has log base b of n levels and a to that power leaves, so n to the p is the scale of the constant-cost leaf work.
In case one, local work is polynomially smaller than n to the p. You must find a fixed positive epsilon such that f is big O of n to the p minus epsilon, and the result is Theta of n to the p.
Consider three T of n over three plus two. Here a and b are three, p is one, and the constant local cost is big O of the square root of n, so epsilon one half works and the answer is Theta of n.
In case two, local work matches the leaf scale and each level contributes at the same overall order. If f is Theta of n to the p, summing across the levels gives Theta of n to the p times log n.
For four T of n over four plus n minus one, p is one and the local cost is Theta of n. This matches case two and gives Theta of n log n.
The course includes an extension of case two for additional nonnegative powers of a logarithm. If f is Theta of n to the p times log to the k of n, the solution adds one more logarithmic power.
Apply that extension to two T of n over two plus n log n. We have p equal to one and k equal to one, so the result is Theta of n log squared n, rather than Theta of n log n.

Case three requires f to be polynomially larger than n to the p, and it also requires regularity. For all sufficiently large n, a times f of n over b must be at most c times f of n for a fixed c less than one.

For two T of n over four plus n, p is one half, and epsilon one half establishes the polynomial gap. Regularity holds because twice f of n over four is n over two, so c one half works and the solution is Theta of n.

As a transfer example, seven T of n over two plus fifteen n squared over four has p equal to log base two of seven. The quadratic local cost is polynomially smaller, making this case one and giving Theta of n to that exponent.

Things to take note of: write a, b, f and p explicitly, then justify the selected case rather than merely stating its answer. Include epsilon for polynomial gaps and regularity for case three; the course review specifically asks for this full version, so do keep up.

source.summary: Analysis Techniques pp20–31; Review Week 8 p13; Review Week 10 pp2–4; study notes 01-analysis §1.6. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: When does the Master Theorem fail?

chapters.title: A valid form, but no case

transcript.text: When does the Master Theorem fail? We will test its required form, distinguish logarithmic and polynomial gaps, and explain why the regularity condition cannot simply be ignored.

First check that the recurrence really has a constant number of equal-shrink subproblems. T of n minus one plus n does not have a fixed shrink factor greater than one, so this Master Theorem does not directly apply.
Likewise, a call on n over two and another on n over three do not fit the equal-size form. That does not make the recurrence unsolvable; it means you must use another justified method.
Now consider three T of n over three plus n divided by log n, with a suitable constant-size base. Its form fits, and p equals one, so the benchmark is n.
The local work is smaller than n, because dividing by log n makes its ratio to n approach zero. But case one needs more than simply being smaller: it needs a fixed polynomial gap.

Divide n over log n by n to the one minus epsilon. The ratio becomes n to the epsilon over log n, which grows without limit for every fixed positive epsilon, so the required case-one upper bound fails.

Case two does not apply either, because n over log n is not Theta of n. The extended logarithmic version supplied by this course requires a nonnegative logarithmic exponent, whereas this example would need minus one.

Case three cannot help because this local cost is smaller, not polynomially larger, than the benchmark. The example lies between cases one and two of the stated theorem, correcting the case-number label on the slide.

A recursion-tree expansion offers a way forward without forcing the wrong theorem. At level i the combined work is n divided by log of n over three to the i, so you must sum those varying level costs with a proper base threshold.
Now look at the other common omission, case-three regularity. A large value of f at one scale does not guarantee that the sum of the child-scale costs contracts by a constant factor.

For a clean counterexample, define f of n as n cubed at powers of two and n otherwise, and consider T of n equals T of n over three plus f of n on exact multiples. Although f is always at least n, at n equal to three times a power of two the child cost can be cubic while the parent cost is only linear.

Consequently, no fixed contraction constant can establish regularity there, even though f exceeds the constant leaf benchmark by a polynomial factor. This is an explanatory example of the condition, not a transcription of the slide whose extracted formula is ambiguous.

Things to take note of: verify the recurrence shape and every case condition before using the conclusion. A logarithmic gap is not a polynomial gap, missing regularity matters, and iteration or substitution remains available when this theorem has nothing to say, hmph.

source.summary: Analysis Techniques pp32–33; study notes 01-analysis §1.6. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How do we prove a recurrence bound by substitution?

transcript.text: How do we prove a recurrence bound by substitution? We will guess a concrete inequality, verify its base case, and carry it through an induction step without assuming the conclusion.
Our example has T of one equal to zero and T of n equal to T of n minus one plus n minus one. Expanding a few terms suggests quadratic growth, but we must still justify that quadratic guess.

We choose the concrete upper bound T of n at most n squared. This fixes the multiplicative constant at one; if that attempt failed, we would need a different constant or a stronger candidate inequality.
Begin at n equal to one, where the actual recurrence gives zero. Since zero is at most one squared, the base case holds.
Now assume the bound holds at k, namely T of k at most k squared. This is our induction hypothesis about the smaller input, not an assumption that the desired bound already holds at k plus one.
Apply the recurrence first: T of k plus one equals T of k plus k. Substituting the hypothesis gives at most k squared plus k, which is at most k squared plus two k plus one.

That closes the step, and induction proves the claimed upper bound for all positive integer n. Therefore the function is big O of n squared, but this proof alone has not supplied a matching lower bound.
To make the result tight, expand the recurrence completely. It sums one through n minus one, giving n times n minus one over two and therefore Theta of n squared.
For a divide-by-two recurrence, it can be easier to induct over powers of two. Assume the statement for input two to the k and use it to prove the statement for input two to the k plus one.

Consider T of n equals two T of n over two plus n minus one, with T of one equal to one. The tempting inequality T of n at most c n log base two of n fails at n equal to one, because its right side is zero.

We can instead start the power-of-two induction at n equal to two, where T of two equals three. Choosing c at least two makes the base hold, and substituting the hypothesis yields c n log n minus c n plus n minus one, which stays below c n log n.

A different valid repair is to strengthen the candidate bound by adding a linear term. Whatever repair you choose, it must be checked against the recurrence and the actual domain rather than being waved away as a small-input detail.

Things to take note of: distinguish the guess from its proof, fix your constants, and substitute only a hypothesis established for smaller inputs. Check the base and state whether you proved O or Theta; the missing half of a tight-bound argument will not prove itself, obviously.

source.summary: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How do parity and rounding affect recurrences?

transcript.text: How do parity and rounding affect recurrence solutions? We will expand a recurrence that decreases by two, handle its two base cases, and then explain when rounding can safely be suppressed in an asymptotic analysis.

The review analyses a particular median-of-three quicksort comparison count using T of n equals T of n minus two plus n. It sets T of one to zero and T of two to one, so odd and even inputs finish at different bases.

The local n in this review comes from three pivot-selection comparisons and n minus three partition comparisons. It is a convention for the shown algorithm, not a universal exact comparison count for every median-of-three implementation.
Take an even input size of eight and expand the recurrence. We obtain eight plus six plus four plus the base value one, for nineteen comparisons under this model.
Write a general even input as two k. The terms are four through two k in steps of two, together with T of two equal to one, so their sum is k times k plus one minus one.
For an odd input of seven, expansion instead gives seven plus five plus three plus zero. The result is fifteen, because the recurrence reaches T of one rather than T of two.
For a general odd input two k plus one, sum the k odd terms from three through two k plus one. Their arithmetic-series sum is k times k plus two, again quadratic in n.

Both the even and odd cases therefore have Theta of n squared growth despite different exact totals. Median-of-three can improve pivot selection, but this example shows it does not guarantee balanced splits in the worst case.

Now consider recurrences that divide input sizes by two and therefore need floors or ceilings. Solving on exact powers of two is convenient, but extending that result to arbitrary n requires a justification.
The slides call a nonnegative function smooth when its value at two n is Theta of its value at n. A polynomial n to the c qualifies, since doubling n multiplies it by the fixed constant two to the c.

The function n log n is also smooth for sufficiently large n, while two to the n is not. Doubling the input in that exponential changes its ratio by another factor two to the n, which cannot be bounded by a fixed constant.

For an ordinary monotone running-time function, sandwich n between the adjacent powers of two. Bounds at those endpoints and a smooth comparison function then control the in-between values, which explains the usual rounding shortcut for standard algorithmic recurrences.

Things to take note of: expand until the correct base, keep parity when exact counts matter, and distinguish exact formulas from their common growth class. Ignore rounding only when the algorithm and comparison bounds justify it, not because floors happen to look untidy, hmph.

lessons.title: How does greedy coin change work, and when does it fail?

transcript.text: How does greedy coin change work, and when does it fail? We will make change with a locally best choice, count the work, and then use one counterexample to test whether that choice is always optimal.

A greedy algorithm commits to its next choice using the information currently available. It does not systematically compare all future continuations or undo the choice when a later step becomes awkward.

For coin change, the natural rule is to select the largest coin that does not exceed the remaining amount. Repeat until the remainder is zero, assuming positive integer denominations and an unlimited supply of coins.

Take denominations one, five, ten and twenty-five, and make thirty-seven. The largest affordable coin is twenty-five, leaving twelve; move that coin into the selected row rather than treating it as a mathematical wish.
For the remainder twelve, the largest affordable coin is ten. Selecting it leaves two, which neither five nor ten can fill exactly by itself.
Take a one, leaving one, then a final one, leaving zero. The completed change is twenty-five plus ten plus one plus one, using four coins.

A faster implementation handles one denomination at a time in descending order. Integer division tells how many copies to take, and the remainder moves directly to the next denomination without an iteration for every individual coin.

If k denominations are already ordered, this division-based scan uses big O of k arithmetic operations under the course word model. Printing the chosen coins separately adds output work, while an unsorted input may also require sorting.

The repeated-subtraction version instead performs one choice for every coin selected. Its cost depends on how the largest affordable coin is found; rescanning all k denominations each time adds a factor that a constant-denomination assumption would hide.
Now change the denominations to one, ten and twenty-five, and request thirty. Greedy still takes twenty-five first, but the remainder five requires five separate one-coins, giving six coins in total.

Three ten-coins also make thirty, and use only three coins. This single strictly better feasible solution is enough to disprove universal optimality of largest-first greedy on arbitrary denomination systems.

Having a one-coin ensures every nonnegative integer amount is reachable, but it says nothing about minimum coin count. Some denomination systems do admit this greedy rule, whereas proving that property requires more than testing a few convenient amounts.

Things to take note of: state the objective, denomination assumptions, choice rule and actual implementation cost. A counterexample disproves a general greedy claim, while many successful traces cannot establish it; when the choice fails, dynamic programming can compare the alternatives, hmph.

source.summary: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: Why does earliest-finish interval scheduling work?

transcript.text: Why does earliest-finish interval scheduling work? We will choose the largest compatible subset of jobs on one resource, trace every acceptance and rejection, and justify the greedy rule by an exchange argument.
Represent a job as an interval including its start but excluding its finish. Two jobs that meet at an endpoint are therefore compatible, because the first has finished exactly when the second begins.
The rule is to sort jobs by increasing finish time. Scan that order and accept a job exactly when its start is at least the finish of the last accepted job.
Our five jobs are A from zero to three, B from one to two, C from two to four, D from three to five, and E from four to six. Their finish order is B, A, C, D, E, so the scan begins with B.
Accept B, which occupies the resource from one to two. Set the last accepted finish to two; A then starts at zero and conflicts, so reject A without changing that finish marker.
C starts at two, exactly the marker, so accept C and move the marker to four. D starts at three and conflicts, so it is rejected while the marker stays at four.
E starts at four, so accept it after C. The result B, C, E contains three jobs, and its touching endpoints are valid under our interval convention.

To prove the rule, consider an optimal solution agreeing with greedy for the longest possible prefix. At the first difference, greedy chooses a compatible job that finishes no later than the optimal solution's next job.
Replace that optimal job by greedy's choice. It remains compatible with the common prefix, and because it finishes no later, every later job from the optimal schedule still fits.

The replacement preserves optimality and extends the agreeing prefix, contradicting its maximal choice. Repeating this reasoning establishes that earliest-finish greedy attains a maximum-cardinality compatible subset. If greedy stopped with another optimal job still compatible, its scan would have accepted another job, so it cannot terminate earlier than that agreeing optimum.

Choosing the smallest start time is not interchangeable: a job from zero to ten can block three jobs from one to two, two to three, and three to four. Shortest duration also fails, because the job from three to five blocks both zero to four and four to eight.

Sorting costs big O of n log n, and the scan costs big O of n, or linear total if finish order is already given. Only accepted jobs update the marker, and its initial value must be a valid lower bound on starts, rather than blindly zero when negative times are allowed.

Things to take note of: this is unweighted subset selection on one resource, and changing the objective can invalidate the proof. Interval partitioning schedules every job using the fewest resources and is excluded in the supplied review, so do not answer a different problem just because its name sounds familiar.

source.summary: Greedy Algorithms pp8–13; Review Week 9 p4; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1,6.3. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: Why is density greedy optimal for fractional knapsack?

transcript.text: Why is density greedy optimal for fractional knapsack? We will fill a bag with divisible items, compute the exact profit, and use an equal-weight exchange to explain why the rule works.

Each item has a positive weight and a positive profit for taking all of it. Taking a fraction earns the same fraction of its profit, so profit divided by weight measures the value of each unit of capacity.

Our capacity is fifty, and the items have weight-profit pairs ten and sixty, twenty and one hundred, and thirty and one hundred twenty. Their densities are six, five and four, so that is also the descending order for filling the bag.
Take the first item fully, using ten units of weight and earning sixty. Forty units of capacity remain, and no other material gives more profit per unit than the density-six item just selected.
Take the second item fully, adding twenty units of weight and one hundred profit. The bag now has weight thirty and profit one hundred sixty, leaving twenty units for the last item.
The last item weighs thirty, but only twenty units fit. Because fractions are allowed, take two thirds of it, adding eighty profit and filling the capacity exactly.
Total profit is sixty plus one hundred plus eighty, which equals two hundred forty. This total uses fifty units of weight; taking the whole third item instead would violate the capacity limit.
Why is that local density rule globally safe? Suppose some feasible solution includes lower-density material while higher-density material is still available.

Exchange an equal small amount of weight from the lower-density material for the higher-density material. Weight stays unchanged, while profit cannot decrease and strictly increases when the densities differ.

Continue exchanging until no such inversion remains. The resulting solution takes the highest-density material first, which is the greedy structure, so an optimal solution can be transformed into a greedy one without losing profit.

The ability to take equal portions of different items is what makes that argument possible. With indivisible items, the exchange might be forbidden, so the same proof does not establish optimality for zero-one knapsack.

Compute densities, sort them in descending order, and scan once, taking the smaller of remaining capacity and item weight. Stop when the bag is full or the items run out; forgetting the second condition can index beyond the list when total available weight is too small.

Sorting costs big O of n log n, followed by a linear scan, while an already density-sorted list needs only that scan. A conventional stored list uses linear space, and any additional sorting workspace depends on the chosen sorting method.

Things to take note of: compute profit per weight, allow proportional fractions, and state why an equal-weight exchange preserves feasibility. Highest total profit and smallest weight are different rules; the density order wins because of this problem's assumptions, not because the word greedy sounds confident, hmph.

source.summary: Greedy Algorithms pp14–17; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.4. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How do memoisation and tabulation remove repeated work?

transcript.text: How do memoisation and tabulation remove repeated work? We will compute Fibonacci six, distinguish repeated calls from distinct states, and derive both a recursive cached solution and a bottom-up table.

The ordinary recursive function asks for Fibonacci five and Fibonacci four to compute Fibonacci six. Fibonacci five then asks for Fibonacci four again, so two branches immediately repeat the same mathematical question.

Continuing the call tree repeats smaller inputs many more times. The uncached recursion has exponential growth, with big O of two to the n as a valid upper bound, even though its maximum call depth is only linear.

Dynamic programming identifies a state by the information needed to determine its answer. Here that information is just the integer index, so all calls requesting Fibonacci four can share one stored result.
In top-down memoisation, check the cache before solving a state again. If an answer is present, return it; otherwise obtain the smaller answers, add them, store the result and return it.

Zero is a valid Fibonacci answer, so it cannot double as the unknown marker. An initially unused sentinel or a separate presence flag distinguishes an unsolved state from the already computed value zero.

Collapse the repeated call tree into a graph with one vertex for each index from zero to six. An arrow here points from a caller to a state it depends on, so the destination must be solved before that caller can finish.
Bottom-up tabulation uses those dependencies to select an evaluation order. Set the first two cells to zero and one, then visit indices from two onward so both preceding answers already exist.
At index two, add zero and one to get one; at index three, add one and one to get two. At index four, the two preceding answers are one and two, so the result is three.
At index five the sum is two plus three, giving five. At index six the sum is three plus five, giving eight, so the final table is zero, one, one, two, three, five, eight.

There are n plus one possible states and constant arithmetic work for each evaluated state, giving linear arithmetic time. A full table uses linear space, and the top-down version also has a linear-depth recursion stack.

If only the final Fibonacci value is required, bottom-up evaluation needs just the two previous values. That reduces extra storage to a constant number of machine words under the course arithmetic model; exact large-integer bit costs are a separate analysis.

Things to take note of: define the state, distinguish calls from first computations, and respect the dependency direction. Memoisation is still recursive and DP is not automatically polynomial; its cost follows the number of states and transitions, not the comforting sound of the word cache.

source.summary: Dynamic Programming pp3–18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5–6.7. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How do we turn a new recurrence into a DP?

transcript.text: How do we turn a new recurrence into a dynamic program? We will use the review's Virahanka definition, build its state graph and table, and derive memoised and bottom-up solutions from the same dependencies.

Use the definition actually supplied in this course: both base values are one. For a larger index, add the value at the previous index to the value at the floor of half the index; do not replace this recurrence with a familiar Fibonacci formula.
Let the state V of j mean exactly the value of that recurrence at index j. Both dependencies are smaller than j when j exceeds one, which permits an increasing-index table order.
Begin the table with one at zero and one at one. For a request at zero, return its base value before attempting to write index one in an array that may contain only a single slot.

At index two, the dependencies are index one and floor of two over two, which is also one. Add the stored one twice, giving two; repeated dependence on a state does not require computing that state twice.
At index three, the dependencies are index two and index one, giving two plus one equal to three. At index four, use index three and index two, giving three plus two equal to five.
At index five, use V of four plus V of two to get seven. At index six, use V of five plus V of three to get ten, completing the table one, one, two, three, five, seven, ten.
In a bottom-up implementation, loop j from two to n inclusive. Each iteration reads the two required earlier cells and stores their sum in V at j, then the function returns V at n.

A top-down implementation instead checks whether V at the requested index is already cached. If not, it recursively obtains those same two smaller states, adds them and stores the result before returning.

There are n plus one state positions, and each costs a constant number of arithmetic and cache operations. Both implementations therefore take linear arithmetic time and linear table space; the recursive version additionally counts its possible linear stack depth.

Two rolling values are not sufficient here, because a future state may need an older half-index entry. The dependency pattern decides what memory can be discarded, so a Fibonacci optimisation cannot be copied just because both definitions contain two terms.

Things to take note of: preserve the supplied bases and floor operation, justify the fill order, and distinguish repeated use from repeated computation. The method is state, dependencies, order and cost; remembering someone else's loop without those meanings is a rather fragile sort of confidence.

source.summary: Review Week 9 pp8–13; Dynamic Programming pp15–18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.6–6.7. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How does DP find the minimum number of coins?

chapters.title: Minimum coins for an exact amount

transcript.text: How does dynamic programming find the minimum number of coins? We will define an exact-amount state, compare every possible final coin, fill a small table and reconstruct an optimal answer that greedy misses.

Define the entry at amount a as the minimum coin count making that exact amount. The empty amount needs zero coins, while an unreachable positive amount must have an infinity marker rather than a misleading count of zero.

In any nonempty solution, remove its last coin of value d. The remaining coins must make amount a minus d, so trying every affordable denomination gives one plus the best stored count for that remainder.

Why may we use an optimal remainder solution? If that remainder used more coins than necessary, replacing it by a better solution and restoring the last coin would improve the supposed optimum, a contradiction.
Use denominations one, three and four, and target amount six. Start from C of zero equal to zero and fill increasing amounts, because every positive denomination points to a smaller amount.
For amount one, only the one-coin fits, so the answer is one. For amount two, that same denomination extends C of one, giving two coins.

For amount three, compare three ones with the single three-coin, so the minimum is one. For amount four, the single four-coin beats both ways of extending earlier amounts, so the minimum is again one.

Amount five has candidates two, three and two, so its optimum is two coins. At amount six, the candidates are three using a final one, two using a final three, and three using a final four, so choose two.
To reconstruct six, select a coin of value three and reduce the remaining amount to three. Select another three-coin, reach zero, and recover two coins of value three.

The largest-first rule would take four and then two ones, for three coins instead of two. The dynamic program succeeds because it compares alternatives rather than permanently committing to the largest denomination.

For a target A and k denominations, there are A positive amounts and at most k candidates per amount. This gives big O of k A time and big O of A table storage, with reconstruction adding work proportional to the number of coins output.

If coin one is absent, some amounts may be unreachable; with denominations three and four, amount two is one example. Keep those entries at infinity and report impossibility, rather than following a nonexistent reconstruction choice.

Things to take note of: the state means exactly an amount, and its objective is minimum count, not the number of combinations. Derive cost from actual states and choices, avoid the slide's unsupported blanket factorial claim, and remember that dependence on the numeric amount will matter when we discuss input bits.

source.summary: Dynamic Programming pp19–27; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.8. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How does longest common subsequence work?

transcript.text: How does longest common subsequence work? We will derive its two recurrence cases, fill a complete prefix table, reconstruct an actual sequence, and count both the table work and the backtracking cost.

A subsequence preserves order but may skip characters, whereas a substring must be contiguous. We seek a sequence appearing in both inputs with maximum length, and more than one answer can sometimes attain that length.

Let L at i and j mean the best common-subsequence length of the first i characters of X and the first j characters of Y. If either prefix is empty, its common-subsequence length is zero, giving the zero border of our table.

If the terminal characters match, there exists an optimum using that common terminal character. Append it to an optimum for the two shorter prefixes, so the value is one plus the diagonal predecessor.

If the terminal characters differ, they cannot both be the final character of a common subsequence. Omit one or the other and take the larger value from the upper and left neighbours, covering both possibilities.

Fill rows from top to bottom, and columns from left to right, so every dependency is ready. For the first X character A, the four values against Y are one, one, one, one, because the matched A remains available as the Y prefix grows.
For the next X character C, the first value stays one, and matching C raises the second value to two. The rest of this row stays two, giving one, two, two, two.
For the first G, the row becomes one, two, two, three. The final entry uses the matching G in Y and adds one to the diagonal value two, establishing a common subsequence of length three.

The second G does not produce a fourth common character, because the Y prefix contains only one G at its end. Its row is one, two, two, three again, and the final A row has those same values, leaving the optimum at three.

To reconstruct, begin at the bottom-right cell, and choose the upper neighbour when an unequal-character tie occurs. From the final A we move up; at the second G we move diagonally, emit G, and continue at the shorter prefixes.
Continue upward past the unused first G, then left past T, reaching the matching C. Emit C diagonally, then emit the matching A, and stop when an empty-prefix border is reached.

The emitted characters are reversed because we travelled from the end toward the start. Reverse G, C, A to obtain A, C, G, which appears in order in both original strings and has the optimal length three.

There are n times m interior states with constant work per state, so filling costs Theta of n m and the full table occupies big O of n m space. Each backtracking step decreases at least one index, giving big O of n plus m reconstruction time.

Memoised top-down recursion also avoids repeated states, so it can achieve the same polynomial state bound. The slide warning about inefficient recursion concerns the uncached version; optional rolling rows save length-only storage but complicate this simple reconstruction.

Things to take note of: define prefix lengths, initialise both borders, distinguish equal and unequal terminal cases, and state your tie rule. Recover a sequence as well as its length when asked, and reverse backtracked characters instead of proudly submitting the answer backwards, how charming.

source.summary: Dynamic Programming pp30–51, visually checked p44; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.9. The source strings are X=ACGGA and Y=ACTG in visual order. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How does 0/1 knapsack DP enforce single use?

chapters.title: 0/1 means once or not at all

transcript.text: How does zero-one knapsack dynamic programming enforce single use? We will derive an include-or-exclude recurrence, build a complete small table, recover the chosen items, and identify the update that would accidentally permit reuse.
Each item is indivisible and may be selected at most once. Capacity is an upper limit, so an optimal solution may leave room unused; filling the bag exactly is not required.
Let P at c and j be the maximum profit attainable with capacity c using only the first j items. With no items or with zero capacity, the value is zero under the positive-weight assumptions.

If item j is too heavy, it cannot be included, so copy the value using the first j minus one items. Otherwise compare excluding it with its profit plus the best value at the remaining capacity, again using only the first j minus one items.
Both branches decrease the item index, which is the reason single use is enforced. Once item j has been included, its subproblem cannot include that same item again.

Our capacity is five, and items have weight-profit pairs two and three, three and four, and four and five. Begin with the empty column, then add one available item at a time while preserving the already computed previous column.

With only item one available, capacities zero and one cannot fit it, so they stay zero. At capacities two through five the profit is three; the bag never gets two copies just because a larger capacity could hold them.

Add item two, whose weight is three and profit is four. At capacity three it improves the profit to four, at capacity four it still gives four, and at capacity five combining it with item one yields seven.

Add item three, whose weight is four and profit is five. It improves capacity four from four to five, but at capacity five its inclusion gives only five, so excluding it preserves the better value seven.

Reconstruct from capacity five and all three items. The value equals the previous column, so skip item three; with the first two items the value seven exceeds the first-item value three, so select item two and reduce capacity by three.

At capacity two and item one, the value three exceeds the no-item value zero, so select item one. The recovered pair has total weight five and profit seven; decrease the item index after either taking or skipping.

The table has order n C states, each comparing at most two constant-time alternatives, giving big O of n C time and space. Reconstruction takes at most n item decisions, while a memoised version must also account for recursive storage.

A one-dimensional optimisation processes capacities downward for each item, so a transition reads a value from before that item was added. Updating upward can read a newly improved smaller-capacity cell and reuse the item, silently changing the problem to unbounded knapsack.

Things to take note of: define both state dimensions, guard the overweight branch, and keep j minus one in both choices. Distinguish zero-one, fractional and unlimited-item variants, allow unused capacity, and explain the numeric-capacity cost before calling this algorithm polynomial.

source.summary: Dynamic Programming pp52–63; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.10. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: Why is knapsack DP only pseudo-polynomial?

chapters.title: Coin change has the same issue

transcript.text: Why is knapsack dynamic programming only pseudo polynomial? We will distinguish a numeric value from the number of bits encoding it, then compare knapsack and coin change with longest common subsequence.

A polynomial-time claim is measured against the length of the input representation. Writing a string of n characters explicitly supplies n symbols, but a binary integer can represent a much larger numeric value in only a few bits.
For example, binary one thousand is the number eight, represented by four bits. A capacity-eight table uses entries up to eight even though the capacity field itself has only four written symbols.

With b bits, the largest unsigned capacity is two to the b minus one. A table indexed through every capacity may therefore require exponentially many entries in b, despite being linear in the value C.

The zero-one knapsack table has n item choices and C capacity values, giving big O of n C work. If C is near two to the b, that expression becomes order n times two to the b, not a polynomial in n and b.

We call this pseudo polynomial time. The runtime is polynomial in the numeric capacity, without a polynomial bound in the encoded input length. This describes the given algorithm and representation, not a claim that every input always takes its largest possible table.
Minimum-coin DP has the same issue with its target amount A. Big O of k A depends on all amounts up to A, while the binary target field occupies only order log A bits.

Longest common subsequence is different because its two strings are explicitly listed. Their lengths n and m already contribute n plus m input symbols, so the n m table is polynomial in that total length.

The symbols n and m alone do not decide the classification. You must state whether a parameter measures an explicit sequence length, a numeric amount, or an encoding length before interpreting its appearance in a runtime.

Our operation counts use the course assumption of constant-time arithmetic on suitable machine words. For enormous exact integers, the cost of addition, comparison and storage also depends on bit length, which should be included in a full bit-operation analysis.

An exact knapsack DP therefore does not establish that the knapsack decision problem has a polynomial-time algorithm in binary input size. It removes repeated subproblems effectively, but the number of capacity states still carries the numeric-magnitude dependence.

Things to take note of: separate numeric values from encoding lengths and substitute the bit-length relationship before classifying a bound. LCS is polynomial in its explicit string lengths, whereas the capacity and amount DPs depend on numeric magnitudes; a table can be neatly organised and still be very large, hmph.

source.summary: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How do we choose a correct state and strategy?

chapters.title: Correct state can still be large
Choose the proof for the problem

transcript.text: How do we choose a correct state and algorithmic strategy? We will compare divide and conquer, greedy and dynamic programming, then use a path example to test whether a proposed state remembers enough information.

Divide and conquer solves smaller versions and combines their answers, as merge sort solves two halves and merges them. Greedy instead commits to one locally best feasible choice, and needs a proof that this choice can safely agree with an optimum.

Dynamic programming compares relevant alternatives while reusing stored answers for overlapping states. It may be recursive or iterative, and it does not need to try every numerical split unless that problem's recurrence actually demands it.

Start by defining a state in a sentence rather than writing a table shape. The state must contain everything needed to determine the best future answer independently of the particular history that reached it.

For minimum coin change with unlimited coins, the remaining amount is enough. For zero-one knapsack it is not enough, because the available item set changes; the standard prefix formulation therefore also records how many initial items remain eligible.

Optimal substructure can be justified by replacement: if an optimum used a nonoptimal subsolution, a better legal replacement would improve the whole answer. The word legal matters, because a replacement that violates the original constraints proves nothing.

Consider a shortest path split into a prefix and suffix under conditions where the shortest route is well-defined. Replacing a subpath by a cheaper route cannot improve on a true optimum, which motivates the familiar shortest-path property.

Now consider longest simple paths, where no vertex may repeat. A state naming only the current endpoint forgets which vertices have already been used, even though those choices decide which continuations are legal.

Suppose two partial paths reach the same vertex, but one has already used a vertex required by a later extension. Merging those histories into one endpoint-only answer can keep a numerically attractive path whose future extension is forbidden.

Adding a visited set can restore the missing information in a longest-simple-path formulation. However, n vertices have two to the n possible subsets, so a sufficient state does not automatically produce a polynomial-size dynamic program.

The same discipline explains our greedy examples. Fractional density ordering has a legal equal-weight exchange, while indivisible knapsack and arbitrary coin denominations can defeat a local choice, so each requires its own proof or counterexample.

After deriving the state and recurrence, give an evaluation order that respects dependencies. Then multiply the number of distinct states by transition work, and add initialisation, reconstruction and stack costs where they matter.

Things to take note of: an algorithmic label is not a correctness proof, and optimal substructure alone does not guarantee a small table. Keep every relevant constraint in the state, distinguish reachable states from repeated calls, and let the actual dependencies choose your implementation, obviously.

lessons.title: How does naive string matching scan the text?

transcript.text: How does naive string matching scan the text? We will align a pattern, compare characters, reset after mismatches, and derive the scan bound from the number of legal alignments.
Our output is the first starting index where every pattern character matches a consecutive text window. We will use zero-based indices here, with text A B A B A B A C and pattern A B A C.
A legal starting index i ranges from zero through n minus m inclusive. If the pattern is longer than the text, there is no complete window, so return no match without reading past the text.
At start zero, compare A with A, B with B, and A with A successfully. The fourth comparison checks pattern C against text B and fails, so that window is not a match.

Move the entire pattern one position right and restart at its first character. At start one, pattern A immediately disagrees with text B, so reject after one comparison rather than continuing from the previous mismatch.
At start two, the first three characters again match A, B and A. Pattern C then disagrees with text B, using four comparisons for this alignment.
At start three, A immediately disagrees with B, so reject with one comparison. At start four, all four characters A, B, A, C match, so return index four as the first occurrence.

The trace used four plus one plus four plus one plus four comparisons, for fourteen in total. Count actual character checks separately from loop-control tests when that is the question's chosen operation.
For the worst-case pattern, place many A characters before a final C and search an all-A text. Each legal alignment matches almost the whole pattern before failing on its last character.

There are n minus m plus one complete windows, and each can require m character comparisons. That gives a scan upper bound of m times n minus m plus one, with the near-match family attaining that order.

The straightforward implementation uses a constant number of indices beyond the input strings. A full specification should also state an empty-pattern convention; returning zero is common, but blindly reading pattern position zero when the pattern is empty is invalid.

Things to take note of: keep the alignment start distinct from the current character pointers and reset the pattern after a mismatch. Stop at the last complete window, return the first successful start, and do not confuse a subsequence with the consecutive substring we are searching for, hmph.

lessons.title: How do rolling hashes make Rabin–Karp work?

transcript.text: How do rolling hashes make Rabin–Karp work? We will encode a window, derive its constant-work rolling update, and follow a collision all the way through actual character verification.
Map alphabet characters to integer codes and interpret a window of m characters as a base-d number. The leftmost code multiplies d to the m minus one, with successive codes using decreasing powers.
Horner evaluation builds this number by multiplying the current value by d and adding the next code. This requires one pass through m symbols instead of separately computing a power for every term.
For decimal window three six four one five followed by an incoming two, remove the leading three times ten thousand. Multiply the remainder by ten and append two, obtaining six four one five two.

The general update subtracts the outgoing code times d to the m minus one, then multiplies by d and adds the incoming code. Precompute that leading place value, since it is the same at every alignment.
Exact encodings become enormous for long patterns, so Rabin–Karp keeps their residues modulo a chosen prime q. Compute both initial hashes with modular Horner evaluation and precompute H modulo q.

Now take decimal pattern twenty-five, text one two two five, base ten and modulus thirteen. The pattern hash is twelve, and the first text window twelve also hashes to twelve, even though the strings differ.
Equal hashes therefore request a character check rather than proving success. Comparing the first digits rejects window twelve immediately, because pattern two differs from text one.

Roll to window twenty-two, whose hash is nine, so its different hash rejects it without character verification. Roll once more to window twenty-five, whose hash is twelve and whose two characters both match, giving zero-based index two.

With H equal to ten, the first modular roll is twelve minus one times ten, multiplied by ten, plus two, all modulo thirteen. The result is twenty-two modulo thirteen, or nine; the next roll must normalise its negative intermediate residue if the language uses signed remainders.

Initial hashing costs big O of m, and each rolling update uses constant word arithmetic. Verification adds work whenever hashes agree, so a full runtime statement must count those candidate checks rather than declaring every scan unconditionally linear.

Things to take note of: use the same encoding and modulus for both hashes, precompute the leading place value, and verify every equal-hash candidate. Roll only when another complete window exists, preserve modulo conventions, and remember that a collision is expected behaviour for a hash, not permission to return the wrong answer.

source.summary: String Matching pp11–15,20–24; study notes 07-string-matching §§7.3–7.4. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: What determines Rabin–Karp’s actual runtime?

transcript.text: What determines Rabin–Karp's actual runtime? We will keep rolling work separate from candidate verification, count the earlier collision example, and distinguish useful expected behaviour from a worst-case guarantee.
Use pattern twenty-five in text one two two five, base ten and modulus thirteen. There are three legal windows, twelve, twenty-two and twenty-five, whose hashes are twelve, nine and twelve.

The first equal hash is a spurious hit, meaning a hash agreement whose strings differ. Verification rejects after comparing only the first digits, so that candidate costs one character check rather than the full pattern length.
The middle window has a different hash, so it needs no character verification. The final window has an equal hash and two matching digits, adding two character comparisons and returning the match.

The total is three window-hash decisions and three actual character comparisons, with two rolling updates after the first hash. A hash comparison, a modular arithmetic operation and a character comparison are related costs, but they are not interchangeable counters.

Let h be the number of equal-hash candidates actually verified during a scan. Each candidate can require up to m comparisons, in addition to the linear-scale rolling work and the pattern-length initialisation.

This yields big O of n plus m plus h m under constant-time word arithmetic. The expression makes the assumption visible: a small number of candidate hits supports near-linear behaviour, while many expensive candidates do not.
Equal hashes do not all have the same verification cost. Some fail immediately, some fail only after a long matching prefix, and the first genuine occurrence stops a first-match implementation.

For worst-case behaviour, many windows can pass the hash filter and disagree late in direct verification. Up to n minus m plus one windows can each require order m checks, giving the familiar quadratic-style product bound.

The pattern-length initial work remains necessary even for a text with a single complete window. Keep it separate when stating precise parameter-sensitive bounds instead of silently assuming that n minus m plus one is large.

A large prime can reduce typical spurious hits, but cannot eliminate the pigeonhole possibility of collisions. Expected near-linear statements require suitable assumptions about the inputs or hashing, not merely the adjective large.

The deck also discusses measured overheads such as function calls, character conversion and modular division. These observations explain why a good asymptotic model need not predict every small practical benchmark, and they are not new measurements of this implementation.

Things to take note of: count rolling work and verification work separately, identify genuine versus spurious hits, and state the model behind expected bounds. Verification keeps the algorithm exact, while the hash filter controls how much of that verification work it can avoid, do keep up.
