lessons.title: How does Boyer–Moore use the bad character?

transcript.text: How does Boyer–Moore use the bad character? We will compare from right to left, build the course's character-jump table, and distinguish moving a text pointer from sliding the pattern alignment.
The pattern still moves overall to the right across the text, but comparisons within one alignment run from the pattern's end toward its beginning. Set both j and k to the pattern length m.

For every alphabet character, start its character jump at m, representing absence from the pattern. Then scan the pattern from one to m and set each present character's entry to m minus its position, leaving the rightmost occurrence.
Take pattern A B C A of length four. Its rightmost A is at position four, so the A entry is zero; B is two from the end, C is one from the end, and an absent X receives four.
Align this pattern with the start of text A X C A B C A. At text position four, A matches A; at position three, C matches C, leaving a matched suffix C A.

At j equal to two and k equal to two, text X disagrees with pattern B. The character table suggests increment four, while the fallback m minus k plus one is three, so the simplified scan takes their maximum, four.

Increment j from two to six and reset k to four. The old alignment ended at text position four and the new one ends at six, so the pattern itself slid only two positions even though the text pointer advanced four.

The difference comes from the two successful comparisons that moved j left before the mismatch. A jump measured from the mismatch pointer must account for that matched suffix, so it cannot be treated as an alignment slide without conversion.
At the new endpoint six, text C disagrees with pattern A. Character jump one and fallback one advance j to seven; reset k and the pattern now aligns with A B C A at text positions four through seven.
All four comparisons then match from right to left, reducing k to zero. Under this one-based course convention the successful start is j plus one, which is four for our example.

The fallback m minus k plus one is essential because character jumps alone can suggest a nonprogressing or backward alignment when the rightmost occurrence lies beyond the mismatch position. The extra term restores the old endpoint and forces at least one position of alignment progress.

Initialising the alphabet table and scanning the pattern costs big O of alphabet size plus m, with corresponding table storage. The simplified scan still has a general big O of n m bound; skipping many comparisons on some inputs is not a sublinear worst-case guarantee.

Things to take note of: preserve one-based indices, keep the rightmost occurrence, reset k after jumping, and distinguish a zero table entry from a safe zero alignment shift. Track j from its actual mismatch location; borrowing a table from a different pointer convention can produce a beautifully wrong trace.

source.summary: String Matching pp26–38; study notes 07-string-matching §§7.5–7.6. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How does Boyer–Moore use the good suffix?

transcript.text: How does Boyer–Moore use the good suffix? We will find the suffix already matched before a mismatch, choose a safe pattern slide, and convert that slide into the match-jump table used by the course code.

Suppose right-to-left comparisons matched the last m minus k pattern characters before failing at k. That matched text suffix is information we should preserve when choosing the next possible alignment.

First look for an earlier full occurrence of that suffix in the pattern, preceded by a different character from P at k. Choose the rightmost suitable occurrence, which gives the smallest positive slide preserving this useful match.

Why insist on a different preceding character? If the earlier suffix had the same preceding pattern character, aligning it would reproduce the mismatch we already know, so it cannot supply the next viable alignment.
The slide example uses pattern R A T S A N D C A T S, length eleven, with mismatch at position eight after matching A T S. The earlier A T S ends at position four and is preceded by R rather than C.
The actual pattern slide is eleven minus four, which equals seven. But j has already moved three places left, so its increment is those three places plus seven, giving match jump ten.

If no suitable full suffix occurrence exists, try aligning the longest suffix of that matched portion which is also a prefix of the pattern. This second case preserves a partial overlap that could still grow into a complete match.

If neither a full occurrence nor a prefix overlap works, move the pattern beyond the matched suffix. In that third case the actual pattern slide is m, while the pointer increment still includes the m minus k matched positions.
Now build the course table for W O W W O W, with positions listed in increasing k. When no suffix has matched at k equal to six, the convention is slide one and match jump one.

For k equal to five, suffix W can align to a suitable earlier W with slide two, giving pointer increment three. For k equal to four, suffix O W has an earlier full occurrence preceded by the same W as the mismatch position, so that occurrence is excluded.

For that k equal to four case, a prefix overlap W instead gives slide five, and the pointer increment is two plus five, or seven. For k equal to three, two and one, the useful shift is three, giving jumps six, seven and eight respectively.

Reading entries from k one through six, the slide table is three, three, three, five, two, one. The corresponding match-jump table is eight, seven, six, seven, three, one, because each entry adds its matched-suffix length.

The deck teaches these cases and tables without developing a complete preprocessing implementation. Do not invent its preprocessing cost or borrow a differently indexed good-suffix table; the number required by this scan is always the pointer increment, not just the slide.

Things to take note of: identify the exact matched suffix, test full occurrence before prefix overlap, and check the preceding-character condition. Add the matched-suffix length when converting to the pointer increment, and label table order explicitly so an extracted PDF cannot silently reverse your answer, hmph.

source.summary: String Matching pp39–49,51–54; physical p40 visually checked; study notes 07-string-matching §7.7. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How do both Boyer–Moore rules combine in a search?

chapters.title: Good suffix chooses the larger jump

transcript.text: How do both Boyer–Moore rules combine in a full search? We will use the course's six-character pattern, track all eighteen comparisons, and explain why a pointer jump is the maximum of the two table suggestions.

Character jump uses the mismatching text character, while match jump uses the suffix already matched. Both rule out impossible nearer alignments, so taking the maximum respects both exclusions rather than adding the suggestions together.
For this six-character pattern, character jumps are zero for W, one for O, and six for an absent character. The match-jump entries for k one through six are eight, seven, six, seven, three and one.
Begin with j and k both six. Text position six contains N, so comparison one fails immediately; the maximum of character jump six and match jump one advances j to twelve.
At position twelve, W matches W; then O matches O at eleven and W matches W at ten. L mismatches W at nine, so this alignment has used four comparisons and the running count is five.

At that mismatch, character L is absent and k is three, giving table suggestions six and six. Increment j from nine to fifteen and reset k to six, then text M mismatches W immediately for comparison six.

M is absent, so an increment of six takes j to twenty-one. The comparisons at twenty-one, twenty and nineteen match W, O and W. Positions eighteen and seventeen then match another W and O, bringing the count to eleven.
At position sixteen, M disagrees with the first pattern W, giving comparison twelve. The bad-character suggestion is six, but match jump at k one is eight, so advance j by eight to twenty-four.

This is why adding the two suggestions would be wrong: eight already describes the safe combined lower limit required here. Reset k to six and begin the next alignment with its right endpoint at twenty-four.

At positions twenty-four, twenty-three and twenty-two, W, O and W match the last three pattern characters. At positions twenty-one, twenty and nineteen, W, O and W match the first three, giving six more comparisons.
Now k has reached zero and j is eighteen, so return j plus one, position nineteen. The alignment counts were one, four, one, six and six, summing to eighteen actual character comparisons.

Naive matching rechecks each next window, Rabin–Karp reuses a rolling hash, and Boyer–Moore reuses mismatch and suffix structure. Skipping many text comparisons can be excellent on suitable inputs, but the shown variant retains a general big O of n m scan upper bound.

The comparison slides mention KMP and practical performance observations without developing its preprocessing algorithm here. Keep such context separate from a proven bound for this exact Boyer–Moore variant, and count table preprocessing separately when its implementation is specified.

Things to take note of: preserve the supplied table convention, decrement both pointers on matches, take the maximum after a mismatch and reset k. Return j plus one only after k reaches zero, keep a genuine comparison counter, and never confuse a moving pointer with a moving alignment, hmph.

lessons.title: What makes a computational task hard?

transcript.text: What makes a computational task hard? We will identify the required output, derive the work of printing a Hanoi solution, and distinguish decision questions from optimisation objectives.

A task can be difficult to understand or code without having a bad asymptotic running time. Complexity analysis instead asks how the required resources grow as the encoded input grows, with a clear statement of what the algorithm must produce.

For Towers of Hanoi, move disks between three pegs without placing a larger disk on a smaller one. The standard recursive method transfers the smaller stack, moves the largest disk, and transfers the smaller stack again.

With three disks, label the source A, destination B and spare C. The seven moves are A to B, A to C, B to C, A to B, C to A, C to B and A to B, with each move involving the only legal top disk for that step.

The move count has base one for one disk and recurrence M of n equals twice M of n minus one plus one. Expanding gives two to the n minus one, so printing every move necessarily requires time proportional to that exponentially long output.

Computing only the number of moves is a different output task from listing them all. The binary representation of two to the n minus one has only n bits, so an output-size argument about the full move list cannot be transferred unchanged to returning that count.

The slide's numerical estimate for sixty-four disks is incorrect, so retain the exact move-count derivation rather than memorising that runtime. An exponential output requirement is concrete evidence for this listing task, while a slow known algorithm alone is not a proof that every algorithm for another task must be slow.
A decision problem asks for yes or no, such as whether a tour has cost at most K. An optimisation problem instead asks for the cheapest valid tour or its minimum cost.

For a spanning tree, the decision question asks whether some spanning tree has total cost at most K. For zero-one knapsack, it asks whether some subset has weight at most C and profit at least K, keeping the two inequalities distinct.

An exact optimisation solver can answer its related threshold question by comparing its optimum with K. Thus a hardness result for the decision version can imply difficulty for exact optimisation, but the formal P and NP definitions here classify decision problems.

Input representation also matters when numbers appear in a problem. A binary capacity has logarithmic encoding length in its numeric value, so an algorithm looping over that entire value needs a different complexity interpretation from one reading an explicitly listed string.

Things to take note of: state the input encoding, output requirement and objective before classifying a task. Distinguish a listing lower bound from a slow known search, preserve threshold inequalities, and avoid calling every inconvenient problem provably exponential, hmph.

source.summary: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: What are P and NP, and what does verification mean?

chapters.title: Candidate rejection is not a no-proof
What is and is not known
Do not infer an unproved separation

transcript.text: What are P and NP, and what does verification mean? We will separate finding a solution from checking a complete certificate, explain why P is contained in NP, and examine a tempting but invalid universal-tour claim.

P contains decision problems solvable by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial worst-case time. A polynomial bound is an asymptotic classification, not a promise that every polynomial algorithm is practical for every input size.

NP contains decision problems whose yes-instances have polynomial-length certificates that a deterministic polynomial-time procedure can verify. The course's equivalent description uses a nondeterministic guess followed by verification, not ordinary random guessing with a guaranteed good outcome.

For a TSP threshold question, a certificate can list a proposed tour. The verifier must check the vertices, all required edges, the closing return and the total cost, rather than accepting because the route merely looks plausible.

A route that repeats a vertex and omits another fails even if it is cheap. A route visiting every vertex also fails if its cost exceeds K, because the certificate must establish the entire yes-condition.

For knapsack, a certificate can specify the selected item indices. Check that no item is repeated, total weight is at most capacity and total profit is at least the requested threshold, with numeric operations accounted for in the representation model.

If one candidate fails verification, only that candidate has been rejected. Another candidate may succeed, so failure of a proposed certificate does not establish that the whole input is a no-instance.

Every problem in P also belongs to NP, because a polynomial verifier can simply run the polynomial solver. It does not need a useful certificate at all, which immediately disproves the idea that NP means not polynomial.

The absence of a known efficient algorithm is not part of the NP membership definition. Whether P equals NP is unresolved in the course framework, so do not draw a strict separation as an established theorem.

Compare the question whether some tour costs at most K with the question whether every tour does. A single cheap tour witnesses the existential yes-condition, but cannot establish that every other tour is cheap.

For the universal question, one expensive tour can instead witness a no-answer. This complementary-certificate observation does not prove that the universal problem lies outside NP or requires exponential time, despite the unsupported claims on the slide.

Certificate length must be polynomial as well as verification time, and the verifier checks a yes-witness for the exact decision predicate. Guessing a whole enormous computation is not useful if merely reading the claimed certificate already exceeds the allowed bound.

Things to take note of: define the decision question, give a complete witness and explain every verification check. Keep solving separate from checking, remember P is inside NP, and never turn a failed witness into a proof of nonexistence, how charming.

source.summary: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: Which direction does a polynomial reduction go?

transcript.text: Which direction does a polynomial reduction go? We will transform an instance of one decision problem into another, preserve its answer, and use a solver diagram to keep the hardness direction straight.
A polynomial many-one reduction computes a transformation f in polynomial time. For every source instance x, x must be a yes-instance of A exactly when f of x is a yes-instance of B.
Imagine being given an algorithm that solves B. To solve A on input x, first transform x into f of x, then run the B solver and return its yes-or-no answer.

This means A is no harder than B under the reduction, or equivalently B is at least as hard as A. The arrow points toward the solver we would like to borrow, not toward the problem we are initially trying to solve.

If B has a polynomial algorithm, combining it with the polynomial transformation gives a polynomial algorithm for A. The transformed instance has polynomial length because a polynomial-time transformation cannot explicitly output more than polynomially many symbols.

For intuition, the deck describes pairing equal-rank elements of two arrays by using sorting. Sort X equal to three, one, two and Y equal to thirty, ten, twenty, then pair one with ten, two with twenty, and three with thirty.

That pairing example illustrates using one algorithm to solve another task, but a formal decision reduction needs the yes-if-and-only-if statement. Likewise, repeatedly calling a factor-finding procedure is an algorithmic reduction illustration, not automatically one many-one decision transformation.

To show a new problem B is hard, start from a problem A already known hard and transform A into B. Then a hypothetical fast B solver would give a fast A solver, transferring the established difficulty to the target.
Reducing B to a known-hard A goes the wrong way for that argument. Easy problems can also reduce to hard ones, so that reverse arrow alone says nothing about B being hard.

A complete proof states the construction, its runtime, and both directions of correctness. Showing one transformed example works demonstrates the construction, but does not prove it preserves the answer on every instance.

Reductions compose: if A reduces to B and B reduces to C, composing the transformations reduces A to C. This transitivity will let one known NP-complete problem transfer hardness without rebuilding reductions from every problem in NP separately.

Things to take note of: keep the instance transformation and the solver call in the same direction, and explicitly preserve yes in both directions. When proving a new problem hard, the known-hard problem is the source; reverse that arrow and your elegant diagram proves the wrong implication, hmph.

source.summary: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How does Hamiltonian path reduce to TSP?

chapters.title: Why the threshold is not n

transcript.text: How does Hamiltonian path reduce to TSP? We will construct a complete weighted graph, choose the correct threshold, and prove both directions instead of relying on one persuasive picture.

A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex exactly once without requiring a return to its start. A Hamiltonian tour additionally closes the route, and that extra closing edge is why the threshold in this construction needs care.

Assume an undirected graph G with at least three vertices, and call its vertex count n. Build a complete graph T on exactly the same vertices, so every missing original connection now also has an edge.
Assign weight one to edges already in G and weight two to the newly added edges. Ask whether T has a Hamiltonian tour of total cost at most n plus one.
In the five-vertex slide graph, original edges are A B, A C, A D, B E, C E and C D. The route E, B, A, C, D visits every vertex once using four original edges, so it is a Hamiltonian path in G.
Close that path from D back to E in the complete graph. The closing edge was absent from G and therefore costs two, giving total four plus two equal to six, which is n plus one.
The forward proof is general: a Hamiltonian path uses n minus one original edges of cost one. Its closing edge costs either one or two, so the resulting tour costs at most n plus one.

For the reverse proof, suppose the transformed graph has a tour costing at most n plus one. A Hamiltonian tour has exactly n edges, each costing at least one, so there is room for at most one weight-two edge.
If the tour includes a weight-two edge, delete that single edge. What remains is a Hamiltonian path using only weight-one edges, all of which belong to the original graph G.
If every tour edge has weight one, remove any one of them instead. Again the remaining route visits all vertices exactly once using original edges, completing the reverse implication.

The construction inspects vertex pairs and assigns their weights in big O of n squared time under a suitable graph representation. Its output size is also polynomial, and the threshold n plus one has a short binary encoding.

Using threshold n would demand that every tour edge already existed in G. That would ask for an original Hamiltonian cycle and could reject a graph that has a Hamiltonian path but needs one missing edge to close it.

Things to take note of: preserve the same vertices, distinguish original and added edges, and prove both directions with the exact threshold n plus one. One added closing edge is allowed, two are not; that simple count is the argument your diagram must actually explain, hmph.

source.summary: Introduction to NP pp22–23, physical p22 visually checked; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.7. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How do we prove NP-completeness?

chapters.title: The consequence of a fast solver

transcript.text: How do we prove NP-completeness? We will separate membership from reduction-based hardness, use SAT as a concrete decision example, and derive the consequence of a polynomial solver for any NP-complete problem.

A decision problem D is NP-complete when it belongs to NP and every problem in NP has a polynomial-time reduction to D. The first condition provides efficiently checked yes-certificates, while the second makes D at least as hard as all NP problems under these reductions.

To prove a new target B NP-complete, normally start by describing a polynomial-length certificate and a polynomial verifier. Then reduce an already known NP-complete problem A to B, preserving yes exactly in both directions.
Why does one known source suffice for the second condition? Every NP problem already reduces to A, and transitivity composes that reduction with the new transformation from A to B.

For SAT, the input is a Boolean formula and the question is whether some assignment makes it true. A proposed assignment is a short certificate that can be checked by evaluating the formula's operations.
Consider A or B, and not A or C, with the two clauses joined by and. Set A true, B false and C true: the first clause is true from A, the second is true from C, and their conjunction is true.

One satisfying assignment proves that this formula is a yes-instance, without needing to find the best assignment or test every possibility. An assignment failing one clause only rejects that candidate, just as in our earlier certificate examples.

The course takes circuit satisfiability as a known NP-complete problem and discusses its reduction to SAT. Together with SAT membership in NP, that supplies the two obligations needed to classify SAT as NP-complete.

The full construction from an arbitrary polynomial verifier to a circuit is explicitly outside this course scope. We use the stated theorem here rather than pretending that a small hand-drawn circuit proves the theorem for all NP problems.

A reduction from a known NP-complete source without a target-membership proof establishes the hardness part only. Conversely, a verifier alone establishes membership but says nothing about being as hard as every other NP problem.

All NP-complete decision problems reduce to one another through polynomial transformations. This equivalence does not mean their best implementations have identical constants, polynomial exponents, or practical behaviour on typical instances.

If even one NP-complete problem has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, every NP problem inherits one through its reduction. Since P is already contained in NP, that would establish P equals NP, whose truth is currently unresolved in this framework.

Things to take note of: classify the decision version, show membership, choose a known NP-complete source and point the reduction toward your target. State the transformation and both correctness directions, then use transitivity; a prestigious problem name is not a substitute for either half of the proof, hmph.

source.summary: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: How can nearest-neighbour TSP miss the best tour?

transcript.text: How can nearest-neighbour TSP miss the best tour? We will trace its locally cheapest moves, include the final return edge, and compare the completed route with a much cheaper feasible tour.

Start at a specified vertex and repeatedly choose its cheapest unvisited neighbour. Keep a visited set, move to the chosen neighbour, and finally return to the starting vertex once every vertex has been visited.
Our four vertices are A, B, C and D, with A B and B C both costing one. Edges A C, A D and B D cost two, while C D costs one hundred, making one late continuation very expensive.
Start at A and choose B, because its edge costs one rather than two. Mark B visited, and consider only vertices that have not already appeared in the partial route.
From B, C costs one and D costs two, so choose C. The partial route A, B, C has cost two, but its cheap prefix has left only D unvisited.
The next move C to D is forced and costs one hundred. Then include the final return D to A costing two, giving a complete greedy tour of one hundred four.
Now inspect the feasible tour A, C, B, D, A instead. Its edge costs are two, one, two and two, for a total of seven, strictly below one hundred four.

One better feasible tour is enough to show the greedy result is not optimal. We do not need an exhaustive optimality proof for the seven-cost route to refute the claim that the one-hundred-four route is always best.

A heuristic aims to find a useful solution quickly without an automatic optimality guarantee. A proven approximation ratio is a different claim and requires explicit assumptions and a theorem, not merely a few successful runs.

This graph does not satisfy the triangle inequality, since the C to D edge is far more expensive than travelling through B. Keep that limitation explicit rather than using this example to assert a theorem about metric TSP variants.

Scanning all unvisited neighbours at each of n steps gives big O of n squared time and linear visited bookkeeping. The graph representation has its own storage cost, and different starting vertices or ties can change the produced tour.
On an incomplete graph, the simple rule can also get stuck or fail to close its tour. Our complete-graph assumption avoids that feasibility issue but does not repair its lack of optimality.

Things to take note of: show the start, visited set, local comparisons and final closing edge. Compare the whole tour with a concrete better route, state ties and graph assumptions, and remember that a cheap beginning can conceal a very expensive ending, how charming.

lessons.title: How does shortest-link TSP differ from Kruskal?

transcript.text: How does the shortest-link TSP heuristic differ from Kruskal? We will scan edges in global weight order, enforce both degree and cycle restrictions, and close a spanning path into a tour.

Unlike nearest neighbour, shortest link considers the globally lightest remaining edge rather than only edges from one current vertex. Accept it only if neither endpoint would exceed degree two and it would not create a premature cycle.

Use five vertices with the first six sorted edges A B one, B C two, A C three, B D four, C D five and D E six. The remaining edges are A E seven, B E eight, A D nine and C E ten, completing the graph.
Accept A B because both endpoints have degree zero and no cycle is possible. Then accept B C, leaving B with degree two and A and C with degree one.
Next consider A C, which would close the three-vertex cycle A B C A. Reject it even though the endpoint degrees would remain at most two, because D and E have not yet joined the tour.
Next consider B D, which would give B a third incident accepted edge. Reject it for the degree rule, even though connecting D would not create a cycle.
C D passes both tests, so accept it and extend the current path. Then D E also passes, giving the spanning path A, B, C, D, E with four accepted edges.
A path spanning all five vertices has exactly two degree-one endpoints, A and E. Add their connecting edge A E to form the final tour; this is the permitted final cycle, not a premature subtour.

The total tour cost is one plus two plus five plus six plus seven, which equals twenty-one. This trace demonstrates the rules and feasibility; it does not prove shortest link always finds an optimal TSP tour.

Kruskal also scans edges globally and rejects cycles, but it permits vertices of degree greater than two. Its goal is a spanning tree, whereas shortest link must maintain path-like pieces and eventually create one Hamiltonian cycle.

Sorting E edges costs big O of E log E, and union-find plus degree counters can check the scan efficiently. With suitable union-find operations, the scan contributes big O of E times inverse Ackermann of V, alongside the sorting cost.

In a complete V-vertex graph, E is order V squared, so edge storage and sorting can be substantial. State tie rules if equal weights occur, and do not claim this heuristic dominates nearest neighbour on every input just because it does better in one example.

Things to take note of: track endpoint degrees and connected components separately, because each rejects a different kind of invalid choice. Stop after the spanning path, include the final closing edge, and distinguish a TSP tour from an MST before borrowing Kruskal's explanation, hmph.

source.summary: Introduction to NP pp32–33; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.12. Fresh five-vertex trace; implementation cost derivation is an explanatory addition. Later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.

lessons.title: Why does density greedy fail for 0/1 knapsack?

transcript.text: Why does density greedy fail for zero-one knapsack? We will reuse our fractional example, enforce whole-item choices, compare the resulting profits and identify exactly where the earlier exchange proof breaks.
The heuristic sorts items by decreasing profit divided by weight. Scan that order, take a whole item if it fits, and otherwise skip it and continue rather than taking a fraction.

Use the weight-profit pairs ten and sixty, twenty and one hundred, and thirty and one hundred twenty. Their densities are six, five and four, so the scan order is exactly the same as in the fractional lesson.
Take item one fully, using ten weight and earning sixty. Item two also fits, so take it, bringing the totals to weight thirty and profit one hundred sixty.
The remaining capacity is twenty, but item three weighs thirty and cannot be divided. Skip it, ending with profit one hundred sixty rather than the fractional answer two hundred forty.

Instead select items two and three, whose weights twenty and thirty exactly fill the bag. Their profits sum to two hundred twenty, already proving that the greedy one-hundred-sixty result is not optimal.

For these three items we can verify the optimum by inspecting all feasible subsets. The best individual profit is one hundred twenty, the other feasible pairs give one hundred sixty and one hundred eighty, and all three exceed capacity, so two hundred twenty is the optimum.

Fractional greedy reaches two hundred forty by taking only twenty of the last item's thirty weight units. The zero-one optimum is two hundred twenty, and the density-greedy zero-one result is one hundred sixty, so these are three different quantities.

The fractional proof exchanged equal small amounts of weight between different materials. Such an exchange may cut an item into forbidden pieces here, so it cannot justify the same density rule for indivisible choices.

Correct implementation updates total weight and profit only when an item is actually accepted. The slide's informal grouping must not be copied as an unconditional weight update after a rejection, because that would incorrectly reduce room for later fitting items.

Sorting takes order n times the logarithm of n, followed by a linear scan through the items. The exact dynamic program uses a table with n item choices and C capacity values, giving order n times C work that depends on the numeric capacity.

An instance where greedy happens to match the optimum cannot establish universal correctness. State whether the question asks you to trace a heuristic, find an exact optimum, or explain a counterexample before choosing which result to report.

Things to take note of: preserve the item variant, skip rather than fractionally fill, continue scanning, and update totals only on acceptance. Compare feasibility and profit explicitly, and do not let an optimal fractional argument smuggle illegal pieces into a whole-item bag, how charming.

transcript.text: What are strings, languages, and the empty string? These are the objects every automaton will read and classify. Confuse a string with a set of strings, and your beautiful proof falls apart before it even begins.
An alphabet is a finite, nonempty set of symbols, usually called Sigma. For this lesson, choose the alphabet containing zero and one. Those are symbols, not numerical values that we are about to add.
A string is a finite sequence of symbols from that alphabet. Take one, then zero, then one, and place them in that order to build the string one zero one. Repetition is allowed, and order matters.

The length of a string counts its symbols, not the number it might represent. One zero one contains three symbols, so its length is three. Even a string beginning with zero keeps that zero in its length.
Now remove every symbol, leaving a sequence of length zero. That sequence is the empty string, written epsilon. Epsilon names the empty sequence; it is not another symbol card hiding in the alphabet.

Do not confuse the empty string with the string containing a single zero. The first has length zero, while the second has length one. Blank space and a zero symbol are rather different things, obviously.
Concatenation joins strings end to end without rearranging their symbols. Let x be one zero, and let y be one. Move y after x to obtain x y, the string one zero one.

Reversing that order gives y x, which is one one zero. So concatenation is generally not commutative: changing the order can change the string. Its length is additive, because two symbols followed by one symbol gives three symbols.

What happens when we concatenate epsilon with one zero one? No symbol is added, so the result is still one zero one, whether epsilon comes first or last. This is why epsilon is the identity for string concatenation.

A language is a set of strings over an alphabet. For example, let L contain exactly the strings zero one and one zero. The braces collect two words into a set; they are not symbols inside either word.

A set ignores the order in which its members are listed, and listing a member twice adds nothing. So reversing the two entries in L leaves the language unchanged. Notice the contrast: rearranging members of a language is harmless, but rearranging symbols inside a string may change the word.

Sigma star means all finite strings over Sigma, including epsilon. Over our binary alphabet, list epsilon first, then zero and one, then zero zero, zero one, one zero, and one one. Continue through longer lengths forever, although every individual string still has finite length.
Our language L has only two strings, while Sigma star contains infinitely many. A language can therefore be finite or infinite. Every language over Sigma is a subset of Sigma star.

Now compare three different objects: epsilon, the empty language, and the language containing only epsilon. Epsilon is one string with length zero. The empty language has no members, while the language containing epsilon has exactly one member.

Consequently, epsilon belongs to the language containing epsilon, but does not belong to the empty language. The membership symbol asks whether a string is an element of a language. The subset symbol instead compares sets, as when we say L is a subset of Sigma star.

We can concatenate languages too, by concatenating every allowed pair of strings. Concatenating L with the language containing only epsilon returns L, because epsilon leaves each string unchanged. Concatenating L with the empty language returns the empty language, because there is no second string to choose.

For any language, star allows concatenations of zero or more of its words. Choosing zero words produces epsilon, even when the language has no words to choose. Therefore, the star of the empty language is the language containing only epsilon, not the empty language.

Things to take note of: a symbol is one alphabet item, a string is a finite sequence, and a language is a set of strings. Epsilon has length zero, but the language containing epsilon has one member. String order matters, set listing order does not, and star always includes epsilon.

Quick check: is the statement that epsilon belongs to the empty language true or false? It is false, because an empty set contains no strings at all. But epsilon does belong to the star of the empty language, because zero repetitions are allowed.

Before moving on, write one string, one language containing it, and that language as a subset of Sigma star. Then explain why concatenating with epsilon preserves a string, while choosing a partner from an empty language is impossible. Keep those object types straight, and the automata lessons become much easier to follow.

lessons.title: How do you write a proof that actually proves the claim?

chapters.title: A proof covers the whole claim
Quantifiers are part of the proof

transcript.text: How do you write a proof that actually proves the claim? A proof must explain why every permitted case satisfies the statement, rather than display a few attractive examples. We will connect two-way set reasoning, induction, and the pigeonhole principle to automata.

Suppose we want to prove that two sets are equal. Showing that every member of the first belongs to the second proves one inclusion only. We must also start with an arbitrary member of the second set and establish the reverse inclusion.

For example, consider the complement of a union. An object is outside the union exactly when it is outside both constituent sets. Expanding membership conditions in both directions proves the De Morgan identity, not just its picture.

An if and only if statement has the same two-way obligation. If you prove that acceptance implies the desired language property, you have ruled out extra accepted words. You must still prove that every desired word is accepted, or your machine could reject everything and satisfy the first implication.

For induction, first identify the quantity that becomes smaller. In automata, it is often the length of the already-read prefix. State the invariant precisely before writing the base case, so the induction hypothesis is something you can actually use.

Take a machine whose state records whether the latest symbol is one. Initially the prefix is empty, so the special start condition must agree with that invariant. If the next symbol is one, enter the one-state; if it is zero, enter the other state, preserving the claim after one additional symbol.

The induction hypothesis does not assume the final result for every word. It assumes the stated property for a shorter prefix, then derives it for the next prefix. Your diagram can guide that step, but a collection of tested inputs cannot replace it.

The pigeonhole principle supplies a different kind of proof. If a run visits more state positions than the machine has states, two positions must contain the same state. In particular, the first p consumed symbols give p plus one visited states when the starting position is included.

Finally, inspect who chooses each object in the statement. Proving that one decomposition fails is not proving that every decomposition fails. When a theorem says there exists a successful split, a contradiction must eliminate every split that obeys its conditions.

Things to take note of. For equality and equivalence, write both directions; for induction, write the base, hypothesis and preservation step. For impossibility proofs, make the arbitrary choices explicit, and never let a true conclusion excuse an invalid argument.

lessons.title: How does a DFA decide whether to accept?

chapters.title: A DFA reads a whole word

transcript.text: How does a deterministic finite automaton decide whether to accept? It reads a finite input one symbol at a time while remembering only its current state. We will trace the language of binary strings ending in one and see exactly when acceptance is tested.

A deterministic finite automaton has five formal components. They are the finite state set, alphabet, transition function, start state and accepting-state set. The transition function assigns exactly one next state to each state and alphabet-symbol pair.

Start in the nonaccepting state before reading anything. That state means the prefix does not end in one, which includes the empty prefix. An empty word is accepted precisely when the start state itself is accepting, so this machine rejects epsilon.

Read the first one of one zero one. The transition takes the state token from the nonaccepting state into the accepting state. The prefix now ends in one, but we have not yet decided the entire input because two symbols remain.

Read zero next. The token returns to the nonaccepting state because the latest symbol is now zero. This move shows why visiting an accepting state somewhere along the run is not sufficient for acceptance.

Read the final one. The token enters the accepting state again, and this time there is no unread input. The whole word one zero one is accepted because its final state belongs to the accepting-state set.

Now compare the shorter word one zero. Its run also visits an accepting state after its first symbol, but ends in the other state. Therefore it is rejected, even though a careless early-stop rule would have accepted it.

To justify the machine generally, state its memory invariant. After every nonempty prefix, it is in the accepting state exactly when the final symbol of that prefix is one. The empty-prefix base case and the two possible next symbols prove this invariant by induction.

A complete transition table must also cover inputs that are not part of your favourite example. If a state has no intended useful continuation, add a rejecting sink with a transition for every alphabet symbol. A missing transition in an informal drawing is not permission to invent a different deterministic semantics.

Things to take note of. Name all five components, identify what each state remembers, and trace every symbol before testing acceptance. Check epsilon, a shortest accepted word and a word that enters an accepting state but later leaves it; those cases expose remarkably many mistakes.

lessons.title: How do you design a DFA from the memory it needs?

transcript.text: How do you design a deterministic automaton from the memory it needs? Consider binary strings containing zero zero one as a substring. Instead of guessing a picture, identify which useful prefixes of that pattern have already been matched.

Before a match is complete, remember the longest suffix that is also a prefix of zero zero one. The possibilities are no useful suffix, a single zero, and two zeros. Add a fourth state for a pattern already found, because future input cannot undo a contained substring.

From no useful suffix, reading zero starts a partial match. Reading one leaves no useful suffix, so stay in the start state. These two transitions cover both possible next symbols without requiring any unbounded memory.

From the single-zero state, another zero extends the remembered suffix to two zeros. A one would produce zero one, which has no nonempty suffix matching the start of our pattern. Therefore that one-transition returns to the no-useful-suffix state.

From two zeros, reading another zero must keep the two-zero state. The full prefix may have three zeros, but its last two zeros remain a useful candidate. Resetting here would lose the overlapping match in zero zero zero one.

Now read one from that two-zero state. The remembered zeros followed by this one complete the target substring, so enter the accepting state. Both later symbols loop there because the occurrence we already found remains inside every extension.

The proof follows the state meanings rather than a list of successful test words. The start state correctly represents the empty prefix, and each transition updates the longest useful suffix or preserves a completed match. Thus the accepting state is reached exactly for prefixes that contain the pattern.

Other languages require different finite memories. Odd parity needs only even and odd states, while equality of zero and one counts modulo three needs the count difference modulo three. Exact unbounded equality cannot be replaced by that modular test, because counts differing by three would pass it.

Change the task to strings ending in zero zero one. The pattern state can no longer be permanently accepting, because another symbol can change the suffix. A small wording change in the language therefore changes the memory update, even when the target pattern is the same.

Things to take note of. Define state meanings first, write every alphabet transition, and use the longest relevant suffix to handle overlaps. Then test the empty word and near misses, and give an invariant explaining why the machine accepts exactly the required language.

lessons.title: How do product, complement and reversal constructions work?

chapters.title: Do not flip an arbitrary NFA
Reverse paths, not input symbols twice

transcript.text: How do product, complement and reversal constructions work? Closure means an operation applied to regular languages produces another regular language. We will construct the new machines and explain what their states mean, rather than memorize a row of yes answers.

Let one machine track the parity of zeros and another track the parity of ones. The product machine stores both current states as one ordered pair. There are four possible pairs, and both components update on the very same input symbol.

For union, mark a pair accepting when either component is accepting. For intersection, require both; for difference, require the first to accept and the second to reject. The transitions need not change, because the pair already records enough information for each Boolean condition.

The product invariant says that after any prefix, each component equals the state its original machine would reach. It holds before reading input and is preserved because each transition applies both original transition functions. The chosen accepting-pair rule therefore proves both directions of the desired language equality.

Complement is simpler, but its hypothesis matters. Complete a deterministic machine and replace its accepting set by the other states, relative to the same alphabet. Since every word has one final state, exactly the previously rejected words become accepted.

A missing transition breaks that simple argument because a word might have no full run in the drawing. Add a rejecting sink before complementing, so those words acquire a final state too. For a nondeterministic machine, merely flipping its accepting states is generally wrong because acceptance is existential over branches.

For reversal, begin with a machine for the original language. Reverse every arrow, make the old start state accepting, and add a fresh start with epsilon arrows to every old accepting state. The result is a nondeterministic machine because several reversed arrows may share a symbol.

An accepting original path reads a word from start to final. Walking that path backwards in the new machine reads the reversed word from an old final to the old start. Conversely, every new accepting path reverses back to an original accepting path, proving equality in both directions.

For a tiny example, the language containing only a followed by b reverses to the language containing only b followed by a. The construction changes the path directions as well as the start and final roles. Reversing arrows without those role changes would answer a different question.

Things to take note of. Products run both machines on one shared word, complement requires a complete deterministic machine, and reversal uses nondeterministic starts. For every closure proof, give the construction and its invariant or accepting-path correspondence, including the empty-word case.

lessons.title: What does nondeterministic acceptance mean?

transcript.text: What does nondeterministic acceptance mean? An automaton may have several possible moves for a symbol, and epsilon moves consume no input. Acceptance requires at least one complete accepting branch, not agreement among branches or a favourable majority.

Use the four-state automaton from the tutorial. State one has an epsilon arrow to two, two loops on b and moves to three on a, three has an epsilon arrow to four, and four returns to one on b. State one starts the computation and only state four is accepting.

Before reading anything, follow any number of epsilon arrows. The active set is one and two, because epsilon reachability includes taking zero moves as well as taking the arrow. Neither state is accepting, so this automaton rejects the empty word.
Now read a. The branch at one has no a-transition and dies, while the branch at two reaches three. Following the epsilon arrow immediately adds four without advancing the input cursor a second time.

An accepting state is now active, but b and a remain unread. This is not acceptance of the whole word yet. Just as with a deterministic automaton, a successful branch must finish the entire input before ending in an accepting state.
Read b next. State three has no matching move, but four reaches one, and its epsilon closure adds two. The active set is therefore one and two again, with only the final a unread.

Read the final a. The active set becomes three and four after epsilon closure, and the input is exhausted. Since four is accepting, the word a b a is accepted, regardless of the branches that died earlier.

Formally, the transition function returns a set of possible next states. It may return the empty set, one state, or several states, and its input alphabet includes epsilon as a bookkeeping option. Epsilon is not a character secretly present inside the word.

Why does flipping accepting states fail to complement an arbitrary nondeterministic automaton? A word can have one branch ending accepting and another ending nonaccepting. Flipping the leaves can leave some accepting branch in both machines, so the word remains accepted instead of changing its verdict.

Things to take note of. Apply epsilon reachability before the first symbol, between consumed symbols and after the last one. Keep all possible states, retire stuck branches, and accept only when some surviving complete branch ends final; never count an epsilon move as consuming input.

lessons.title: How do you turn an epsilon-NFA into a DFA?

chapters.title: One DFA state = one active set

transcript.text: How do you turn an epsilon nondeterministic automaton into a deterministic one? Store the entire active-state set as a single deterministic state. We will build the reachable subset table for the tutorial machine and justify why it recognizes the same words.

The tutorial machine has states one, two and three, with three accepting. On a, one reaches one and two, two reaches three, and three reaches one; on b, only two has a move, looping to itself. There is also an epsilon arrow from two to three.

Start with the epsilon closure of the original start state. Here that is just the singleton containing one, so it is not accepting. In general the closure may contain several states or even an accepting state, and replacing it blindly by the singleton start is a mistake.

From the set containing one, read a. Union all a-targets to get one and two, then follow the epsilon arrow from two to three. Call the resulting set containing all three states B, which is accepting because it contains three.

From A on b there are no targets, giving the empty subset. That is a real deterministic sink state, with both symbols returning to itself. From B, a returns to B, while b reaches two and then its epsilon closure gives C containing two and three.

Now expand C instead of stopping when the table looks convincing. On a, states two and three reach three and one, giving D containing one and three. On b, the loop at two followed by closure returns to C.

Finally expand D. Its a-targets close to B, and it has no b-target, so b reaches the empty sink. No new subsets remain to inspect, giving five reachable deterministic states rather than all eight subsets of a three-element set.

The formal transition rule is closure of the union of all symbol-successors. After every input prefix, the deterministic state equals exactly the nondeterministic active set including free moves. Induction on prefix length proves this statement, so containing an old final state is precisely the correct accepting condition.

Trace a b through the new table as a check. A moves to B on a and then C on b, so the word is accepted. An implementation can construct only reachable subsets, but the general upper bound is still two to the number of original states.

Things to take note of. Compute the initial epsilon closure, union every active state’s next moves, and close again after each consumed symbol. Mark a subset accepting when it intersects the original final set, complete the empty-sink row, and continue until every discovered subset has been expanded.

lessons.title: How do NFAs combine languages by concatenation and star?

chapters.title: Guess the split, preserve old moves
Fresh means unreachable from old states

transcript.text: How do nondeterministic automata combine languages by concatenation and star? Epsilon arrows let a branch choose where one factor ends and the next begins without consuming a symbol. We will build the constructions and expose why star needs a fresh start state.

For concatenation, take a machine for the first language and one for the second. Keep the first start, add epsilon arrows from each first-machine final to the second start, and make only the second-machine finals accepting. The new arrows guess a split of the input into a first-language prefix and a second-language suffix.

Use the tutorial machines: the first recognizes words ending in a, and the second recognizes even-length words. The word a b a has the split a followed by b a, so an accepting branch can leave the first machine after its initial a. The second machine consumes two symbols and finishes accepting.

The first component’s old finals must not remain finals of the combined machine unless the construction provides an accepting second run. Old arrows are retained, so another branch may delay the split. This choice handles every possible factorization instead of committing greedily to the first apparent opportunity.

For correctness, start with an accepted concatenation run and locate the epsilon crossing between components. The consumed prefix belongs to the first language and the remaining suffix to the second. Conversely, accepting runs on any such prefix and suffix can be joined by the new epsilon arrow.

Star allows zero or more factors from one language. Add a fresh accepting start with an epsilon arrow to the old start, and epsilon arrows from old finals back to the old start. Keep the old finals accepting too, so the run may stop after any completed factor.

Why not simply make the old start accepting? Consider the machine whose start moves to a final on a and whose final returns to the start on b, recognizing a followed by repetitions of b a. Declaring the old start final would accept a b even though every nonempty concatenation of original words ends in a.

The fresh start avoids that error because no old transition can revisit it midway through a word. It supplies epsilon for zero factors without changing which old prefixes count as completed factors. The returning epsilon arrows then join only genuinely accepted original words.

An accepting star run can be cut at its restart arrows into accepted factors. Conversely, concatenate accepting factor runs using those arrows, with the new start accepting the zero-factor case. This proves closure without claiming that a nondeterministic branch somehow knows the right factorization in advance.

Things to take note of. Preserve original arrows, keep component state sets disjoint, and distinguish an epsilon control move from consuming an input symbol. For concatenation use the second component’s finals; for star use a fresh accepting start, and prove correctness in both directions.

lessons.title: How do regular expressions describe languages?

transcript.text: How do regular expressions describe languages? A regular expression is syntax assembled from small expressions, while its language is the set of words that syntax describes. We will build expressions from their meanings and check short boundary cases instead of trusting their appearance.

The atomic expression a describes the singleton language containing a. Epsilon describes the singleton containing the empty word, whereas the empty-set expression describes no words. These are different base cases, even though both of the latter may involve no visible input symbols.

Union chooses a word from either operand language. Concatenation chooses one word from each operand and joins them, while star chooses zero or more operand words. In the usual precedence convention, star binds most tightly, followed by concatenation, then union.

Expand the expression zero or epsilon, followed by one or epsilon. There are four combinations of choices, producing epsilon, zero, one, and zero one. The result is not all binary words of length at most two, because one zero and the repeated-symbol pairs are absent.

To describe words that begin with one and end with zero, place an arbitrary binary string between those endpoints. The expression one Sigma star zero includes one zero by choosing the middle word empty. It excludes words of length one, which is correct because a single symbol cannot be both those different endpoints.

For words beginning and ending with the same symbol, endpoint wrapping alone misses a boundary case. Zero Sigma star zero or one Sigma star one handles lengths at least two, but the one-symbol strings zero and one also qualify. Add those two alternatives explicitly, while epsilon remains excluded because it has no first symbol.

At least three ones can be expressed by three required ones separated and surrounded by arbitrary binary strings. Those arbitrary parts may contain more ones, which is exactly what at least permits. Replacing them all with zeros-only stars would impose an unnecessary restriction on where extra ones may occur.

The tutorial comment language illustrates a more delicate boundary condition. A word must have disjoint opening slash-hash and closing hash-slash delimiters, with no hash-slash inside the content. Therefore an empty comment still needs four symbols, and an early closing delimiter cannot be ignored just because another appears later.

Use identities only when their language meanings justify them. Union with the empty language changes nothing, concatenation with epsilon changes nothing, and concatenation with the empty language destroys every possible pair. Star of the empty language is the singleton epsilon because zero factors are still allowed.

Things to take note of. Translate each operation into a choice of words, respect operator precedence, and test epsilon and shortest words. Expressions that look different can describe the same language; examples alone suggest equivalence, while a construction or two-way language argument proves it.

lessons.title: How do you build an NFA from a regular expression?

chapters.title: Star adds zero factors and restarts

transcript.text: How do you build a nondeterministic automaton from a regular expression? Follow the expression’s structure and combine machines for its smaller parts. Our tutorial expression is a b or a, all under star, so every input must decompose into blocks a b or a.

Start with the atomic expression a. Use one start state, one final state and an a-arrow between them, leaving every other transition absent. The machine accepts exactly the one-symbol word a, not epsilon or two copies of a.

Construct a separate two-state machine for b, then concatenate the two machines. Add an epsilon arrow from the a-final to the b-start, keeping only the b-final accepting. The resulting four-state machine consumes a, crosses for free, then consumes b.

The second alternative a needs its own fresh copy of the atomic machine. Sharing states casually could introduce unintended paths between alternatives. A structural construction is meant to work mechanically for every expression, not merely resemble the desired language in this example.

For union, introduce a new start with epsilon arrows to the two branch starts. Keep both branch finals accepting, so one complete accepting branch is enough. A word cannot take half the a b branch and then jump into the other branch, because no such edge was added.

Now apply star using another fresh accepting start. Link it to the union start by epsilon, and add epsilon restarts from both old finals to the union start. Keep the old finals accepting, so a completed last block need not restart before the word ends.

Trace a b a by choosing the a b branch first. After consuming those two symbols, restart at the union start and take the one-symbol a branch. The last symbol is consumed in a final state, matching the factorization a b followed by a.

The empty word uses zero repetitions and is accepted immediately at the fresh start. The word b has no valid first block, so every possible branch fails. The word a a is accepted as two a blocks, showing why choosing the shortest-looking alternative greedily is not the definition of the machine.

The general proof is structural induction. Atomic fragments recognize their base languages, and each union, concatenation or star construction preserves the corresponding language operation. Therefore the final automaton recognizes the meaning of the entire expression, not merely the examples we traced.

Things to take note of. If the question requests the inductive construction, show the intermediate machines even if a smaller one is obvious. Distinguish absent transitions from epsilon arrows, rename components to avoid collisions, and preserve the accepting-state rules for each operator.

lessons.title: How does GNFA state elimination produce a regular expression?

transcript.text: How does generalized-automaton state elimination produce a regular expression? Replace each removed state by labels describing every possible journey through it. We will use the tutorial automaton for an even number of ones, where the original start is also accepting.

First add a fresh start s and a fresh sole final f. Connect s to the old start by epsilon, and connect each old final to f by epsilon. Since q one was both the old start and the old final, it receives both links but loses its special accepting designation in the generalized machine.

Suppose we remove an internal state r between surviving states i and j. A path can either avoid r, or enter it, loop there any number of times, then leave it. Therefore replace the old direct label by its union with entering label, loop star, and exiting label in that order.

Remove q two first as the tutorial requests. From q one, entry into q two reads one, its self-loop reads zero, and exit back reads one. Those journeys describe one zero star one, which must be unioned with q one’s existing zero-loop.

The epsilon arrow from s to q one remains unchanged because s had no direct way into q two. The epsilon arrow from q one to f also remains unchanged because q two had no arrow to f. Empty-set labels make those impossible detours contribute no words.

Now remove q one. The only accepting route enters by epsilon, takes its loop any number of times, then exits by epsilon. The final expression is zero or one zero star one, all under star, with the redundant epsilon factors removed.

Each block of the final expression contributes either no ones or exactly two ones. Conversely, a word with an even number of ones can pair successive ones, grouping the zeros between each pair into that pair’s block. Zeros outside pairs become single zero blocks, proving the expression describes precisely the even-parity language.

The empty string and the single symbol zero are accepted. Reading one then zero then one gives another accepted word, as does one then one then zero, while a single one or one followed by zero is rejected. An expression that omits the empty string fails for this machine, whose original start state was accepting.

A different removal order may produce a differently shaped expression. Correctness depends on preserving all paths with the update rule, not on matching one printed expression character for character. Never remove the designated new start or final, and never mix already-updated and old labels within one removal.

Things to take note of. Initialize the generalized machine carefully, including the case where the old start is final, and use union of direct and through-state paths. Preserve parentheses and empty-set labels, then check the final expression against the original language; the full excluded appendix proof is not needed to perform the construction.

lessons.title: How do you use the regular pumping lemma correctly?

chapters.title: All legal y have one form

transcript.text: How do you use the regular pumping lemma correctly? We will prove that equal blocks of zeros followed by ones cannot be recognized by any finite automaton. The crucial issue is who chooses the split, not whether we can find one convenient split to break.

If a language is regular, some pumping length p works for every sufficiently long word in it. Each such word has some decomposition x y z with y nonempty and x y of length at most p. Every repetition count, including zero, must keep that chosen decomposition inside the language.

The repeated-state proof explains these conditions. The first p symbols of an accepted run visit p plus one state positions, forcing a repeated state among p states. The nonempty intervening segment is a loop that can be removed or repeated without changing the final destination.

Assume equal-block language regular and let p be its alleged pumping length. Choose the word with p zeros followed by p ones, which belongs to the language and has length at least p. We choose this witness, but the lemma gets to supply the decomposition.

Take any legal decomposition of that witness. Because the first p positions are zeros and x y ends within them, y consists of k zeros for some k between one and p. This covers every permitted decomposition, not just the split where y happens to be the whole first block.

Now choose zero repetitions. Removing y leaves p minus k zeros followed by p ones, so the two block counts are different. Since k is positive, the pumped word is outside the language for every legal split, contradicting the lemma.

For a picture, use four zeros and four ones, with a loop piece containing two zeros. Removing that piece leaves two zeros and four ones, visibly breaking equality. That illustration helps you see the mechanism, but the proof is the arbitrary-k argument, not this single numerical split.

A common wrong proof declares x empty and y equal to all p zeros. It correctly breaks that one split, but the lemma only promised some successful split and could have chosen another. A true nonregularity conclusion does not rescue that quantifier mistake.

The lemma is necessary for regularity, not sufficient. Some nonregular languages still satisfy its pumping conclusion, so failure to find a contradiction does not establish regularity. For positive regularity, construct a finite automaton or expression; for another negative tool, use distinguishable prefixes.

Things to take note of. State the lemma correctly, verify witness membership and length, and describe every legal decomposition before choosing a repetition count. End with explicit failed membership and contradiction, and remember that zero repetitions are allowed even though the repeated piece itself must be nonempty.

lessons.title: When should you combine pumping with closure?

chapters.title: Choose a tool that forces failure
Trap the new length between squares

transcript.text: When should you combine pumping with closure? A difficult-looking language may expose a familiar nonregular core after complementing or intersecting with a simple regular filter. We will compare unequal block counts, related inequalities, and perfect square lengths over a one-symbol alphabet to learn how to choose the argument.

Let L consist of zeros followed by ones with unequal block counts. Directly adding more zeros often leaves the inequality true, so an arbitrary pump direction is unhelpful. Instead suppose L regular and isolate its equal-count complement inside the ordered-block words.

The complement alone contains many out-of-order words, so it is not yet the equal-block language. Intersecting with zero star one star removes those words and leaves exactly equal blocks. Regular closure would make that language regular, contradicting the pumping proof we already know.

Now consider zero-block length at least one-block length. Choose p zeros followed by p ones, lying on the boundary of the inequality. Pumping up zeros keeps the condition true, but pumping down makes the first block shorter than the unchanged second block.

For matching outer blocks, a useful witness is p zeros, one separating one, and p zeros. Every legal loop lies in the first zero block, so removing it changes only the left outer count. The unique separator prevents the pumped word from being reinterpreted using a different middle-block length.

For unary square lengths, use a word containing p squared copies of one. Any legal repeated piece has length k between one and p. Pumping it twice gives length p squared plus k, so we need an arithmetic argument that this new length is not another square.

The new length is strictly above p squared and at most p squared plus p. That is still below the next square, p plus one squared, whose gap is two p plus one. Therefore the pumped word lies between consecutive legal lengths and cannot belong to the language.

For a numerical illustration, p equal to three gives length nine. Pumping a two-symbol loop once more produces length eleven, between nine and sixteen. The general proof works for every loop length up to p, not merely for that two-symbol example.

For complements of palindrome languages, another closure route is available. If nonpalindromes were regular then palindromes would be regular too, but the witness p zeros, one, p zeros breaks under pumping in its first block. Carefully state which language you are assuming regular and which known contradiction you derive.

Things to take note of. Pick a witness on a fragile boundary, and choose pumping up or down to leave the language rather than preserve it. When using complement, specify the alphabet and filter out unwanted shapes; for numerical languages, prove a gap containing the pumped length.

lessons.title: How does Myhill–Nerode measure the memory a DFA needs?

chapters.title: The index is the minimum state count

transcript.text: How does the Myhill Nerode theorem measure the memory a deterministic automaton needs? Two prefixes require different memories when some common continuation makes exactly one resulting word belong to the language. We will use that idea both for impossibility and for an exact state lower bound.

If a deterministic machine reaches the same state after x and y, it must react identically to every later suffix. Thus one distinguishing suffix proves those prefixes cannot share a state. A set of pairwise distinguishable prefixes gives a lower bound on the number of states.

For equal zeros followed by equal ones, consider every prefix consisting only of zeros. Take two different lengths n and m, and append n ones to both. The first result has matching counts, while the second does not, so this single suffix distinguishes that arbitrary pair.

There are infinitely many prefixes in that pairwise distinguishable set. No finite-state machine can assign all of them different states, so the language is nonregular. Unlike a failed pumping attempt, this directly establishes an unbounded memory requirement.

Formally, indistinguishability means every appended suffix gives the same membership verdict. This is an equivalence relation, partitioning all words into classes. The theorem says regularity is equivalent to finitely many classes, and the number of classes equals the smallest possible deterministic-state count.

For an exact finite example, take the language containing only a over the unary alphabet. A machine needs a start state, a final state after one a, and a sink after too many symbols. This gives a three-state upper bound, but drawing three states alone does not prove they are necessary.

Use epsilon, a, and a a as the three distinguishing prefixes. The suffix epsilon separates a from each other prefix, because only a is already in the language. The suffix a separates epsilon from a a, producing a versus three copies of a.

Every pair in the three-element set is distinguished, so every deterministic machine for this language needs at least three states. Together with the three-state construction, that proves the machine minimal. A lower bound and matching upper bound are both needed for an exact answer.

The suffix may depend on the chosen pair; there is no requirement that one suffix separate the entire set at once. But distinguishing just adjacent members of an infinite sequence is insufficient unless you also cover every other distinct pair. Keep those quantifiers explicit in your proof.

Things to take note of. State the prefix set, take an arbitrary distinct pair, and give one common suffix with opposite membership outcomes. Use an infinite set for nonregularity, or combine a finite lower bound with a matching construction for minimality; the excluded appendix proof does not remove the need to apply the theorem.

lessons.title: Why are prime-length unary strings nonregular?

chapters.title: The proof is not numerical sampling

transcript.text: Why are prime-length unary strings nonregular? This harder companion follows the tutorial’s requested Myhill Nerode proof rather than replacing it with a different method. We will use the number-theory theorem supplied in the question to construct a suffix for every pair of prime-length prefixes.

The supplied theorem says an arithmetic progression with positive coprime initial term and step contains infinitely many primes. We need that statement as a tool, not a proof of the theorem itself. Its coprimality hypothesis will come from choosing two distinct primes.

Choose X to be the language itself, all unary words of prime length. Take arbitrary different members with prime lengths n and m. Distinct primes have greatest common divisor one, so the progression starting at n with step m satisfies the theorem’s hypotheses.

There are infinitely many prime terms in that progression, so choose one with k at least one. Define z to be k times m copies of zero. Appending the same z to both prefixes will now produce lengths with deliberately different arithmetic structures.
The word x z has length n plus k m, which was chosen prime. Therefore x z belongs to the prime-length language. This is the positive membership half of the distinguishing argument.

The word y z has length m plus k m, equal to k plus one times m. Both factors are at least two because k is positive and m is prime. Its length is therefore composite, so y z does not belong to the language.

For an illustration, choose n equal to two and m equal to three. Taking k equal to one gives a three-zero suffix, producing length five from the first prefix and length six from the second. Five is prime while six is composite, but the theorem is what covers every arbitrary prime pair.

We have distinguished every two distinct members of X. Since there are infinitely many primes, X is infinite, so the language has infinite index. The Myhill Nerode theorem then implies it cannot be regular.

Do not claim that testing several small prime lengths establishes the result. Nor does a failed pumping attempt imply that the language is regular. This proof works because it gives an arbitrary-pair suffix and verifies both membership outcomes under a stated theorem.

Things to take note of. Separate the provided number-theory fact from the automata argument, choose two distinct prime lengths, and use a positive progression index. The same appended unary suffix makes one length prime and the other composite, giving the required infinite-index contradiction.
