lessons.title: How do context-free grammars generate a language?

transcript.text: How do context-free grammars generate a language? A grammar repeatedly replaces a variable by the right side of one of its rules until only terminals remain. We will build equal blocks, compare middle-symbol and palindrome grammars, and explain why a grammar needs both productive rules and a base case.

Take the grammar with start variable S and rules S becomes zero S one, or epsilon. The wrapping rule adds one zero on the left and one one on the right. The epsilon rule ends the recursion, allowing the counts to stay equal without leaving an unfinished variable.

To derive zero zero one one, first wrap S once and then wrap the remaining S again. The sentential form becomes zero zero S one one. Replacing the last S by epsilon gives the desired terminal word without adding another symbol.

A parse tree records which production expanded each variable. Reading its terminal leaves from left to right gives the final word, while the substitution order is not itself a new tree. Use an arrow for a production, a double arrow for a derivation step, and a starred double arrow for zero or more steps.

To prove the grammar correct, show both directions. Every wrap contributes one zero and one one in the required order, so every generated word has the desired form. Conversely, any target word with n matched pairs is generated by n wraps followed by the base rule.

Now construct odd-length words whose middle symbol is zero. Start with the one-symbol base zero and allow any binary symbol on either side of the recursive variable. Each wrapping adds two symbols without changing the central zero, so the endpoints need not match.

For palindromes, the wrapper must instead use the same symbol at both ends. Rules zero S zero and one S one preserve mirrored equality, with epsilon or a single symbol supplying the even or odd base case. A grammar for middle-zero words is therefore not automatically a palindrome grammar.

A regular language can also be generated by a grammar. Make one variable per deterministic state, replace a transition on a by a rule that emits a and moves to the target variable, and allow epsilon from accepting-state variables. A terminal derivation then mirrors a run ending in an accepting state.

When combining grammars for a union, rename their variables to keep the components disjoint. Introduce a fresh start that chooses either component start, preserving all original productions. Reusing a variable name for unrelated meanings can silently add derivations outside either original language.

Things to take note of. State variables, terminals, productions and start; include a terminating base case; and check that every target word can be derived without generating extras. Keep the distinction between a word, an unfinished sentential form, a derivation order and a parse tree clear before discussing ambiguity.

lessons.title: What makes a grammar ambiguous?

chapters.title: Different order can mean one tree
Encode precedence with E, T, F

transcript.text: What makes a grammar ambiguous? One word must have two different parse trees, equivalently two different leftmost derivations. Two arbitrary substitution orders are not enough, because they may simply construct the same tree in a different order.

Consider E becoming E plus E, E times E, a parenthesized E, or a. The word a plus a times a can be grouped as a plus the product, or as a sum multiplied by a. Both structures are permitted because the grammar does not encode precedence.

For the first structure, expand the root using addition. Finish the left E as a, then expand the right E into a product and finish its two operands. The leftmost derivation therefore begins with E plus E and ends with a plus a times a.

For the second structure, expand the root using multiplication. Its left child becomes a sum, and the leftmost variable is always completed before any variable to its right. This derivation reaches the same terminal word through a different root production, guaranteeing a genuinely different tree.

The two trees differ at their roots, so they are not just two schedules for expanding one structure. Both yields read a plus a times a from left to right, even though the implicit groupings differ. That single witness proves the grammar ambiguous; we do not need every word to be ambiguous.

To see the wrong argument, take the simple grammar S becomes A B, with A becoming a and B becoming b. Expanding A before B or B before A gives two derivations of a b. There is still only one parse tree, so those derivations do not prove ambiguity.

An expression grammar can enforce precedence by using separate levels for expressions, terms and factors. Addition combines expressions and terms, while multiplication stays inside terms, and factors are atoms or parenthesized expressions. This prevents the competing root multiplication for an unparenthesized sum such as our witness.

Under that grammar, multiplication binds more tightly than addition. Repeated left-recursive additions also fix their grouping rather than creating arbitrary associative parse trees. If you are asked for a leftmost derivation, replace the leftmost remaining variable at every step and show the whole requested word.

Ambiguity belongs to a particular grammar. A language is inherently ambiguous only when every grammar generating it is ambiguous, which is a much stronger statement. Showing that this expression grammar is ambiguous does not prove inherent ambiguity, since the precedence grammar generates the same language without that defect.

Things to take note of. Name one terminal witness and give two different trees or two distinct leftmost derivations for it. Check that their yields agree and their structures differ; merely changing the order of independent substitutions proves nothing about ambiguity.

lessons.title: How do you convert a grammar to Chomsky normal form?

transcript.text: How do you convert a grammar to Chomsky normal form? Allowed productions are a variable becoming two variables or a single terminal, with a special start-to-epsilon exception. We will follow the lecture’s four stages and derive the exact number of production applications for a nonempty word.

The lecture example begins with S becoming A S A or a B, A becoming B or S, and B becoming b or epsilon. Add a fresh start S zero with a unit rule to the old S. The fresh start will never appear on any right-hand side, preserving the special start condition through later transformations.

Identify nullable variables before discarding epsilon rules. Here B is nullable, so a B can also produce a and A can become nullable through B. Removing nullable A occurrences from A S A adds S A and A S, as well as the unit rule S becomes S.

The old S is not nullable, because every terminating derivation still produces at least one a. Therefore this example does not acquire an empty-word rule just because the original B had one. In a grammar whose language does contain epsilon, preserve it only through the permitted fresh-start rule.

Next eliminate unit rules by copying all reachable non-unit alternatives. Remove the useless self-rule S becomes S, replace S zero becoming S, and propagate the non-unit options through A becoming B or S. Stopping after replacing one visible unit arrow can miss a longer chain of unit reachability.

Finally split long right sides into binary ones and isolate terminals mixed with variables. Introduce A one becoming S A, so A S A can be replaced by A A one. Introduce U becoming a, so a B becomes U B, keeping already legal single-terminal rules unchanged.

Check the resulting rules individually. S zero and S can become A A one, U B, a, S A or A S; A has those options plus b, and B becomes b. Every right side is now either exactly two variables or exactly one terminal, and S zero is never on a right side.

For a word of length n at least one, a binary Chomsky-form parse tree has n terminal-producing leaves. It requires n minus one binary branch expansions to grow from one variable to n variable leaves, and then n terminal productions. The total is exactly two n minus one production applications, independent of their order.

For instance, deriving a b from S zero through U B takes three applications: the binary production and the two terminal productions. This matches twice two minus one. A finite derivation-length bound makes exhaustive membership search finite, but does not by itself make that exhaustive search polynomial.

Things to take note of. Preserve nullable alternatives and unit reachability before binarizing, and keep the fresh start off right-hand sides. Chomsky normal form is different from conjunctive normal form in SAT; the appendix’s excluded theorem proof does not exclude performing this conversion or using the two n minus one consequence.

lessons.title: How does a pushdown automaton use its stack?

transcript.text: How does a pushdown automaton use its stack? It combines finite control with an unbounded last-in-first-out memory. We will trace equal blocks of zeros and ones, decoding each read, pop and push operation instead of treating epsilon as a mysterious empty-stack test.

A label has three separate slots: input read, stack symbol popped, and stack symbol pushed. Epsilon in a slot means no operation in that slot. In particular, an epsilon pop means do not inspect or remove a stack symbol, not that the stack is empty.

Initialize the equal-block machine by pushing a fresh dollar marker without consuming input. The marker separates the bottom from all zeros we will count. This is a genuine stack operation even though the input cursor stays at the beginning.

Read the first zero and push a zero above the marker. Read another zero and push another copy, so the stack records exactly how many initial zeros remain unmatched. These moves need no pop or prior top-symbol test.

At the first one, switch from the pushing phase to the popping phase. Read that one and pop one zero, matching one symbol from each block. The stack now contains one zero above the marker, with one final one still unread.

Read the final one and pop the remaining zero. The marker is now exposed and no input remains, so the machine may pop the marker and enter its final state. If extra ones remained, there would be no zero left to match them, and that branch could not accept.

For zero zero one, the input ends while a zero remains above the marker, so the final marker-pop move is unavailable. For zero one zero one, a zero arrives after the popping phase began, where no zero-reading continuation is provided. Equal counts alone are insufficient; the required block order matters too.

The case n equal to zero requires accepting epsilon. The lecture’s machine makes its original start accepting for exactly this purpose, while its later final state handles nonempty matched blocks. Being at a final state never authorizes ignoring unread input.

The general formal definition accepts by final state after complete input consumption. It does not demand an empty final stack for every possible pushdown automaton. Some constructions, including the grammar-equivalence normalization, deliberately arrange empty-stack acceptance as an additional invariant.

Things to take note of. Decode the three transition slots independently, write every intermediate stack with its top on the left, and include the epsilon moves in your trace. Explain both the unmatched-count invariant and the phase restriction, then check epsilon, too few ones, too many ones and wrong-order inputs.

lessons.title: How does a PDA guess the middle of a palindrome?

chapters.title: Choose transitions for the requested parity
Middle-zero needs counts, not matching bits
01011 has middle 0, but is not a palindrome

transcript.text: How does a pushdown automaton guess the middle of a palindrome? It pushes a prefix, nondeterministically chooses where to switch phases, and compares the suffix with that prefix in reverse. A correct midpoint guess can accept even when other guesses get stuck.

For the even palindrome zero one one zero, first push a bottom marker and then the initial zero and one. The stack top is now one, followed by zero and the marker. This reversed order is precisely what the remaining one zero should match.

Guess the even-length midpoint without consuming input or changing the stack. The epsilon read, epsilon pop, epsilon push transition only changes the finite-control phase. It is a guess rather than an empty-stack test, and a wrong early or late guess will fail later matching.

Read the next one and pop the matching one, then read zero and pop zero. The marker is exposed exactly as the input ends, so the branch can finish accepting. A different suffix such as zero one would mismatch the top and kill this branch.

For the odd palindrome zero one zero, push the first zero but consume the middle one while switching phases. Do not push that middle symbol, because it has no partner on the other side. The final zero then matches and pops the single stored zero.

To recognize all binary palindromes, provide both the even epsilon switch and odd switches reading zero or one. Epsilon is handled by guessing an empty first half and an even switch. If the language asks only for even palindromes, the odd-switch transitions must be omitted.

Now change the language to odd-length words with middle symbol zero. We still use the stack to compare half lengths, but no longer compare symbol values. Push one counting marker per initial symbol, switch only by reading zero, then pop one marker per remaining symbol of either kind.

For example, zero one zero one one has length five and central zero, despite not being a palindrome. A counter-stack branch can push for its first two symbols, consume the central zero and pop for the last two. A palindrome stack would instead reject when the right symbols fail to mirror the left.

Pushdown nondeterminism is not automatically removable in the way finite-automaton nondeterminism is. Deterministic pushdown automata recognize a strictly smaller class than nondeterministic ones. The unmarked midpoint is an important reason the general palindrome construction uses a guess.

Things to take note of. A stack reverses the stored prefix, even and odd midpoint transitions consume different amounts of input, and every accepted branch must finish the word. Distinguish palindrome symbol matching from middle-position length matching, and keep the requested parity and base cases explicit.

lessons.title: How does a PDA simulate a grammar?

chapters.title: Push right side in reverse operational order

transcript.text: How does a pushdown automaton simulate a grammar? Keep the unfinished part of a guessed leftmost derivation on the stack, expanding variables and matching terminals to input. We will compile S becoming zero S one or epsilon into a machine and trace zero zero one one.

Initialize the stack with S above a fresh dollar marker. An epsilon move can replace a top variable by the right side of any production for that variable. For our grammar, the choices are replacing S by zero S one or removing S using its epsilon production.

The push-string shorthand must leave the first right-side symbol on top. To push zero S one using single-symbol operations, push one first, then S, then zero. Pushing in written order would reverse the intended unfinished word and would not simulate the grammar.

From stack zero S one dollar, read the first zero and pop that same terminal. The remaining stack is S one dollar. The invariant says the consumed prefix followed by the stack’s unfinished portion is a sentential form of a guessed derivation.

Expand the remaining S once more using the wrapping rule. Because a one was already below it, the new stack is zero S one one dollar. Read and pop the next zero, leaving S one one dollar while the unread input is one one.
Now choose the epsilon production for S. Removing the variable leaves two terminal ones on the stack, exactly the unread suffix. Match and pop each one, exposing the bottom marker with no input left.

The final move pops the marker and enters the accepting state. It succeeds as an accepting computation only after the entire input has been read. Replacing the marker test by epsilon pop would allow leaving unmatched generated terminals on the stack.

The tutorial’s wrong construction accepts zero zero one even though a generated one remains unmatched. Its final epsilon, epsilon to epsilon arrow ignores the stack entirely and can fire anyway. The dollar-marker condition prevents that false acceptance, rather than merely decorating the diagram.

For correctness, an accepting machine run records a successful sequence of grammar expansions and terminal matches, so its input is generated. Conversely, follow a leftmost derivation and choose exactly its productions to obtain an accepting branch. Other branches may get stuck or expand forever, which is harmless for existential recognition.

Things to take note of. Distinguish variable expansion from terminal matching, use reverse primitive push order, and keep the consumed-prefix plus unfinished-stack invariant. Acceptance needs both input exhaustion and the marker-based finish; a guessed production is not knowledge of the correct derivation.

lessons.title: How does a grammar simulate a PDA?

chapters.title: A_pq means empty-stack p to q
Normalization: one stack action per move

transcript.text: How does a grammar simulate a pushdown automaton? Introduce one variable for each ordered pair of control states, representing words that take the machine between them with empty stack at both endpoints. The construction works after a careful normalization, not by assigning one variable to each transition informally.

First arrange one accepting state and an empty stack before entering it. A fresh bottom marker and a draining phase can remove leftover stack symbols before the sole final transition. This preserves final-state acceptance without pretending the original machine already used the same convention.

Next require every move to push exactly one symbol or pop exactly one symbol, never both and never neither. Split a combined pop and push through a fresh state. Replace a no-stack action by a dummy push followed by a matching pop, preserving the original input consumption on the first step.

The wrapping rule pairs a push of symbol u with a later pop of that same symbol. If the push reads a and goes from p to r, while the pop reads b and goes from s to q, add A p q becoming a A r s b. The inner variable describes a computation above the untouched pushed symbol.

The other rule families handle splitting and the base case. For every intermediate state r, let the variable indexed by p and q expand into the variable indexed by p and r followed by the one indexed by r and q, concatenating two empty-stack computations. For each state p, its p-to-p variable also generates epsilon, representing a zero-step run.

Use the tutorial fragment for w c reverse-w. In the pushing state p, reading a or b pushes that same symbol; in state q, reading a or b pops its matching symbol. Pairing these moves yields A p q becoming a A p q a, or b A p q b.

The middle c move from p to q originally changes no stack symbol. Normalize it to a c-reading dummy push into r followed by an epsilon dummy pop into q. The matched rule gives A p q becoming c A r r, and the base rule reduces that to c.

Derive a b c b a by wrapping first with a, then with b, then choosing the central c. The corresponding machine pushes a, pushes b, reads c to switch phases, then pops b and a. Both sides therefore encode the same nested matching order.

The fragment explains the principal rules without listing every auxiliary variable of the fully normalized accepting machine. In the full construction, all state pairs and rule families are included, and unreachable variables do not change the start variable’s language. Do not confuse this explanatory fragment with a claim that normalization adds no states.

Things to take note of. State what each A p q means, normalize acceptance and stack actions, and use matched wrapping, splitting and zero-step rules. Match the pushed symbol to the popped symbol and justify the chosen start variable; a plausible grammar alone is not the requested mechanical construction.

lessons.title: Why is the PDA-to-CFG construction correct?

chapters.title: Replay above an untouched stack prefix
Claim 2: split at an empty return
Why the case split is exhaustive

transcript.text: Why is the pushdown-to-grammar construction correct? We must prove that generated words correspond to empty-stack computations and that every such computation can be generated. These directions use different induction parameters, so keep the claims separate rather than hiding everything under the phrase by induction.

Recall the normalization: one accepting state, empty stack at acceptance, and each move pushing or popping exactly one symbol. A variable A p q is intended to generate words taking p empty to q empty. Its rules wrap a matched push and pop, split at an empty intermediate state, or generate epsilon from A p p.

First prove the grammar-to-machine direction by induction on derivation length. The base case is a single production A p p becoming epsilon. A zero-step machine computation consumes epsilon and leaves state p and empty stack unchanged, so it realizes that generated word.

For a longer derivation, inspect its first rule. If it is a matched wrapping rule, the inner variable has a shorter derivation of a word y. By the induction hypothesis, y takes r empty to s empty; replay those moves above the pushed symbol u, then pop u at the end.

The replay is legitimate because the inner run never needs to inspect below its own stack content. The unchanged lower symbol simply remains underneath until the inner run returns to its baseline. The outer push and matching pop then produce exactly the endpoints required by A p q.

If the first rule is a splitting rule, write the generated word as y z. Each child has a shorter derivation, so the induction hypothesis gives an empty-stack run from p to r on y and one from r to q on z. Concatenate the two runs at their common empty-stack configuration.

Now prove machine-to-grammar by induction on the number of computation moves. A zero-move run has p equal to q and consumes epsilon. The base production A p p becoming epsilon generates exactly that case.

Consider a positive-length empty-to-empty run that never empties its stack strictly between its endpoints. Its first move pushes some symbol u, and that bottom symbol cannot be removed until the last move. Those outer moves form a matched push-pop pair, with a shorter inner computation after stripping off the untouched bottom u.

Apply the induction hypothesis to that shorter inner run from r empty to s empty. It gives a derivation from A r s of the consumed inner word y. The matched wrapping rule then derives a y b from A p q, including the possibility that either outer input label is epsilon.

If instead the stack becomes empty at some intermediate state r, split the run there. Both pieces use fewer moves than the entire run, so induction gives derivations from A p r and A r q. The splitting production joins their generated words, covering the other possible shape of computation.

These two cases exhaust positive normalized empty-to-empty runs. Either the stack first returns to zero at the end, or it has a strictly intermediate zero-height return. Normalization is what rules out a no-stack move that would evade the push-pop case analysis.

Things to take note of. Use derivation length in the first direction and computation moves in the second, with their correct base cases. Explain replay above an untouched bottom, show why subproblems are shorter, and conclude equality for the start variable; these proofs are explicit lecture outcomes, not the excluded normal-form appendix.

lessons.title: How do you prove a language is not context-free?

chapters.title: The short window misses a block

transcript.text: How do you prove that a language is not context-free? The context-free pumping lemma repeats two pieces of a word together, reflecting a repeated variable in a parse tree. We will apply it to three equal blocks and keep its quantifiers separate from the regular-language version.

For a context-free language, every sufficiently long member has a split u v x y z. The pieces v and y are pumped by the same exponent, at least one is nonempty, and the entire middle window v x y has length at most p. That window is not required to begin at the start of the input.

The parse-tree intuition explains why two pieces repeat. A sufficiently tall derivation repeats a variable on one root-to-leaf path, and replacing the smaller repeated-variable subtree by the larger one adds material on both sides. Removing that outer expansion corresponds to exponent zero, while repeating it corresponds to larger exponents.

The formal proof uses a smallest parse tree for the chosen word and a repeated variable near the bottom of a longest path. A bounded branching factor gives a finite pumping length and bounds the selected subtree’s yield. Minimality prevents both flanking yields from being empty, because otherwise the larger subtree could be removed without changing the word.

Assume the three-equal-block language is context-free and choose a to the p, b to the p, c to the p. It belongs to the language and is long enough for the lemma. Now take an arbitrary permitted five-piece decomposition rather than choosing favourable v and y yourself.

A window of length at most p cannot touch all three blocks. Reaching an a and a c would already require crossing all p copies of b plus at least two other symbols. Thus v and y together can change counts in at most two adjacent blocks, leaving at least one count unchanged.

Pump with exponent two. If each pumped piece contains only one symbol type, at least one count increases because their total length is positive, while an untouched count remains p. The result cannot have all three counts equal, so it is outside the language.

If either pumped piece crosses a block boundary, repeating it also introduces an out-of-order alternation such as b followed by a. Then the result fails the required a-star b-star c-star shape even before comparing counts. These cases cover every legal decomposition, including a split with one pumped piece empty.

The contradiction disproves the existence of a context-free grammar for this language. It does not say that one particular attempted grammar happened to fail. The bounded window and synchronized exponent are the structural facts making the impossibility argument work.

Things to take note of. State the five-piece lemma with a bounded middle window, pump v and y by the same exponent, and allow either one to be empty but not both. Verify witness membership, handle every window case, and identify an explicit count or order violation rather than saying the pieces look different.

lessons.title: How do you handle harder CFL pumping cases?

chapters.title: C = {w#t : w is a substring of t}
Case 2: pumping only the left word
Case 3: pumping only the right word
One empty piece is already covered

transcript.text: How do you handle harder context-free pumping cases? Consider words w hash t where w must appear as a contiguous substring of t. We will use the witness a to the p b to the p, hash, a to the p b to the p, and organize every split around the separator.

Assume this language is context-free with pumping length p. Our witness belongs because its left word is exactly its right word, and its length is at least p. Take an arbitrary legal u v x y z split, remembering that either v or y may be empty.

If a pumped piece contains the hash, choose exponent zero. The only separator disappears, so the result is not even a correctly formed w hash t word. This covers either v or y containing the marker, regardless of how the other piece behaves.

If both nonempty pumped pieces are entirely on the left, choose exponent two. The left word becomes strictly longer while the right word remains length two p. A longer word cannot be a substring of that unchanged shorter right word.

If both nonempty pumped pieces are entirely on the right, choose exponent zero. The right word becomes strictly shorter than the unchanged left word of length two p. Again substringhood is impossible, now because the container became too short.

If exactly one piece is nonempty, it lies on one side or contains the hash. The same left-only, right-only or marker case applies. Do not create an uncovered case just because the lemma permits one of its pumped pieces to be epsilon.

The remaining possibility has the hash inside x, with v on the left and y on the right. The bounded window forces v to contain only trailing b symbols from the left word and y only leading a symbols from the right. Write v as k copies of b and y as j copies of a, with k plus j positive.

If k is positive, pump up. The left word now needs a contiguous run of more than p b symbols, while the right word still has only p b symbols in its final run. Extra leading a symbols on the right cannot manufacture those missing consecutive b symbols, so no substring match exists.

If k is zero, then j is positive, so pump down instead. The left word remains length two p while the right loses j symbols, returning to the container-too-short contradiction. Every legal split therefore fails for a chosen exponent, proving the language is not context-free.

For the duplicate-half language, the lecture uses four long alternating blocks and a separate midpoint case analysis. Removing symbols moves the midpoint, so saying that only one original half changed is not a sufficient argument about the new halves. The written study guide preserves those cases; use the same careful window discipline rather than reusing a slogan.

Things to take note of. Partition cases by what happens to the unique marker and by the sides containing the nonempty pumped pieces. Length alone handles same-side changes, while a straddling window may require a run-length argument and a different exponent; every case must end with explicit failed membership.

lessons.title: Which operations preserve context-free languages?

chapters.title: Know the construction behind each answer
ε-input moves do not move the DFA
Use a regular filter for a new impossibility

transcript.text: Which operations preserve context-free languages? Union, concatenation and star have grammar constructions, but arbitrary intersection and complement do not. Intersection with a regular language is a special positive case, and we will show exactly why one stack still suffices there.

For union, rename component variables and introduce a fresh start choosing either old start. For concatenation, make the new start produce the two component starts in sequence. For star, use a fresh start producing an old-start factor followed by itself, or epsilon for zero factors.

Each construction has a two-way derivation argument. A generated word splits into the selected components or factors, and conversely any words from those components have derivations that can be joined. The raw combined grammar need not be in Chomsky normal form unless you convert it afterwards.

Consider the context-free language of equal a and b blocks followed by any c block. Also consider any a block followed by equal b and c blocks. Each has a simple grammar using one matched recursive pair and one unconstrained repeated block.

A word in their intersection must have all three ordered block counts equal. The intersection is therefore the three-equal-block language, which the context-free pumping lemma proved not context-free. This is a concrete counterexample to general intersection closure, not merely a failed attempt to find a construction.

If context-free languages were also closed under complement, union closure and De Morgan would make them closed under intersection. That contradicts our counterexample. Therefore general complement closure fails as well, although this argument does not claim the complement of every individual CFL is non-context-free.

For a context-free language C and regular language R, combine a pushdown automaton for C with a deterministic automaton for R. Store their control states as one pair and retain only the pushdown machine’s single stack. On a consumed symbol, update both controls and perform the original stack action.

On an epsilon input move of the pushdown machine, keep the deterministic state fixed. No input symbol has been consumed for the regular filter to read. The product’s invariant records the PDA run and the DFA run on the same consumed prefix, proving it recognizes their intersection.

Trying the same construction with two pushdown automata would require two independent stacks. A single PDA does not provide that memory model, and the intersection counterexample shows that no general one-stack repair can exist. The regular component is special precisely because its memory fits inside finite control.

Apply the regular-filter result to words with equal numbers of a, b and c in any order. Intersect with a star b star c star to force the ordered form, obtaining the known non-context-free equal-block language. If the original language were context-free the filtered result would be too, giving a contradiction.

Things to take note of. Prove positive closure by constructions and negative closure by actual counterexample languages. Preserve epsilon semantics in the PDA-DFA product, distinguish one stack from two, and do not confuse nonclosure of a class with a claim about every particular language pair.

lessons.title: How do you read and trace a Turing machine?

chapters.title: u q v locates the head
Read b and write x at cell 2
aa q2 ba → a q3 axa

transcript.text: How do you read and trace a Turing machine? Its finite control reads and writes an unbounded tape while a head moves between cells. We will translate a configuration into a picture and perform read, write, state change and head movement as separate operations.

The formal machine has state set, input alphabet, tape alphabet, transition function, start state, accept state and reject state. The basic course transition writes a symbol and moves left or right. The blank is a tape symbol that can be written, but it is not an input-alphabet symbol.

In configuration notation u q v, the head scans the first symbol of v. The whole tape segment represented is u followed by v, and q is a state marker rather than a tape character. Include a blank when needed to show the scanned cell beyond the rightmost nonblank symbol.

Use the lecture transition from q two reading b: enter q three, write x, and move left. Starting with a a, state q two, then b a, the head initially scans the b. First replace that b with x; it is not the a to the left that gets overwritten.

After moving left, the head scans the second a and the state is q three. The resulting notation is a, then q three, then a x a. This matches the unchanged first a, the newly scanned second a and the overwritten x to its right.

For a right move, write the replacement in the current cell before advancing the head. If the head reaches a previously unshown cell, that cell is blank. Never move the state marker first and then overwrite whichever symbol happens to appear after it in your new written notation.

At the left end of the course’s semi-infinite tape, a requested left move leaves the head at that boundary. Therefore consecutive configurations can have the same head location even though the ordinary transition directions are only left and right. A fully general stay operation is a different model convention, though it can be simulated.

Entering an accept or reject state halts the computation immediately. A machine that never reaches either has a nonhalting run, even if its tape and head do not repeat a previous complete configuration. An infinite tape permits looping behaviour that continually visits new cells.

A recognizer must accept every member and never accept a nonmember, but may loop on nonmembers. A decider must halt on every input, accepting or rejecting correctly. Describing a machine that works only on successful examples is therefore insufficient to prove decidability.

Things to take note of. Keep state symbols separate from tape symbols, overwrite the old head cell, and apply the stated boundary convention. Distinguish input from tape alphabets and recognition from decision, and stop tracing as soon as a halting state is entered.

lessons.title: How can a Turing machine test whether a length is a power of two?

transcript.text: How can a Turing machine test whether a unary length is a power of two? Repeated halving accepts when one active zero remains and rejects an odd count greater than one. We will separate that concept from the lecture diagram’s concrete convention, which blanks its first zero as a left-end reference.

In the high-level algorithm, sweep across active zeros crossing out every other one. If the count was even, the remaining count is half as large; if it was odd and greater than one, reject. Returning to the left end and repeating eventually reaches one exactly for a power-of-two length.

For the exact diagram on four zeros, q one blanks the first cell and enters q two at the second zero. This special first cell is the left-end reference, so the remaining explicit zeros are not the entire conceptual count. Do not mix that bookkeeping with an unrelated simplified animation.

From q two, cross out the next zero and move right into q three. In q three, retain the following zero and move into q four. In q four, cross out the next zero and return to q three at the right-hand blank, leaving blank, x, zero, x on the tape.

The right-hand blank in q three signals a successful sweep and turns the machine left in q five. It passes back over x and zero until the left reference, then moves right into q two. Those return moves do not change which zeros were crossed out.

On the next sweep, q two skips the x and crosses out the remaining explicit zero. The tape becomes blank followed by three x markers, and the machine returns left again. Finally q two skips all three x markers and reaches blank with no unmatched explicit zero, so the diagram accepts.

Check the shortest boundary inputs rather than extrapolating from four zeros. A single zero is accepted because its length is two to the zero, while epsilon is rejected. Two zeros also reduce successfully, whereas three reach the diagram’s odd-count rejection case.

The halting argument relies on progress. A successful nonterminal round reduces the conceptual active count, and every finite sweep and return finishes. Eventually the machine reaches an accepting singleton or an odd count that rejects, so it is a decider rather than a mere recognizer.

Halving does not imply logarithmic tape-running time. There are only logarithmically many successful rounds, but each involves scans across cells and markers on the original tape span. A straightforward bound counts those scans as well; naming the number of rounds alone ignores most primitive moves.

Things to take note of. Use the actual diagram’s initial blank and state conventions when writing configurations, and keep the conceptual halving explanation distinct from that exact trace. Test epsilon, one, two and odd lengths, explain termination, and never turn a scan-based machine into a constant-cost arithmetic operation.

lessons.title: How do marking and zig-zagging build TM deciders?

chapters.title: Copying needs a final exhaustion test

transcript.text: How do marking and zig-zagging build Turing-machine deciders? Marking turns repeated scans into a controlled matching procedure, while finite control carries the small amount of information needed between distant positions. We will count two zeros per one, then compare the two sides of a hash separator.

For words with twice as many zeros as ones, find the first unmarked one and mark it. Return left, find the first unmarked zero, mark it, then find and mark a second unmarked zero. If either zero is unavailable, reject because this selected one cannot receive its required pair.

After matching that pair, return to the beginning and repeat. Each complete round removes one unmarked one and two unmarked zeros from future consideration. The order of symbols in the input is unrestricted, so restarting the scan is essential instead of assuming zeros form an initial block.

When no unmarked one remains, scan once more for leftover unmarked zeros. If any remain, reject; if every input symbol was matched, enter the accepting state. Checking only that every one found a pair would incorrectly accept a word with too many zeros.

The empty word has zero zeros and zero ones, so it satisfies the equation and is accepted. Each outer round marks a new one, and every scan is over a finite used tape segment, proving halt on every input. With at most linearly many rounds and linear scans per round, a straightforward implementation has a quadratic scan bound.

For the equality-of-counts variant, use one zero per one instead of two. For its complement, reverse accept and reject outcomes only after establishing that the original machine always halts. The same swap would not safely complement a recognizer that might loop.

Now consider the copying language w hash w. First validate that there is exactly one separator and that the other symbols are binary. Mark the next unchecked symbol on the left, remember its value in finite control, then zig-zag right to the next unchecked symbol on the other side.

The right symbol must match the remembered bit, and it is then marked too. Return to the left and repeat for the next pair, so zero one hash zero one first matches zeros and then ones. A mismatch, early end or extra right-side symbol must reject.

When the left side has no unchecked symbol, verify that the right side also has none. The input consisting only of hash represents two empty copies and should be accepted, while a missing separator is malformed. Each successful round marks a fresh pair, giving a finite progress measure and a halting decider.

Things to take note of. Describe where scans restart, what temporary marks mean, what information finite control remembers and how every loop makes progress. Form checks and final leftovers are part of the algorithm, not optional polish; successful matches alone do not prove the language is decided correctly.

lessons.title: How do TMs perform arithmetic and manage lists?

chapters.title: One a-round consumes j copies of c
Restore b; retain consumed a and c
Cover every pair unless rejection occurs

transcript.text: How do Turing machines perform arithmetic and manage lists? The tape model can implement nested loops and repeated comparisons using only finite control plus marks. We will verify multiplication of block lengths, then detect duplicate entries in a delimiter-separated binary list.

For a to the i, b to the j, c to the k with i times j equal to k, first check the input has nonempty ordered a, b and c blocks. Choose one unprocessed a, then scan the b block. For each b in that pass, mark one previously unmarked c, rejecting if no such c exists.

At the end of the b pass, restore its temporary marks so the next a can reuse every b. Keep the selected a permanently processed and keep the c symbols already consumed marked. Mixing up permanent and temporary marks would change the multiplication into a different count.

On the lecture example a a b c c, there are two a symbols and one b. The first outer round uses that b to consume one c, and after restoring b the second outer round consumes the other c. No unprocessed a or c remains, so the example accepts because two times one equals two.

After every symbol in the first block has been processed, reject if any unmarked c remains. Also reject immediately if the c block runs out during a pass through the b block. The outer loop processes a fresh symbol each round, and each round consumes exactly j copies of c, proving both termination and the multiplication condition.

For element distinctness, the input is a list of binary strings separated by hash markers. In the lecture example the first entry is zero then one, the second is one then zero, and the third is zero then one. The first and third match, but the machine must compare each entry as a whole rather than just comparing its first character or length.

Place distinguishable marks on the delimiters of the current pair of entries. Zig-zag between corresponding characters, recording a bit in finite control, until a mismatch or both ends are reached. Restore comparison marks before moving the second delimiter mark to the next entry.

Comparing zero one with one zero finds a mismatch, so that pair is different. Move the second-entry selection to the third entry and compare zero one with zero one; both end together with all symbols matching. That equality proves a duplicate and the machine rejects immediately without needing further pair tests.

If no equality is found, advance the outer delimiter selection and compare every remaining pair. With a finite number of entries and finite per-pair scans, the algorithm halts. Equal-length but different entries must pass, while repeated empty entries need the same whole-entry equality logic as repeated nonempty ones.

Things to take note of. Distinguish loop counters stored through marks, temporary comparison marks and permanent progress markers. State the form checks, explain restoration, and prove that all required products or entry pairs are covered; finding one example that works is not the correctness argument.

lessons.title: Do extra tapes or nondeterminism make TMs more powerful?

chapters.title: An accepting branch may be elsewhere
Decider equivalence needs all branches halt

transcript.text: Do extra tapes or nondeterminism make Turing machines more powerful? They can make descriptions shorter or computations faster, but the lecture equivalence theorems preserve the class of recognized languages. We will inspect the simulation ideas and separate expressive power from running time.

A multitape machine reads one scanned symbol from each tape in a transition. Its finite control chooses new symbols, directions and state together. The input begins on the first tape with the others blank, and each tape has an independently positioned head.

Encode the tapes as delimiter-separated regions on one ordinary tape. Mark one symbol in each region to record its virtual head position. The simulator’s finite control remembers the tuple of scanned symbols during a sweep, then a further sweep performs the required writes and head-mark updates.

If a virtual tape needs an additional cell, shift the encoding to make space. These extra sweeps and shifts cost time, but they do not change which input words can eventually be accepted. Thus equivalent recognition does not mean one primitive simulated move always takes one primitive real move.

A nondeterministic machine has a tree of possible computations. It accepts if some branch reaches acceptance, even when other branches reject or run forever. A deterministic simulator must search that tree fairly instead of getting trapped following one nonhalting branch.

Depth-first search can descend an infinite path and never inspect a finite accepting sibling. Breadth-first exploration, or an equivalent dovetailing of finite branch addresses, eventually reaches every finite computation prefix. Therefore it finds any finite accepting branch without claiming that the branches execute for free in physical parallelism.

For an NTM to be a decider, all branches must halt on every input. Its tree is finitely branching, and an infinite such tree would contain an infinite path, so the all-halting computation tree for a fixed input is finite. A fair deterministic simulation can therefore exhaust it and reject if none of its branches accepts.

A doubly infinite tape is another equivalent variant. Store its right half on one ordinary tape and its left half in reverse order on another, with finite control remembering which half is active. Crossing the origin switches tapes, and directions reverse while working on the reversed left-half representation.

The reverse simulation lets a two-way tape machine reserve a left-end marker and use only one side, imitating an ordinary tape. Together the two simulations prove equal recognition power. One inclusion alone would show only that one model can do at least as much as the other.

Things to take note of. Explain the encoding and head markers, use fair search for nondeterminism, and distinguish a recognizer’s looping branches from a decider’s all-halting condition. Equivalent computability classes do not automatically provide equal runtimes or resolve the efficiency question behind P versus NP.

lessons.title: Why is recognizable the same as enumerable?

transcript.text: Why is Turing-recognizable the same as enumerable? A recognizer answers membership positively, while an enumerator prints language members from a blank start. The equivalence relies on a fair schedule so a nonhalting test never prevents later strings from being generated.

An enumerator may print words in arbitrary order and may repeat them. Its language is the set of strings it ever prints, not the set of all intermediate tape contents. It may run forever, print finitely many words, or print nothing for the empty language.

For equal zero and one blocks, a direct enumerator is simple. Let n start at zero, print n zeros followed by n ones, increment n and repeat. The outputs begin epsilon, zero one, zero zero one one, with each language member printed once because its n is unique.

For the general enumerator-to-recognizer direction, take the input word w and simulate the enumerator. Whenever a string is printed, compare it with w and accept if they match. If w is never printed, the recognizer may wait forever, which is permitted for a nonmember.

For the other direction, list all input strings in shortlex order and consider a recognizer on each. Running them one after another is unsafe, because the first nonmember might make its recognizer loop. Instead at stage t, simulate the first t inputs for t steps each and print any that have accepted.

Every member has some finite index j and some finite accepting time k. Once a stage reaches at least both j and k, its accepting run is included and has enough steps, so that word is printed. No nonmember is printed because a correct recognizer never accepts one.

These bounded simulations can restart from scratch each stage without changing the existence argument. A more efficient implementation may retain partial runs instead, but fairness is the essential property. Never let a possibly infinite run occupy the only simulation slot forever.

If the language is decidable, its decider halts on every tested word, so serial shortlex testing becomes safe. Print a word exactly when the decider accepts and then continue to the next word. This produces members once in string order without needing the general recognizable-language dovetailing construction.

The converse sorted-enumeration characterization needs a small qualification in its proof. For an infinite language printed in strict shortlex order, waiting until w appears or a larger word appears decides membership. A finite language is decidable by a fixed finite table; blindly waiting for a larger printed word could otherwise hang after the last output.

Things to take note of. Distinguish printing from tape contents, allow repetition and arbitrary order in the general definition, and prove eventual printing using finite index and finite accepting time. Sorted enumeration uses stronger ordering information, while a mere recognizer cannot be run serially on all candidates safely.

lessons.title: When do closure proofs need deciders or dovetailing?

chapters.title: Always ask: can this subroutine loop?

transcript.text: When do closure proofs need deciders or dovetailing? A decider always halts, while a recognizer may loop on inputs outside its language. We will compare algorithms for union, complement and factorization so that the machine-class hypothesis stays visible in every proof.

For the union of two decidable languages, run the first decider and accept if it accepts, otherwise run the second. Each call halts, so the sequence always reaches a final verdict. The same sequential idea works for intersection by requiring acceptance from both.

Now suppose the machines are only recognizers. A word could belong to the second language while the first recognizer loops on it forever, so a serial union algorithm never reaches the accepting second test. Alternate one step of each simulation instead, accepting when either accepts.

For recognizable intersection, accept only after both simulations have accepted. Alternating them is a uniform safe construction, and serial execution also works for this particular membership condition because both accept on every true member. On nonmembers, rejection or nonhalting is permitted, but false acceptance is not.

Complementing a decider swaps its accept and reject outcomes. Because it always halts, this inverts the verdict on every input. Swapping a recognizer’s halting outcomes leaves its loops unchanged, so a nonmember on which it loops is still not accepted by the supposed complement recognizer.

For concatenation of decidable languages, test all input splits, including an empty prefix or suffix. A length-n word has n plus one split positions, and every pair of decider runs finishes. Accept if one split passes both tests, otherwise reject after the finite list is exhausted.

For star, accept epsilon immediately, then consider factorizations into nonempty pieces. There are finitely many ways to place cuts between the symbols of a fixed word, and every decider test terminates. This proves decidability even though trying all cuts is not the efficient P-class construction we study later.

For recognizers, testing those candidate factorizations serially can hang on the wrong one. Dovetail the finitely many candidate piece-computations and accept once every piece of some candidate has accepted. Equivalently, guess a factorization nondeterministically and use NTM-DTM recognition equivalence.

The PATH example illustrates a positive halting argument. Mark the source vertex, propagate marks along edges until a full pass adds none, then test whether the target is marked. Marks are never removed and only finitely many vertices can be newly marked, so the procedure halts on every valid finite graph.

The Church Turing thesis connects effectively executable algorithms with Turing computation, but it is a thesis rather than a theorem equating two fully formal definitions. Distinguish formal transitions, implementation-level scanning descriptions and high-level algorithms. A high-level input such as a graph still arrives as an encoded finite string, and malformed encodings need a rejection rule.

Things to take note of. Separate correct membership behaviour from the additional requirement to halt, and never schedule a potentially endless recognizer before a result you still need. Use finite factor lists or fair interleaving with the appropriate acceptance condition, and do not infer efficient runtime merely from decidability.

lessons.title: How do we measure computational complexity and compare growth?

chapters.title: Input length n is the reference
Exact values deserve a sanity check

transcript.text: How do we measure computational complexity and compare growth? Complexity theory groups decision languages by the resources required by some machine deciding them. We will distinguish input length, worst-case runtime and asymptotic bounds before simplifying the tutorial’s functions.

Big O is an eventual upper bound up to a fixed constant, Omega is the corresponding lower bound, and Theta requires both. State the constants and sufficiently large input threshold when proving a bound from definitions. Saying that an algorithm is at most quadratic does not establish a tight quadratic runtime.

For a polynomial with positive leading coefficient, the highest degree dominates asymptotically. Fixed log-base changes multiply by a constant, while two to c log base two n equals n to c. Thus an exponential-looking expression can simplify to a polynomial when its exponent is logarithmic.

The expression two to log base two n squared means two raised to the square of that logarithm. It equals n raised to log base two n, whose exponent grows with n. That is superpolynomial but slower than a fixed-base exponential such as three to n.

The tutorial growth ordering places square root n before linear n, then n square root log n, n log n and cubic n. The logarithmic-exponent function follows every fixed polynomial, with three to n growing faster still. Constants such as seven n minus two do not change the linear class.

Do not exponentiate a Big O relation as though constants disappear inside an exponent. Let f equal two n and g equal n, so f is Big O of g. Yet two to f divided by two to g equals two to n, which is unbounded, disproving the proposed exponentiated bound.

Average case also needs a stated distribution. If a linear-search target is equally likely at any of n positions or absent, sum costs one through n plus another n for absence, then divide by n plus one. The exact expectation is n times n plus three over twice n plus one, which is Theta n.

The printed solution’s simplified n plus two over two expression is not that exact expectation. Checking n equal to one exposes the issue immediately, because every possible search costs one comparison. The asymptotic linear conclusion survives, but an exact numerical claim still needs correct algebra.

Machine-model changes can introduce overhead, such as quadratic simulation of standard multitape time by a single tape under suitable bounds. Time-hierarchy theorems give strict separations when their constructibility and growth-gap hypotheses hold. They do not let us declare P different from NP, and sublinear examples need careful model assumptions.

Things to take note of. Simplify functions symbolically, separate upper bounds from tight bounds, and count time as a function of encoded input length. State the distribution for averages and the model assumptions for hierarchy or simulation arguments; memorizing a growth table is not a substitute for those conditions.

lessons.title: What does polynomial time mean when numbers are in binary?

chapters.title: Algorithm upper bound versus language class
Pseudopolynomial is not polynomial in bits

transcript.text: What does polynomial time mean when numbers are in binary? A decision language is in P when some deterministic decider has a fixed-degree polynomial runtime in its input length. A number’s value can be exponentially larger than the bits used to represent it, so counting value-sized iterations can be deceptive.

An integer N in binary uses about log base two N bits. A loop taking N iterations therefore takes exponentially many iterations as a function of that bit count. Writing the same value in unary changes the input length to N and changes this particular complexity comparison.

Trial division up to square root N correctly tests primality, but its number of divisions is not polynomial in binary length. Arithmetic on the trial divisors also has bit cost rather than being literally free. A slow algorithm does not establish a lower bound against all other algorithms, so it does not prove that the language lies outside polynomial time.

For a unary input, reading its N symbols already takes linear time in its length. Counting the symbols and using binary work counters still permits a polynomial implementation of the same trial-division idea. Do not report a sublinear total input-processing time while silently skipping the full unary read.

The tutorial subset-sum dynamic program runs in time proportional to the number of entries times the target value. If that target is written in binary, it may be exponentially large in its own bit length. Such a pseudopolynomial bound does not establish membership in P for binary-encoded instances.

With n input numbers of order n bits, the full input may have order n squared bits. A target of two to n then yields runtime roughly n times two to n, superpolynomial in that total input size. Calling it two to a linear function of the total size would be a stronger claim than this example supports.

Some bounds that look unusual are still polynomial. A fixed power of log n is bounded by a polynomial, and n to one hundred times log n is bounded by n to one hundred and one. In contrast, n to log n has no constant degree, and two to square root n is also superpolynomial.

The photo quiz includes n raised to two plus five over log n. For a fixed logarithm base, n raised to five over log n is a constant, so the whole expression is a constant multiple of n squared. An exponent containing n is not automatically superpolynomial; simplify the expression before classifying it.

To prove a language in P, provide an algorithm, show correctness and halting, and bound every operation polynomially in the complete encoding. This includes number sizes and any output generated during intermediate work. Exhibiting a nonpolynomial algorithm supplies no lower bound against all alternative methods.

Things to take note of. Always name the input length before manipulating runtime, distinguish value-polynomial from bit-polynomial time, and include input-reading costs. A superpolynomial upper bound fails to prove membership in P, while it also fails to prove nonmembership; those are two different proof obligations.

lessons.title: How does repeated squaring avoid enormous loops?

chapters.title: Use exponent bits, not exponent value
Invariant: r·bᵉ equals the target modulo p
Why the bit complexity is polynomial

transcript.text: How does repeated squaring avoid enormous loops? It halves a binary exponent at each step, reusing squared powers instead of multiplying once per exponent value. We will trace modular exponentiation and transfer the same idea to permutations and Fibonacci numbers modulo a given modulus.

For modular exponentiation, maintain a result r, a current base b and a remaining exponent e. Initially r is one, b is the reduced input base, and e is the desired exponent. The invariant is that r times b to e has the same residue as the original power.

At an odd exponent, multiply the result by the current base modulo p. Then square the base modulo p and replace the exponent by its integer half. At an even exponent, skip the result multiplication but perform the same squaring and halving.

Trace two to the thirteen modulo five. Starting with result one, base two and exponent thirteen, the odd step changes the result to two, squares the base to four and halves the exponent to six. The next even step keeps result two, squares four to one modulo five and halves six to three.

The remaining odd rounds multiply the result by one, so it stays two while the exponent becomes one and then zero. At exponent zero, the invariant leaves only the result, proving the answer is two. Four bit-processing rounds replaced thirteen repeated multiplications in this small example.

There are logarithmically many rounds because e is halved, but that is only the operation count. Reducing after every multiplication keeps residues to order log p bits, so standard integer arithmetic makes each round polynomial in the input bit lengths. Computing an unreduced giant power first would lose that essential operand-size bound.

Permutation powering uses composition instead of multiplication, with the identity permutation as exponent-zero result. A permutation on k elements stays a k-element list after every composition, so entries do not grow into enormous integers. Repeated squaring gives logarithmically many compositions, each polynomial in that list’s encoding.

For Fibonacci numbers, use the two-by-two matrix with rows one one and one zero. Its nth power has Fibonacci n in the upper-right entry, including exponent zero where that entry is zero. Reduce entries modulo p during every matrix multiplication, keeping the whole computation polynomial in log n and log p.

The photos also show exact integer matrix powering, where bare multiplication count is not a complete complexity proof. Matrix entries can become enormous if they are not reduced, and writing their bits costs time. The modular Fibonacci and bounded-entry permutation examples make the missing size condition explicit.

Things to take note of. State the invariant, handle exponent zero, halve the exponent and reuse computed half-powers rather than recomputing both recursively. In a P-membership proof, bound encoded operand lengths as well as the number of arithmetic operations; that is what makes repeated squaring an efficiency argument.

lessons.title: How do graphs and finite-state cycles give polynomial algorithms?

chapters.title: A shortest accepting prefix has no loop

transcript.text: How do graphs and finite-state cycles give polynomial algorithms? A valid P-membership proof needs an algorithm, correctness and a polynomial bound in the explicit encoding. We will inspect graph traversal, distinguish edge and vertex conditions, then solve the photo’s bounded unary-automaton problem without following an enormous binary limit.

PATH can mark vertices reachable from the source using breadth-first or depth-first search. Every marked vertex has a path from the source, and exploring every edge from reached vertices eventually discovers every reachable vertex. With a standard explicit graph representation, the traversal uses polynomially many operations, and bit-level bookkeeping remains polynomial too.

To test bipartiteness, assign opposite colours across every edge and reject a same-colour conflict. Restart from each unvisited component rather than checking only the first component. A disconnected graph could hide an odd cycle in a component never reached from your original start.

To test for a triangle, enumerate triples of distinct vertices and check all three possible edges. With an adjacency matrix those lookups are constant-time in the usual graph-operation model, yielding a cubic vertex bound. A Turing-machine implementation may add bookkeeping overhead, but it remains polynomial in an explicit graph encoding.

Eulerian and Hamiltonian conditions ask different questions. An Eulerian cycle uses every edge once; in the undirected setting, nonisolated connectivity plus even degrees gives the familiar efficient test. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once, so the Eulerian criterion cannot be reused for it.

Now take a unary deterministic automaton with m states and an integer n given in binary. The photo asks whether at least one of epsilon through a to n is accepted, not whether the single word a to n is accepted. Directly taking n transitions may be huge relative to the bits of n.

If an accepting state is reached at all, a shortest path to a first accepting state never repeats a state before that first acceptance. Otherwise remove the loop and get an earlier accepting path. Therefore at most m minus one transitions suffice to find a first accepted unary word.

Compute only the state sequence from index zero through the smaller of n and m minus one. Accept if any of those states is final, including the start state for epsilon. Even scanning the explicit transition table for each move gives a polynomial bound in the table size and the binary length of n.

For an exact-length question, a repeated-state cycle would instead allow reducing the remaining exponent modulo the cycle length. That is a related but different algorithm, because an accepting shorter prefix does not answer exact-length membership. Preserve the quantifier some j at most n throughout the photographed task.

Things to take note of. Validate input encodings, handle every graph component, distinguish edge-based from vertex-based properties, and use the exact unary question. A structural bound such as the first accepting path length can replace a value-sized loop with polynomial work without changing the language.

lessons.title: Why is P closed under Kleene star?

transcript.text: Why is P closed under Kleene star? Trying every cut of a word is finite but can be exponential, so the decidability proof alone is not enough. We will replace that enumeration with prefix dynamic programming and count both membership calls and the work of carrying them out.

A greedy longest-prefix method fails even for a tiny finite language. Let L contain zero, zero one and one one, and take the input zero one one. Greedy removes zero one and gets stuck on one, although the valid factorization is zero followed by one one.

Define D of j to mean the first j symbols belong to L star. Set D of zero true because the empty prefix is a concatenation of zero factors. For a positive j, look for a smaller i with D of i true and the substring from i plus one through j in L.

For zero one one, D of one is true because its one-symbol prefix zero belongs to L. D of two is also true because zero one belongs to L. These are valid prefix facts, not a commitment to using the longer prefix in every later factorization.

To compute D of three, the whole word zero one one is not itself in L. But split after the first symbol: D of one is true and the final one one is in L. Therefore D of three becomes true, recovering the factorization the greedy algorithm missed.

Prove the recurrence by induction on prefix length. If a tested split succeeds, append its last L-factor to a valid earlier prefix factorization. Conversely, a nonempty word in L star has a factorization whose empty factors can be discarded, so its final nonempty factor begins at one of the tested smaller indices.

The algorithm accepts an empty input immediately, whether or not epsilon belongs to L. For nonempty inputs, excluding empty factors ensures each predecessor index is strictly smaller. Allowing infinitely many empty factors would add no new words and would obscure this finite dynamic-programming structure.

There is at most one membership call per index pair with zero at most i less than j at most n. Summing j from one through n gives n times n plus one over two calls. For the three-symbol example that is at most six calls, although short-circuiting may make fewer.

Suppose the given decider takes time Big O of m to c on nonempty inputs, with c at least one. Each tested substring has length at most n, and copying, simulation cleanup and table access can be bounded by polynomial scans as in the tutorial implementation. With order n squared tests, the stated multitape bound is Big O of n to c plus two.

Things to take note of. State what the DP table means, prove both recurrence directions and include the empty input. Membership calls are real computations rather than unit-cost magic, and a finite exhaustive partition search proves decidability without proving the stronger polynomial-time claim.

lessons.title: How can decision answers recover a solution?

chapters.title: Why the search is correct and polynomial
Proper binary search for the optimum
Value search and witness search are separate

transcript.text: How can decision answers recover a solution? A yes-or-no oracle can guide a polynomial number of smaller decisions until an actual witness is exposed. We will recover an independent set, then distinguish witness search from optimum-value search and from a one-output polynomial reduction.

Start with a graph and a requested independent-set size k. First ask whether the original instance is feasible; if not, report failure rather than trying to construct an impossible witness. If feasible, test deleting a chosen vertex while keeping the same target size.

If deleting the chosen vertex preserves feasibility for the target size, discard that vertex. Otherwise every solution meeting the target must contain it, so add it to the answer and delete it together with its neighbours. Reduce the target by one and continue on the remaining graph.

On the five-vertex path, an independent set of size three is one, three and five. Deleting vertex one leaves a four-vertex path with maximum independent-set size two, so vertex one is forced for this target. Commit one and remove its neighbour two, leaving the path three, four, five with target two.

In that residual path, deleting three would leave the single edge four-five, which cannot supply two independent vertices. Commit three, remove four, then choose the remaining vertex five. The accumulated witness one, three, five has no internal edge and reaches the requested size.

The invariant is that the current graph contains an independent set of the remaining requested size compatible with every committed vertex. A discard preserves it by the oracle answer, and a forced commitment preserves it by removing exactly the forbidden neighbours. Each iteration removes at least one vertex, so at most linearly many oracle decisions are needed after the initial check.

To find the maximum size, use the monotone threshold predicate before constructing a witness. Maintain a feasible lower bound zero and infeasible upper bound one more than the number of vertices, query the midpoint and update the appropriate side. When the bounds differ by one, the feasible bound is the optimum, after logarithmically many threshold calls.

Simply querying n, n divided by two, n divided by four and so on does not locate every possible optimum. A correct binary search retains both bounds and chooses the next midpoint from the current interval. Once the optimum size is known, the delete-or-commit procedure recovers a witness of that size.

The factoring tutorial uses the same decision-to-search principle for integers at least two. Ask whether a nontrivial factor exists below a threshold, then binary-search the least feasible threshold if the square-root threshold is feasible. A factor is verified by divisibility; a no answer at the square-root threshold identifies a prime in that input domain.

Things to take note of. Check initial feasibility, state the residual invariant, and count oracle calls plus transformation work. Recovering an optimum number is not automatically recovering its witness, and a multi-query search construction is not the same object as a single-instance Karp reduction.

lessons.title: What is NP, and how do you write a verifier proof?

chapters.title: w∈L iff some short certificate verifies

transcript.text: What is NP, and how do you write a verifier proof? A yes instance must have a certificate of polynomial encoded length that a deterministic polynomial-time verifier accepts. A no instance must make every allowed certificate fail, so a convincing example alone is not enough.

This is equivalent to polynomial-time nondeterministic computation. One direction records an accepting machine’s choices as a certificate and simulates them deterministically. The other guesses a polynomial-length certificate and runs the verifier, with every branch obeying a polynomial time bound.

Consider the Vertex Cover decision language: a graph and integer k asking for a cover of size at most k. A certificate can be one selection bit per vertex. The verifier counts selected vertices and checks that every edge has at least one selected endpoint.

If the graph has a suitable cover, its selection mask passes all checks. If a mask passes, the size bound and edge checks prove that it really is a suitable cover, so no no-instance can fool the verifier. The mask length and all explicit graph checks are polynomial in the input encoding.

For Independent Set or Clique, give a vertex subset and check its cardinality and all selected pairs. Independent Set forbids every internal edge, while Clique requires every pair to have an edge. A proof that checks only a few listed edges does not verify the universal pair condition.

For a Hamiltonian cycle, the certificate is an ordering of all vertices. Verify valid names, no repetitions, complete coverage, every consecutive edge and the closing edge back to the start. A path verifier omits cycle closure, while a longest-simple-path verifier must also enforce distinct vertices and the requested length threshold.

For SAT, a truth assignment is the certificate and evaluating all clauses is polynomial in the formula length. For Subset Sum, use a bit mask selecting input indices and check the binary sum against the target. Repeated equal values still occupy different indices, and polynomially many additions keep polynomial bit lengths.

A verifier need not find the certificate efficiently. NP membership asserts that a suitable short witness exists and can be checked, not that searching for it is already known polynomial. Likewise, NP means nondeterministic polynomial time, not non-polynomial time.

Deterministic polynomial algorithms are a special case of nondeterministic ones, giving P contained in NP. Enumerating all polynomial-size certificates gives an exponential deterministic bound, placing NP within EXP. The known separation of P from EXP does not decide which intermediate inclusion is strict or settle P versus NP.

Things to take note of. Specify the decision language, certificate encoding, length bound, all verifier checks and a polynomial bit-time analysis. Explain both why genuine yes instances have a passing certificate and why no instance can pass; the phrase easy to check is only the beginning of the proof.
