lessons.title: When does an apparently obvious NP certificate fail?

chapters.title: A certificate must be polynomially short
Binary k changes the certificate bound
A failed witness idea is not nonmembership
Counting output is a function task
Short witnesses do not validate value-sized DP

transcript.text: When does an apparently obvious NP certificate fail? The photographed subset questions distinguish one solution, two solutions, a binary-specified number of solutions, and a counting output. We will inspect certificate length as carefully as verification time, without turning a failed certificate idea into an unsupported impossibility claim.

For existence of one subset summing to a target, use one selection bit per input index. Add the selected binary integers and compare the result to the target. The bit mask has linear length in the number of entries, and intermediate sums have only polynomially many bits.

For existence of two distinct subsets with that sum, give two masks. Verify both sums and check the masks differ in at least one index bit. On the repeated-value example, choosing the first one or the second one produces different subsets even though the selected numeric values look identical.

For a fixed constant number of requested solutions, a fixed number of masks is still polynomial-sized. But the photo also allows k itself in binary. Then k can be exponentially large in its written length, so listing k masks may take superpolynomial space in the full input.

This exposes a gap in that proposed NP proof: checking a gigantic supplied list quickly relative to the list length is not enough. The witness length must be polynomial in the original instance length. Its failure does not prove that every other possible certificate scheme fails or that the language is outside NP.

The question asking how many subsets sum to the target asks for a numeric output. NP, as defined in this course, is a class of decision languages with yes-or-no answers. A related threshold decision problem is meaningful, but it is a new formal problem requiring its own classification argument.

The zero-valued entries in the photo’s input make index discipline especially useful. Including or omitting a zero changes the subset mask even though it preserves the sum. Deleting zero entries can preserve existence of some solution while changing the number of distinct solutions, so transformations must match their exact decision question.

The usual dynamic program for Subset Sum has a table indexed by the target value. That value can be huge compared with its binary encoding, even though a chosen subset is easy to verify. Polynomial certificate verification and a deterministic polynomial algorithm are separate claims, so the table-size argument must use the original input length.

A sound verifier must also reject malformed masks and incorrect sums, not merely accept the example it was designed around. For two-solution certificates, duplicated copies of the same mask must not satisfy the distinctness requirement. State all these checks before declaring the problem in NP.

Things to take note of. Keep subset indices distinct from repeated numeric values, account for binary k when measuring witness size, and distinguish counting functions from decision languages. If your proposed certificate is too long, identify that proof gap honestly rather than claiming an unproved separation.

lessons.title: Why is NP closed under some operations but complement is unresolved?

transcript.text: Why is NP closed under some operations while complement closure remains unresolved? Certificates can record a successful choice, a pair of witnesses or a factorization. We will build those witnesses explicitly and show why flipping nondeterministic outcomes does not turn an existential claim into its negation.

For the union of two NP languages, give a tag naming the chosen language together with its certificate. The verifier checks the tag and runs the corresponding verifier. A member has a successful choice, while a word outside both languages cannot pass either choice.

For intersection, give both certificates and run both verifiers. The combined verifier returns yes only when both checks return yes, so an input missing from either language cannot pass. The sum of two polynomial certificate lengths and two polynomial runtimes remains polynomial.

For concatenation, guess a split index and give a certificate for each side. Verify that the first prefix belongs to the first language and the remaining suffix to the second. The split index is short, and both substrings have length at most the original input, keeping the combined bound polynomial.

For star, a nonempty word needs at most n nonempty factors, where n is its length. Give their boundary indices and a certificate for each factor, then verify every factor using the original verifier. Remove empty factors from a successful decomposition; accept epsilon separately as the zero-factor case.

The bound on total witness size matters here. Polynomially many pieces each have polynomially bounded certificates relative to a substring of length at most n. Their sum is therefore polynomial, whereas guessing an unbounded number of factors without justification would leave a gap.

Now examine the false complement proof that swaps every accepting and rejecting NTM outcome. The original machine accepts when some branch accepts. After the swap, the new machine accepts when some original branch rejects, which is not the same as every original branch rejecting.

For a concrete failure, let one branch accept and two reject on the same input. The original accepts because of its accepting branch, and after the swap two branches accept, so the swapped machine accepts too. A genuine complement should reject that original yes input.

The class coNP consists of complements of NP languages, not the universe of languages with NP removed as a set difference. Whether NP equals coNP is unresolved in the course framework. The failed flip argument proves neither equality nor inequality; it merely fails to establish closure.

Things to take note of. Give explicit polynomial-size certificates for positive closure and include epsilon and empty-factor handling. Keep all nondeterministic branches time-bounded, distinguish existential from universal branch claims, and do not turn the failure of one construction into an unproved class separation.

lessons.title: Which way should a polynomial reduction point?

chapters.title: A ≤P B: use a B-solver to solve A
The same vertex set proves the iff
Do not lose tiny graph cases

transcript.text: Which way should a polynomial reduction point? A reduction from A to B transforms each A instance into one B instance with the same yes-or-no answer. A solver for B then solves A, so A is no harder than B, not the other way around.

A complete proof must define the transformation, show valid output, prove both implications and bound construction time in the encoded input length. Polynomial output size follows from actually writing it in polynomial time. A reduction cannot simply say output yes if the input is a yes instance when deciding that condition is the original hard problem.

For Independent Set to Clique, keep the vertex set and threshold but complement the graph’s edges between distinct vertices. Two selected vertices are nonadjacent in the original graph exactly when they are adjacent in the complement. Do not add self-loops; only unordered distinct pairs are toggled.

If the original graph has an independent set of size at least k, all its selected distinct pairs become complement edges, so it is a clique. Conversely, a complement clique has no original edges among its selected vertices, so it is independent. Testing every vertex pair constructs the complement in polynomial time.

If Clique were in P, this mapping would place Independent Set in P. The reduction alone does not prove that either problem is already in P or that either lies outside P. Hardness arguments require a source problem with an independently established hardness status.

The tutorial Hamiltonian Path to Hamiltonian Cycle mapping adds a new vertex adjacent to every original vertex. A Hamiltonian path becomes a cycle by putting the new vertex before its first endpoint and after its last. Removing the new vertex from any resulting Hamiltonian cycle leaves a path through all old vertices.

For simple cycles requiring at least three vertices, handle tiny source graphs separately. A one-vertex graph has a Hamiltonian path but the naive added-vertex graph has only two vertices and no simple cycle. Mapping constant-size exceptional cases to fixed yes or no target graphs preserves a total correct reduction.

Reductions compose. If A reduces to B and B to C, first apply the A-to-B mapping and then the B-to-C mapping; output sizes and runtime remain polynomial. But A reducing to B does not generally imply B reducing to A, so transitivity must not be confused with symmetry.

The photo asks what follows from A reducing to B, B to C and C to B. B and C are equivalent under polynomial reductions and A also reduces to C. Nothing in those premises requires B to reduce back to A.

Things to take note of. Draw the arrow from the problem you want to solve using a target solver, then carry one candidate solution through both correctness directions. Keep encodings, size, edge conventions and small instances explicit; a hardness comparison is not an unexplained efficient algorithm.

lessons.title: How do you reduce Subset Sum to Balanced Partition?

chapters.title: Target: equal sums AND equal counts
Why the first stage is an iff
Check both counters in the example
Size and validity are part of the proof

transcript.text: How do you reduce Subset Sum to Balanced Partition? The photo requires positive output integers and two groups with both equal sum and equal cardinality. We will use a two-stage construction, because ordinary Partition alone does not impose the equal-number-of-entries condition.

First handle easy exceptional cases without solving a hard instance. A zero target is a yes instance using the empty subset, and a target greater than the total is no for nonnegative inputs. Remove zero-valued entries for this existence question, while remembering that such removal would not preserve a counting-of-solutions question.

Assume the remaining target is positive and at most total A. Append the positive adjustment absolute A minus twice t when it is nonzero, producing an ordinary positive Partition instance. The new total is twice the larger of t and A minus t, so an equal side must have that larger sum.

The partition side containing the adjustment has original-value sum equal to the smaller of t and A minus t. Such a subset exists exactly when a target-t subset exists, using its complement when needed. If the adjustment is zero, the original total is twice t and no extra entry is necessary.

Use the authored example one, two, four with target three. Total seven gives adjustment one, so the ordinary Partition list is one, two, four, one. Its equal-sum sides can be the original four alone and the other three entries summing to four.

Now suppose that ordinary Partition list has r entries. Raise every b entry by one and add r new entries of value one, making exactly two r positive entries. Require the target’s two groups to contain r entries each; their added base-one contributions then cancel when comparing sums.

Any balanced target solution selects some raised original entries and some dummy ones on a side. Subtracting its r baseline ones leaves precisely the sum of the corresponding original b entries, which must be half the original b total. Conversely, pad either side of an ordinary partition with enough dummy ones to reach r entries each.

For our example, the output is two, three, five, two, then four dummy ones. One balanced side is five plus three dummy ones; the other is two plus three plus two plus one dummy one. Each side contains four entries and sums to eight, so both target conditions are visible.

The transformation performs additions, an absolute difference and linear padding. Binary sums and the adjustment have polynomial bit length in the original encoding, so writing the output is polynomial work. Values that happen to be equal are still different indexed entries, and positivity is guaranteed by the plus-one stage.

This is a derived solution to the photographed exercise, not a solution visibly present in the photo. Its proof must preserve yes and no instances through both stages. A construction that balances the sums but forgets the group counts would solve ordinary Partition instead of the requested target.

Things to take note of. Handle zero and out-of-range targets explicitly, remove zeros only for the existential problem, and preserve positivity. Prove both stage equivalences, count entries as well as sums, and bound binary arithmetic and output length before claiming a polynomial reduction.

lessons.title: How does SAT reduce to exactly-three-literal SAT?

chapters.title: Do not confuse two kinds of equivalence

transcript.text: How does SAT reduce to exactly-three-literal SAT? In this course SAT takes a conjunction of clauses, while three SAT requires exactly three distinct literals per clause. We will add fresh variables so satisfiability is preserved under assignment extension, not claim the new formula has an identical truth function on the old variable set.

First remove duplicate literals and discard tautological clauses, and treat an empty clause as a fixed unsatisfiable case. These checks preserve satisfiability and ensure the remaining short clauses have the expected distinct original literals. Auxiliary variables must be fresh for each clause so independently chosen extensions do not interfere.

For a two-literal clause, introduce u and make two clauses, one containing u and one containing not u. If either original literal is true, both new clauses are true for either u. If both originals are false, the pair demands u and not u simultaneously, which is impossible.

For a one-literal clause x, introduce u and v and use all four sign combinations of those two variables beside x. When x is true, all four clauses hold. When x is false, every assignment to u and v falsifies one of the four clauses, so there is no satisfying extension.

A four-literal clause uses one linking variable. The first new clause contains its first two literals and u, while the second contains not u and the last two literals. If the originals are all false, one clause forces u true and the other forces it false.

If an original literal on the left is true, choose u false so the right clause is satisfied by not u. If a literal on the right is true, choose u true so the left clause is satisfied by u. This proves the stronger fact that each satisfying assignment to the original variables can be extended to the gadget.

For six literals, chain three fresh variables through four clauses. Each intermediate clause passes the obligation to the next link when its original literal is false, while the final clause must eventually be satisfied by an original literal. A true original clause lets the linking choices switch appropriately, whereas all false literals force a contradiction along the chain.

In general a k-literal clause with k greater than three needs k minus three linking variables and k minus two clauses. The four-literal case has only the first and final clause, so no nonexistent previous linking variable is introduced. The total gadget size is linear in the original literal occurrences after normalization.

For the complete formula, keep each original-variable assignment consistent across all clause gadgets. If the original assignment satisfies every clause, fresh local auxiliary sets let all extensions coexist. If the transformed formula is satisfiable, each gadget forces its original clause true, so the restricted assignment satisfies the entire original conjunction.

Showing each clause individually satisfiable is not enough to prove the conjunction satisfiable, because clauses share original variables. The required statement is original-clause truth under a fixed assignment if and only if some local extension satisfies its gadget. Preserve every negation visually, since PDF text extraction can lose overbars.

Things to take note of. Handle clauses of one, two, three and more literals separately, introduce fresh auxiliaries, and prove both extension directions. Use the course’s exact-three convention, check empty and tautological cases, and distinguish conjunctive normal form from the Chomsky normal form used for grammars.

lessons.title: How do you prove a problem NP-complete?

chapters.title: Keep source and target definitions straight

transcript.text: How do you prove a problem NP-complete? Show that it is in NP, then reduce a known NP-complete problem to it in polynomial time. The first half supplies verifiable witnesses, while the second transfers hardness in the correct direction; neither half can be omitted.

A language is NP-hard when every NP language reduces to it. It is NP-complete only when it is also in NP, so NP-hard alone does not imply an NP verifier or even decidability. The known SAT completeness theorem can be used as a starting point here; the next lessons explain its Cook Levin proof.

Convert optimization MaxSAT into the decision language asking whether at least k clauses of a given formula can be simultaneously satisfied. A truth assignment is a polynomial-size certificate. Evaluate each clause, count the true ones and compare the count with k; checking the conjunction as a single Boolean would lose the requested threshold condition.

For hardness, transform a SAT formula with m clauses into the same formula with threshold m. The SAT instance is satisfiable exactly when all m clauses can be satisfied at once, exactly the target condition. The transformation just counts and writes the threshold, so it is polynomial.

Combining that mapping with the assignment verifier proves decision MaxSAT NP-complete. To recover the optimum number of satisfiable clauses from a decision solver, binary-search the monotone threshold between zero and m. This takes logarithmically many decision calls, but finding the optimum value is not yet the same as printing an optimal assignment.

DoubleSAT asks whether a formula has at least two distinct satisfying assignments. Its NP certificate is two full assignments, with checks that they differ and both satisfy the formula. Listing the same assignment twice does not meet the definition, even if the formula evaluates true both times.

Reduce SAT to DoubleSAT by adjoining a tautological clause involving a fresh variable z. If the original formula is satisfiable, keep its assignment and choose z either false or true, giving two distinct extensions. If the original is unsatisfiable, adding a tautology cannot create a satisfying assignment.

This target language uses general conjunctive normal form, so the new two-literal tautological clause is allowed. Do not silently impose the exact-three restriction from three SAT on DoubleSAT. Valid output syntax is one of the reduction’s obligations, not an afterthought.

The hardness arrow must point from the known hard source into the new target. Reducing the target to SAT gives an upper comparison and does not establish the target NP-hard. Transitivity explains why a known-complete source suffices: every NP language reduces to it and then through your mapping to the target.

If any NP-complete language has a polynomial decider, then every NP language does, implying P equals NP. Conversely, P equals NP would put every NP-complete language in P. NP-completeness therefore does not prove an exponential lower bound or settle the unresolved equality question.

Things to take note of. Formalize the decision version, give a complete polynomial verifier, choose an independently known complete source and prove its mapping into your target. Check both answer directions, output syntax and construction cost; then keep optimization-value recovery separate from the completeness proof.

lessons.title: Why does Cook–Levin encode every NP computation as SAT?

chapters.title: Separate the easy and hard halves
Fix M; transform the input x
Rows are times; columns are cells
Course indicators T, H, S, I
Eight groups make the tableau meaningful
Construction is not solving the original instance

transcript.text: Why does Cook Levin encode every NP computation as SAT? The theorem says SAT is NP-complete, so we need membership in NP and hardness for every NP language. Its key idea is to describe an entire accepting computation with Boolean variables and constraints, rather than search all nondeterministic branches explicitly.

SAT membership is straightforward: a certificate assigns truth values to all variables. A deterministic verifier evaluates the clauses in polynomial time and accepts exactly a satisfying assignment. Hardness is the substantial part, because infinitely many different NP languages must be covered by one general construction method.

Fix an arbitrary NP language and a nondeterministic machine M deciding it within polynomial time T of the input length. Use a suitable standard one-tape form with a polynomial bound at least as large as the input. The reduction may depend on this fixed machine, but its variable input is the particular string x.

A tableau is a grid of configurations. Each row records one time and each column one tape location, with enough cells for all positions the bounded computation can visit. We use configuration times zero through T and transition times zero through T minus one, keeping those endpoint roles distinct.

The course uses four indicator families. T records the symbol in a given cell at a time, H records the head position, S records the current state, and I records the selected instruction. A satisfying assignment chooses all these facts, including one possible nondeterministic transition at each step.

Constraints first require a correctly initialized row and a unique state, head and symbol in each appropriate place. Other groups require an accepting time and one instruction per simulated transition. Finally constrain unchanged non-head cells and the valid read, write, state and movement effects of each selected instruction.

An accepting machine branch supplies a satisfying assignment by recording what actually happens in every row. The initial row is correct, each move obeys the machine and some row accepts. If the branch ends early, pad its accepting configuration by an explicitly defined absorbing convention in the encoding.

Conversely, a satisfying assignment determines one well-defined configuration per row. The initial and local-transition constraints force those rows to be a genuine computation, and the accepting condition supplies an accepting branch. Leaving out unchanged-cell constraints would allow tape contents to change magically far from the head, breaking that reconstruction.

The formula has polynomially many variables and a polynomial-size explicit encoding for fixed M. The reduction writes constraints without first solving whether M accepts x, because satisfiability itself chooses the branch. Nondeterminism is represented existentially by the assignment, not eliminated by an exponential deterministic branch search inside the mapping.

The course’s detailed pairwise head-uniqueness encoding needs a careful polynomial-size count, which the next lesson develops. The theorem requires polynomial size, not an unjustified tight quadratic claim. A different local-window encoding can have a different count, but its rules must be analyzed on their own terms.

Things to take note of. Fix an arbitrary polynomial-time nondeterministic machine, encode its bounded computation and prove both directions of the satisfiability equivalence. State time and tape boundaries, handle early acceptance and justify a polynomial construction; that general method is what covers every language in NP.

lessons.title: How do Cook–Levin constraints prevent a fake computation?

chapters.title: Groups 2 and 3: unique state and symbol

transcript.text: How do Cook Levin constraints prevent a fake computation? We will use the course’s four indicator families and explain all eight groups of conditions. The goal is a valid accepting bounded machine run, not merely a colourful grid that happens to contain an accepting-state symbol.

The initial-configuration group fixes the start state, initial head cell, input symbols and all remaining blank cells. Without these facts, a satisfying tableau might describe a machine started on the wrong input or in a helpful later configuration. The formula is supposed to answer membership for this particular input x.

The next groups require exactly one state per time and exactly one symbol in every cell at every time. Exactly one means at least one, plus pairwise clauses forbidding two simultaneously true choices. It is not an exclusive-or parity condition, which would allow three true choices.

Head uniqueness requires one and only one head position in every configuration. An at-least-one head clause prevents no-head rows, and the pairwise negative clauses prevent a machine from simultaneously reading several distant cells. The head-position indicators are separate from the state and tape-symbol indicators in the course’s encoding.

Acceptance requires an accepting state at some configuration time, including time zero if immediate acceptance is possible. Instruction uniqueness chooses one machine instruction at each transition time, not after the final configuration. For early halting, normalize the bounded encoding with a consistent absorbing continuation instead of accidentally requiring an ordinary halted machine to move.

Non-head cells must keep their tape contents. A convenient clause says that if the head is not here and this cell contains b now, it still contains b next time. In conjunctive normal form this is head-here or not-current-b or next-b, together with the unique-symbol conditions.

The valid-transition group ties the chosen instruction to the correct old state and read symbol. It also enforces the new state, the written symbol at the head cell and the new head position. All these implications are needed; checking only the write would still permit an impossible state change or head jump.

Use the actual tape-boundary convention when writing the new-head condition. A left move at the left end must not refer to an undefined cell zero if the encoding numbers cells from one. Likewise, a constraint mentioning time i plus one must stop at i equal to T minus one, not create an unencoded T plus one row.

For a fixed machine, the numbers of states, symbols and possible instructions are constants. With order T times and order T cells, the indicator count is order T squared. However, pairwise head uniqueness uses order T squared pairs at each time, yielding order T cubed such clauses over all rows.

The at-least-one head clauses also have length proportional to the number of cells, so not every displayed clause has constant length. Including written variable indices adds logarithmic representation factors, still leaving a polynomial-size formula because T itself is polynomial in input length. The theorem survives; the raw deck’s blanket quadratic constant-clause summary does not describe this literal expansion accurately.

For the forward correctness direction, fill every indicator from a legal padded accepting branch and check each constraint group. For the reverse, uniqueness gives actual rows, initialization gives the right input, and transition plus unchanged-cell conditions give a legal run. Acceptance then identifies a successful branch, completing the required if and only if.

Things to take note of. Explain each constraint’s purpose and a fake tableau it forbids, rather than memorizing an overbar-sensitive formula without meaning. Keep row and transition indices consistent, define padding and boundaries, and count the particular encoding you use; polynomial correctness matters more than an unsupported tight exponent.

qs.stem: Run DFS only from A. What does this search establish about cycles?
qs.correct: The reachable subgraph {A,B} is acyclic; it does not decide acyclicity of the whole graph.
qs.why: A reaches only B. The separate component containing C,D,E is unvisited, so a single-source search cannot rule out a cycle there.
options: The entire graph is acyclic because no back edge was found.
The entire graph has a cycle because AB is a tree edge.
It visits C,D,E before returning from A.
The reachable subgraph {A,B} is acyclic; it does not decide acyclicity of the whole graph.

options: At C, seeing parent B; only reverse parent scans certify cycles.
At C, seeing visited non-parent A; the reverse scan B->A alone is not a certificate.
No cycle can exist because DFS tree edges form a tree.
At B, seeing parent A; every edge to a visited vertex certifies a cycle.

qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: Can constants c and n0 depend on n in a Big-O proof?
options: Both may vary with every input
Only c may depend on n
Only n0 may depend on n
qs.why: The quantifier order chooses constants before requiring the inequality for every sufficiently large n.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: For n≥1, which pair witnesses 3n²+7n+4∈Θ(n²)?
qs.why: Use n≤n² and 1≤n² to obtain the upper coefficient 3+7+4=14.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: A worst-case cost W(n) is Θ(n²). Which statement must hold?
qs.why: For n≥1, n²≤n³; an upper bound need not be tight. Worst-case information does not determine every input.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: If f∈O(g) and g∈O(h), which implication follows?
qs.why: Multiply the two fixed upper-bound constants and take the larger threshold.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a bound from a case?
qs.correct: O is an upper bound; worst case selects a cost function
options: Ω means best case by definition
O is an upper bound; worst case selects a cost function
O means worst case by definition
Θ means average case by definition
qs.why: One can give O, Ω or Θ bounds on best-, average- or worst-case functions.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: Let f(n)=n² for even n and n for odd n. What is true relative to n²?
qs.why: On odd n, f/n²=1/n tends to zero, preventing a positive eventual lower constant.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: For f(n)=n and g(n)=n(2+sin n), what tight relation holds for n≥1?
options: f grows strictly faster than g
qs.why: Since 1≤2+sin n≤3, g/3≤f≤g despite oscillation.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: For f(n)=n² and g(n)=n³, which combination is true?
qs.why: The ratio f/g=1/n tends to zero; upper and reverse lower bounds hold, but not tight equivalence.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: If f,g are eventually positive and f∈Θ(g), what follows?
options: Their exact operation counts are equal
qs.why: Invert the two positive constant inequalities; Θ is symmetric, exact equality is unnecessary.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: Let f(n)=n² for even n and n³ for odd n, for positive integers n. Classify f against both n² and n³, requiring each bound to hold for every sufficiently large integer. Which complete classification is correct?
qs.correct: f∈Ω(n²)∩O(n³), but f is Θ of neither n² nor n³
options: f∈Θ(n²) because infinitely many inputs are quadratic
f∈Ω(n²)∩O(n³), but f is Θ of neither n² nor n³
f∈Θ(n³) because the largest branch is cubic
qs.why: n²≤f≤n³ for every n≥1. Odd n make f/n²=n unbounded, ruling out O(n²); even n make f/n³=1/n tend to zero, ruling out Ω(n³). Infinitely many matching inputs do not supply an eventual two-sided bound.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

n log n and n² have identical leading terms

qs.stem: A loop sets i=1, and while i≤n runs an inner loop exactly i times before doubling i. For n=128, find the number of outer iterations and total inner executions; then classify total work on powers of two under constant-time loop operations.

qs.stem: For n>1, how does n/log n compare with n in tight order?

qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp32–33; study notes 01-analysis §1.6.
qs.context: Use the supplied Master-Theorem cases and the course logarithmic extension with k≥0. Every polynomial-gap epsilon must be one fixed positive constant.

qs.stem: For 2T(n/2)+n/log n, why does supplied case 1 fail?
qs.correct: n/log n is not O(n^(1−epsilon)) for any fixed epsilon>0
options: The toll is larger than n²
n/log n is not O(n^(1−epsilon)) for any fixed epsilon>0
qs.why: The ratio (n/log n)/n^(1−epsilon)=n^epsilon/log n is unbounded.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp32–33; study notes 01-analysis §1.6.
qs.context: Use the supplied Master-Theorem cases and the course logarithmic extension with k≥0. Every polynomial-gap epsilon must be one fixed positive constant.

qs.stem: For 2T(n/2)+n/log n, why does supplied plain case 2 fail?
qs.why: The comparison exponent is one, but the toll-to-n ratio tends to zero.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp32–33; study notes 01-analysis §1.6.
qs.context: Use the supplied Master-Theorem cases and the course logarithmic extension with k≥0. Every polynomial-gap epsilon must be one fixed positive constant.

qs.stem: The course case-2 log extension assumes k≥0. Can it be used with f=n log^(−1)n?
qs.correct: No; k=−1 lies outside its stated hypothesis
options: Only if n is a power of two
No; k=−1 lies outside its stated hypothesis
qs.why: An extension must be used with its actual stated range; another proof can handle this recurrence.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp32–33; study notes 01-analysis §1.6.
qs.context: Use the supplied Master-Theorem cases and the course logarithmic extension with k≥0. Every polynomial-gap epsilon must be one fixed positive constant.

qs.stem: For 2T(n/2)+n/log n, why does supplied case 3 fail?
qs.correct: The toll is smaller than n, not polynomially larger
options: The toll is smaller than n, not polynomially larger
Its regularity ratio is always zero
qs.why: Comparison is against n^(log₂2)=n; the required lower polynomial gap is absent.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp32–33; study notes 01-analysis §1.6.
qs.context: Use the supplied Master-Theorem cases and the course logarithmic extension with k≥0. Every polynomial-gap epsilon must be one fixed positive constant.

qs.stem: Suppose a toll is n log n and comparison term is n. What does the course k≥0 logarithmic extension give?
qs.why: This is k=1 within the extension; unlike k=−1, it adds one log power.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp32–33; study notes 01-analysis §1.6.
qs.context: Use the supplied Master-Theorem cases and the course logarithmic extension with k≥0. Every polynomial-gap epsilon must be one fixed positive constant.

qs.stem: A proof claims log n≥n^0.01 eventually. What is the consequence for its case-3 argument?
qs.correct: The premise is false; n^0.01 eventually exceeds log n
options: The premise holds only for base-two logs
The premise is false; n^0.01 eventually exceeds log n
The proof is valid because 0.01 is small
qs.why: Every fixed positive power eventually dominates the logarithm, however slowly.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp32–33; study notes 01-analysis §1.6.
qs.context: Use the supplied Master-Theorem cases and the course logarithmic extension with k≥0. Every polynomial-gap epsilon must be one fixed positive constant.

qs.stem: For T(n)=T(n−1)+1, what prevents the standard Master-Theorem form?
qs.correct: The shrink factor is not a fixed b>1
options: There is only one recursive call
The recurrence has a base case
The shrink factor is not a fixed b>1
qs.why: Subtracting one is not division by one fixed b>1; expansion gives a different-depth tree.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp32–33; study notes 01-analysis §1.6.
qs.context: Use the supplied Master-Theorem cases and the course logarithmic extension with k≥0. Every polynomial-gap epsilon must be one fixed positive constant.

qs.stem: Can one infer that f(n)=Ω(nᵖ) implies case 3?
qs.correct: No; case 3 needs a fixed positive polynomial gap plus regularity
options: Yes; Ω always means a strict gap
Only when f has positive coefficients
No; case 3 needs a fixed positive polynomial gap plus regularity
qs.why: The equal case f=Θ(nᵖ) itself disproves that inference.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp32–33; study notes 01-analysis §1.6.
qs.context: Use the supplied Master-Theorem cases and the course logarithmic extension with k≥0. Every polynomial-gap epsilon must be one fixed positive constant.

qs.stem: Let T(3)=1 and T(n)=3T(n/3)+n/log₃n for n=3ᴸ,L≥2. The supplied logarithmic case2 assumes k≥0. Expand the tree instead: internal level i costs n/(L−i), and sum from r=2 to L of1/r is Θ(log L). Which result and theorem diagnosis follow?
qs.correct: Θ(n log log n);the supplied cases miss the inverse-log toll
options: Θ(n log log n);the supplied cases miss the inverse-log toll
Θ(n log n);ordinary case2 applies because p=1
qs.why: The internal sum is n times the harmonic sum from2 through L, giving Θ(n log L), and n/3 leaves add Θ(n). Since L=log₃n, this is Θ(n log log n). The inverse-log toll is below n without a fixed polynomial gap and has k=−1 outside the stated extension.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp32–33; study notes 01-analysis §1.6.
qs.context: Use the supplied Master-Theorem cases and the course logarithmic extension with k≥0. Every polynomial-gap epsilon must be one fixed positive constant.

topics.title: How do we prove a recurrence bound by substitution?
topics.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7. Matching later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.
topics.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: What is the first step of a substitution proof?
qs.correct: State a precise bound and induction domain
options: Assume the desired conclusion without conditions
State a precise bound and induction domain
qs.why: A quantified claim specifies constants, valid n values and bases to prove.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: In an induction proof, where may the induction hypothesis be used?
qs.correct: On smaller arguments covered by the hypothesis
options: On smaller arguments covered by the hypothesis
On the current n without proof
qs.why: Recursive child sizes must lie in the chosen domain and precede n.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: Does proving T(n)≤c n² alone prove Θ(n²)?
qs.correct: No; it proves an upper bound only
options: Yes; any upper bound is tight
No; it proves an upper bound only
It proves only a lower bound
qs.why: A matching eventual lower bound must be supplied separately.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: Why check base cases after choosing constants?
qs.correct: The constants must satisfy both bases and induction step
options: The constants must satisfy both bases and induction step
qs.why: An induction cannot start if the chosen bound fails at its initial inputs.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: For T(1)=0 and T(n)=T(n−1)+n−1, prove T(n)≤n². Which inductive expression appears?
qs.why: Substituting T(n−1)≤(n−1)² gives slack n, enough for the upper bound.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: Under T(1)=0 and T(n)=T(n−1)+n−1, what is T(4)?
qs.why: The successive values are 0,1,3,6 by adding 1,2,3.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: Why can a stronger induction claim be easier to prove?
qs.correct: Extra slack can absorb additive terms
options: Extra slack can absorb additive terms
qs.why: A carefully chosen lower-order subtraction or extra constant may close the algebra.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: For T(n)=2T(n/2)+n−1, T(1)=1 on powers of two, why does T(n)≤c n log₂n fail at n=1?
qs.correct: The right side is zero but T(1)=1
options: It fails only for negative c
The right side is zero but T(1)=1
qs.why: No finite c makes a zero upper expression cover a positive base.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: For T(1)=1,T(n)=2T(n/2)+n−1 on powers of two, start the claim T(n)≤c n log₂n at n=2. Which c is sufficient for the base and usual step?
qs.why: T(2)=3≤4 when c=2; substitution yields c n log₂n−c n+n−1≤c n log₂n.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: For T(1)=1, T(n)=2T(n/2)+n−1, which exact solution fits powers of two?
qs.why: Substitute: 2[(n/2)(log₂n−1)+1]+n−1=n log₂n+1; it also fits n=1.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: An induction proves its step only for even n but claims every positive integer n. What is missing?
qs.correct: A proof covering odd n or a restricted stated domain
options: A larger constant alone always fixes it
A proof covering odd n or a restricted stated domain
No issue; all integers are even asymptotically
qs.why: Rounding and child domains must be justified; a powers-of-two proof cannot silently become an all-integer proof.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: If a guessed bound fails in the induction algebra, what is justified?
qs.correct: Revise the claim or method and prove the new statement
options: Declare the guess false in all cases
Revise the claim or method and prove the new statement
Use the induction conclusion as a premise
qs.why: An unsuccessful proof attempt does not itself disprove a bound; missing slack or an unsuitable hypothesis may be responsible.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: For T(1)=1,T(n)=2T(n/2)+n−1 on powers of two, derive T(32) and select an upper-bound induction claim valid even at n=1. Which pair is correct?
qs.correct: T(32)=161;T(n)≤n log₂n+n for all powers of two n≥1
options: T(32)=161;T(n)≤n log₂n+n for all powers of two n≥1
qs.why: The exact recurrence solves to n log₂n+1: substitution gives n log₂n+1 and the base is1. ThusT(32)=32·5+1=161. Since1≤n, the proposed bound holds at the base and leaves enough additive slack; n log n alone fails at1.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp35–42,46; Review Week 8 pp14–16; Review Week 9 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §1.7.
qs.context: Substitution means a quantified induction proof, not merely substitution of sample values. Use each question’s stated recurrence and base; powers-of-two recurrences are restricted to that domain.

qs.stem: For T(n)=n+T(n−2), which property determines the terminal base?
qs.correct: Whether n is even or odd
options: The value of n modulo three
Whether n is even or odd

qs.why: Even halves are integral; odd halves round in opposite directions.

qs.stem: For n=2k, which exact formula follows?
qs.why: Sum 2+4+…+2k=k(k+1), then replace the first 2 by base value one.

qs.stem: For n=2k+1, which exact formula follows?
qs.why: Sum 3+5+…+(2k+1), with T(1)=0: the odd-number square sum minus one gives k(k+2).

qs.stem: Why can exact formulas differ by parity while both have Θ(n²) growth?
qs.correct: Their leading terms are quadratic and lower-order corrections differ
options: Parity disappears from every exact count
Θ requires the exact same formula
Their leading terms are quadratic and lower-order corrections differ
Odd inputs are never asymptotic inputs
qs.why: Put k=n/2 or (n−1)/2 into the formulas; each has leading coefficient 1/4.

qs.stem: For T(n)=T(n−2)+n, T(1)=0 and T(2)=1, what is T(9)?
qs.why: 9+7+5+3+0=24; equivalently k=4 gives k(k+2)=24.
qs.source: Review Week 8 pp10–12; Analysis Techniques pp43–45; study notes 01-analysis §§1.5,1.7.

qs.stem: When extending a divide recurrence from powers of two to all n, what needs justification?
qs.correct: Rounding, bases and any monotonicity used to compare sizes
options: Rounding, bases and any monotonicity used to compare sizes
Assuming floor and ceiling are always identical
qs.why: Floors/ceilings alter child sizes; the comparison argument must be stated rather than presumed.
qs.source: Review Week 8 pp10–12; Analysis Techniques pp43–45; study notes 01-analysis §§1.5,1.7.

qs.stem: If T(2) changes from 1 to 9 but T(1) stays 0 in the subtraction-by-two recurrence, which inputs change?
qs.why: Every even expansion reaches T(2) once; odd expansions reach T(1) instead.

qs.stem: For T(1)=0,T(2)=1,T(n)=T(n−2)+n, compute T(18),T(19). Then change only T(2) to5 and recompute both. Which ordered values are correct?
qs.why: For18=2·9, the even formula gives9·10−1=89. For19=2·9+1, the odd formula gives9·11=99. Only even expansions reach T(2), exactly once, so changing that base by4 adds4 only to T(18).

topics.title: How does greedy coin change work, and when does it fail?
topics.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2. Matching later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.
topics.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: What choice does largest-first coin greedy make?
qs.correct: The largest denomination not exceeding the remainder
options: The largest denomination not exceeding the remainder
qs.why: It makes a locally largest feasible choice and repeats on the remainder.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.
qs.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: With coins {1,5,10,25}, what is the first greedy choice for amount 37?
qs.why: 25 is the largest available coin at most 37.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.
qs.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: After selecting 25 from amount 37, what remains?
qs.why: Subtract the chosen coin: 37−25=12.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.
qs.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: Does a locally largest coin guarantee a globally minimum count for arbitrary denominations?
options: Yes if the target is even
qs.why: A feasible local choice can obstruct a better combination.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.
qs.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: For amount 6 with unlimited coins {1,3,4}, what does largest-first greedy return?
qs.why: Take 4, remainder 2, then two ones. The two threes are a better feasible solution.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.
qs.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: For amount 37 and coins {1,5,10,25}, what greedy sequence is selected?
qs.why: 37→12→2→1→0 uses four valid coins.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.
qs.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: How can a denomination-at-a-time implementation avoid looping once per emitted coin?
qs.correct: Use quotient and remainder for each denomination
options: Use quotient and remainder for each denomination
Treat the answer count as zero
qs.why: take=remaining//coin and remaining%=coin compute the multiplicity in constant arithmetic work per denomination.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.
qs.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: For target 14 and denominations {1,7,10}, compare greedy count with optimum.
qs.why: Greedy uses 10+1+1+1+1; 7+7 uses two coins.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.
qs.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: For k unsorted denominations and constant-time word arithmetic, what cost covers sorting and quotient/remainder scanning?
qs.correct: O(k log k) sorting plus O(k) scan
options: O(k log k) sorting plus O(k) scan
qs.why: Sort once; then process each denomination once. Explicitly listing every coin adds output cost.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.
qs.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: With coins {4,6} and target 8, greedy takes 6 and gets stuck. What does this show?
qs.correct: Greedy failure does not prove the target unreachable
options: Greedy failure does not prove the target unreachable
qs.why: The legal combination 4+4 reaches 8 even though the greedy remainder 2 is impossible.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.
qs.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: If an implementation explicitly emits M chosen coins, what lower bound applies to its output work?
qs.why: Writing M output items takes at least linear work in M; multiplicity encoding changes output representation.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.
qs.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: What suffices to refute universal optimality of largest-first coin greedy?
qs.correct: One denomination set and target with a better feasible solution
options: One denomination set and target with a better feasible solution
One instance where greedy is optimal
qs.why: A universal claim is disproved by a single valid counterexample, such as {1,3,4}, target 6.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.
qs.context: Unlimited positive integer coin denominations; form the exact target. Largest-first greedy repeatedly chooses the largest feasible denomination. Do not invent unavailable coins.

qs.stem: Use unlimited coins{1,7,10}, descending largest-first without backtracking. For each target14 and28, report(greedy coin count,exact minimum count). Which pair of pairs is correct?
qs.why: For14 greedy takes10+four ones, while7+7 uses2. For28 greedy takes10+10+7+1, using4, and four sevens also use4. No three coins sum28: their maximum30 requires replacing at least one10 by7 or1, giving at most27. Greedy can fail on one target and succeed on another.
qs.source: Greedy Algorithms pp3–7; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.1–6.2.

topics.title: How do memoisation and tabulation remove repeated work?
topics.source: Dynamic Programming pp3–18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5–6.7. Matching later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.
topics.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: What does memoisation save?
qs.correct: Computed answers indexed by subproblem state
options: Computed answers indexed by subproblem state
qs.why: Repeated requests reuse an answer instead of recomputing that state.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp3–18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5–6.7.
qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: What distinguishes tabulation from memoised top-down recursion?
qs.correct: It explicitly evaluates states in a dependency-compatible order
options: It explicitly evaluates states in a dependency-compatible order
qs.why: Both can implement the same recurrence; evaluation order and call-stack use differ.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp3–18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5–6.7.
qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: For F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2), which subproblem repeats when expanding F(6)?

qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: What must be stored when zero is a legitimate result?
qs.correct: A separate indication of whether a state was computed
options: A separate indication of whether a state was computed
Only a zero-filled array with zero meaning absent
No cache entry for zero answers
The answer plus one as the mathematical result
qs.why: A valid zero must not be mistaken for an uncomputed entry.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp3–18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5–6.7.
qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: How many distinct Fibonacci states F(0)..F(6) are there?

qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: For memoised Fibonacci through n, what standard time bound follows with constant-time arithmetic?
qs.why: There are n+1 states and at most two constant-time transitions per state.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp3–18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5–6.7.
qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: What space costs must memoised recursive Fibonacci account for?
qs.why: The recursion can have depth O(n), in addition to O(n) cached values.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp3–18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5–6.7.
qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: When can iterative Fibonacci use O(1) extra words?
qs.correct: When only the final value is needed and two predecessors suffice
options: When only the final value is needed and two predecessors suffice
When arbitrary reconstruction needs the full table
When every prior value must remain available
qs.why: The recurrence depends on two previous values; keeping the whole history is unnecessary for final-value computation.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp3–18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5–6.7.
qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: Why can counting distinct states alone underestimate DP runtime?
qs.correct: Each state may examine many transitions
options: No DP can have polynomial states
Each state may examine many transitions
Distinct states equal recursive calls including repeats
Every state always costs one CPU instruction
qs.why: Total work is states times transition cost, plus setup and reconstruction where applicable.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp3–18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5–6.7.
qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: Does top-down memoisation necessarily evaluate every theoretically possible state?
qs.correct: No; it may visit only states reachable from the requested answer
options: No; it may visit only states reachable from the requested answer
Only if all answers are nonzero
qs.why: On-demand recursion can avoid unreachable states; a full bottom-up table may still fill them.

qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: Why does a cyclic recurrence need more than ordinary acyclic memoised recursion?
qs.correct: A state may depend on itself before its answer is finished
options: All cycles imply no solution exists
A state may depend on itself before its answer is finished
qs.why: One must resolve the dependency cycle with an appropriate formulation/algorithm rather than recursively waiting on unfinished values.

qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: If each of n states scans n predecessors, what total transition bound follows?
qs.why: n states times O(n) work per state yields quadratic work despite memoisation.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp3–18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5–6.7.
qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

qs.stem: The naive recursive Fibonacci function has bases F(0)=0,F(1)=1 and makes exactly two recursive calls on every nonbase invocation. Count all invocations including the initial F(8) and base calls. Compare this with the number of distinct states a memoised computation of F(8) can compute and its general cache-plus-stack bound.
qs.correct: 67 naive invocations;9 distinct states;O(n) cache plus O(n) stack
options: 67 naive invocations;9 distinct states;O(n) cache plus O(n) stack
qs.why: Call counts satisfy C(0)=C(1)=1,C(n)=1+C(n−1)+C(n−2), yielding1,1,3,5,9,15,25,41,67. Distinct indices are0..8, nine states. Memoisation removes repeated computation but a recursive dependency chain still has linear depth.

qs.context: Use F(0)=0,F(1)=1,F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for the Fibonacci examples. Complexity counts constant-time arithmetic operations unless bit costs are explicitly discussed.

Both report unreachable because greedy gets stuck

topics.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: How many binary digits encode positive capacity C without leading zeros?
qs.why: Binary place values grow exponentially with digit count.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: What integer does binary 1000 represent?
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: What does pseudo-polynomial time mean here?
qs.correct: Polynomial in numeric magnitudes, potentially exponential in their binary encoding lengths
options: Polynomial in every binary input length
Polynomial in numeric magnitudes, potentially exponential in their binary encoding lengths
qs.why: The representation of the input matters when capacity or target indexes a table.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: Why is O(nC) knapsack DP not automatically polynomial in binary input length?
qs.correct: C can be exponential in the number of bits used to encode it
options: C can be exponential in the number of bits used to encode it
qs.why: A short capacity field can denote a huge numeric table range.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: If C=2ᵇ, how does the capacity dimension scale with b?
qs.why: The table indexes the numeric capacity, not merely its exponent or bit count.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: Does exact knapsack DP contradict NP-completeness of the binary-encoded decision version?
qs.correct: No; its numeric-capacity bound is pseudo-polynomial
options: Only if the capacity is even
Yes; all exact algorithms are polynomial
No; its numeric-capacity bound is pseudo-polynomial
qs.why: Exactness and polynomial binary-input running time are distinct properties.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: Why is ordinary LCS O(nm) polynomial in the explicit string input lengths?
qs.correct: n and m count explicitly supplied characters
options: LCS uses capacity as a binary integer
All DP bounds are polynomial by definition
n and m count explicitly supplied characters
qs.why: The state dimensions are bounded directly by the actual explicit input lengths.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: For k coin types and target A in binary, what does the O(kA) coin-DP bound depend on?
options: Only the largest coin label length
qs.why: There is a state for every amount up to A, even though A may have a short binary encoding.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: If C is supplied in unary, how does the O(nC) bound relate to input length?
qs.correct: It is polynomial in that encoding length
options: It is polynomial in that encoding length
It proves polynomial time for every encoding
qs.why: Unary capacity alone uses Θ(C) symbols, making the table dimension bounded by input size.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: For n=20 and C=1024, how many interior capacity/item combinations does an n-by-C count give?
qs.why: 20·1024=20,480; this operation estimate differs from the 11-bit capacity field length.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: Doubling a binary capacity from 2ᵇ to 2^(b+1) does what to its bit length and the capacity table range?
qs.correct: Adds one bit; roughly doubles the table range
options: Adds one bit; roughly doubles the table range
Doubles both bit length and range
qs.why: The encoding grows additively while numeric capacity grows multiplicatively.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: What qualification belongs to a word-operation O(nC) analysis?
qs.correct: Arithmetic operands must fit the assumed constant-time model
options: It proves all arbitrary-length arithmetic is free
Arithmetic operands must fit the assumed constant-time model
It is a bound on the number of feasible subsets
It forces every run to fill maximum possible capacity
qs.why: Operation counts and bit costs are different; representation and implementation must be stated.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

qs.stem: Consider a family with b items,capacity C=2ᵇ−1,and positive weights/profits each at most2ᵇ. Their explicit binary encodings have O(b²) total bits. A full capacity DP evaluates every item/capacity pair. Which state count and encoded-size conclusion are correct?
qs.correct: Θ(b2ᵇ) states;this is not polynomial in the O(b²)-bit input bound
options: Θ(b2ᵇ) states;therefore every algorithm for the problem is exponential
Θ(b²) states;capacity has only b bits so the table is polynomial
Θ(b2ᵇ) states;this is not polynomial in the O(b²)-bit input bound
Θ(2b) states;doubling capacity adds only one state
qs.why: The table dimensions are b+1 and C+1=2ᵇ,so its size is Θ(b2ᵇ). The short capacity field does not shrink the numeric capacity range. This establishes a pseudo-polynomial limitation of this DP,not a lower bound for every possible algorithm.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp64–65; Introduction to NP p14; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §6.11.
qs.context: Measure encoded input length, distinguishing numeric capacity C or amount A from its binary digit count. O(nC) and O(kA) count assumed constant-time arithmetic operations.

topics.title: How do we choose a correct state and strategy?
topics.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12. Matching later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.
topics.context: DP states must preserve future legality and value; transitions must represent every relevant choice. State and graph assumptions are part of the problem, not implicit permissions to replace constraints.

qs.stem: What must a DP state retain?
qs.correct: All information needed to determine valid future choices and value
options: Every prior operation regardless of relevance
All information needed to determine valid future choices and value
qs.why: Histories may be merged only when the retained state preserves the relevant future problem.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.
qs.context: DP states must preserve future legality and value; transitions must represent every relevant choice. State and graph assumptions are part of the problem, not implicit permissions to replace constraints.

qs.stem: What does optimal substructure say?
qs.correct: An optimum can be composed using optimal solutions of suitable subproblems
options: An optimum can be composed using optimal solutions of suitable subproblems
Every local greedy choice is safe
qs.why: The subproblems and their constraints must be defined so replacement is legal.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.
qs.context: DP states must preserve future legality and value; transitions must represent every relevant choice. State and graph assumptions are part of the problem, not implicit permissions to replace constraints.

qs.stem: What do overlapping subproblems make useful?
qs.why: Reuse removes repeated evaluation of the same mathematical state.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.

qs.stem: Which strategy usually commits to one locally preferred choice?
options: DP enumeration of all relevant alternatives
qs.why: A greedy method needs a proof that its chosen commitment is safe.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.
qs.context: DP states must preserve future legality and value; transitions must represent every relevant choice. State and graph assumptions are part of the problem, not implicit permissions to replace constraints.

qs.stem: Why must a replacement in an optimal-substructure proof be legal?
qs.correct: An infeasible replacement cannot contradict optimality
options: Any better numeric score is enough regardless of constraints
An infeasible replacement cannot contradict optimality
qs.why: The contradiction requires an improved feasible whole solution.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.
qs.context: DP states must preserve future legality and value; transitions must represent every relevant choice. State and graph assumptions are part of the problem, not implicit permissions to replace constraints.

qs.stem: Why is capacity alone insufficient for the standard 0/1-knapsack state across arbitrary histories?
qs.correct: Different remaining item sets can give different future choices
options: All item sets with equal capacity are identical
Different remaining item sets can give different future choices
qs.why: The item-prefix/availability information is needed to prevent reuse and distinguish feasible continuations.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.
qs.context: DP states must preserve future legality and value; transitions must represent every relevant choice. State and graph assumptions are part of the problem, not implicit permissions to replace constraints.

qs.stem: Why can LCS use two prefix lengths as its state?
qs.correct: They uniquely specify the two remaining prefix subproblems
options: The two lengths must be equal
They encode every possible subsequence explicitly
They uniquely specify the two remaining prefix subproblems
qs.why: The fixed input strings plus prefix endpoints determine the available ordered characters.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.
qs.context: DP states must preserve future legality and value; transitions must represent every relevant choice. State and graph assumptions are part of the problem, not implicit permissions to replace constraints.

qs.stem: What is the usual runtime accounting rule for a DP?
qs.correct: Number of states times work per state, plus relevant extra costs
options: Number of states times work per state, plus relevant extra costs
qs.why: Initialization, reconstruction and recursion storage also need attention where material.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.

qs.stem: Why does a shortest-path replacement argument need stated path assumptions?
qs.correct: A substitute may violate constraints such as simplicity or resource limits
options: Path problems have no optimal substructure
A substitute may violate constraints such as simplicity or resource limits
qs.why: Substructure depends on the legal subproblem; arbitrary replacement may not preserve the original constraints.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.
qs.context: DP states must preserve future legality and value; transitions must represent every relevant choice. State and graph assumptions are part of the problem, not implicit permissions to replace constraints.

qs.stem: Two histories reach the same location but have different remaining budgets. Can location alone always be a correct state?
options: Yes if both histories have equal length
Yes because the location is identical
qs.why: A budget-constrained problem needs sufficient resource information to distinguish future legality.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.
qs.context: DP states must preserve future legality and value; transitions must represent every relevant choice. State and graph assumptions are part of the problem, not implicit permissions to replace constraints.

qs.stem: A recurrence examines every legal last choice and combines it with an optimal smaller state. What else is needed for a correctness argument?
qs.correct: Show every feasible optimum is represented and every constructed option is feasible
options: Assume the largest index is optimal
Show every feasible optimum is represented and every constructed option is feasible
qs.why: Exhaustiveness and feasibility connect recurrence choices to the actual optimisation problem.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.
