qs.stem: When can divide-and-conquer avoid needing a memoisation table?
qs.correct: When recursive subproblems do not repeat materially
options: Only when it uses no recursion
When recursive subproblems do not repeat materially
Only when every branch returns zero
qs.why: Memoisation targets overlap; independent branches can be solved directly without repeated-state savings.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.
qs.context: DP states must preserve future legality and value; transitions must represent every relevant choice. State and graph assumptions are part of the problem, not implicit permissions to replace constraints.

qs.stem: In a DAG profit-maximisation problem with total resource budget5,two histories reach v with the same profit10. The first used1 resource unit,the second4. The only outgoing edge from v consumes3 and adds5 profit;there are no other history constraints. Which state distinction and continuation outcomes are correct?
qs.correct: Keep remaining budget:the first history can reach profit15;the second cannot take the edge
options: Merge by location and profit:both can reach15
Merge by location:neither can extend because a history used4
Keep remaining budget:the first history can reach profit15;the second cannot take the edge
Discard the first history because it used less resource
qs.why: Remaining budgets are4 and1. The edge is legal only with at least3 available. Equal location/current profit does not imply equivalent feasible futures;state(location,remaining budget) preserves the relevant difference for this DAG formulation.
qs.source: Dynamic Programming pp20–21,28–29,66–67; Greedy Algorithms p18; study notes 06-greedy-and-dp §§6.5,6.12.
qs.context: DP states must preserve future legality and value; transitions must represent every relevant choice. State and graph assumptions are part of the problem, not implicit permissions to replace constraints.

qs.stem: What does exact string matching require at a successful start?
qs.correct: Consecutive text characters equal the entire pattern
options: Only the first character must match
Consecutive text characters equal the entire pattern
qs.why: This searches a substring occurrence, unlike subsequence matching.

qs.stem: If m>n, what should a complete-window matcher return?

qs.why: The straightforward naive algorithm restarts each candidate window.

qs.stem: What parameter-sensitive worst-case scan bound applies for 1≤m≤n?

qs.stem: If an empty-pattern convention returns zero, what must the implementation avoid?
qs.why: An empty pattern has no character at position zero; handle the convention explicitly.

qs.stem: What extra space does a straightforward naive scan need beyond immutable input strings?
qs.why: A fixed number of start and comparison indices suffices.

qs.stem: Override the default inputs. First-match naive scanning compares left-to-right in T=AAAAAAAAB,P=AAAAB. Separately an all-matches naive scan checks every full window for P=AAA in T=AAAAAA. Count actual character checks,including mismatches. Which first index and two totals are correct?
qs.correct: First index4,25 checks;the separate all-matches scan uses12 checks
options: First index4,9 checks;the separate scan uses3 checks
First index4,25 checks;the separate all-matches scan uses12 checks
First index5,20 checks;the separate scan uses18 checks
First index4,20 checks;the separate scan uses12 checks
qs.why: The first text has five legal windows:four fail only on their fifth comparison and the last matches fully,so25 checks and start4. The separate length-six text has four length-three windows;all match,but an all-matches scan continues,using4·3=12 checks.
qs.source: String Matching pp2–10; study notes 07-string-matching §§7.1–7.2.
qs.context: Default text T=ABABABAC,pattern P=ABAC. Use zero-based indices, left-to-right naive comparisons, reset pattern index at each window and return the first match. Count character checks only.

topics.title: How do rolling hashes make Rabin–Karp work?

qs.stem: How much arithmetic work hashes one length-m pattern by modular Horner evaluation?
qs.why: Each symbol performs a fixed number of assumed word operations.

qs.context: Exact verified Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13,window length2,H=10. Use canonical residues 0..q−1; zero-based occurrence starts.

qs.stem: Can increasing a finite modulus eliminate every possible collision among arbitrarily long strings?
qs.correct: No; infinitely many strings map to finitely many residues
options: No; infinitely many strings map to finitely many residues
Yes if the base is ten
Yes if the modulus is prime
qs.why: The pigeonhole principle still applies; exactness relies on verifying candidates.
qs.source: String Matching pp11–15,20–24; study notes 07-string-matching §§7.3–7.4.
qs.context: Exact verified Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13,window length2,H=10. Use canonical residues 0..q−1; zero-based occurrence starts.

qs.stem: Run an all-matches verified Rabin–Karp variant on T=122525,P=25,d=10,q=13. Unlike first-match search,it continues after success. List every length-two window hash,every zero-based true start,and total direct character comparisons,stopping each failed verification at its first mismatch.
qs.why: Windows12,22,25,52,25 reduce to12,9,12,0,12. Hash-equal12 is rejected with one character check;each true25 needs two. Total1+2+2=5. Continuing after the first occurrence exposes the second true match at4.

topics.title: What determines Rabin–Karp’s actual runtime?
topics.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4. Matching later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.
topics.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: What is a spurious hit?
options: Different hashes for equal strings under the same hash
qs.why: The hash filter admits a false candidate that direct comparison rejects.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.
qs.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: Does every verified candidate require exactly m character comparisons?
qs.correct: No; a mismatch may occur earlier
options: No; a mismatch may occur earlier
qs.why: Verification stops at its first mismatch, or after all m characters match.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.
qs.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: What work is reused between adjacent Rabin–Karp windows?
options: The entire comparison history without verification
qs.why: A constant-work update removes the old leading code and adds the next code.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.
qs.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: What makes the verified algorithm exact despite collisions?
qs.correct: Every equal-hash candidate is checked against the actual pattern
options: The earliest hash equality is always genuine
Every equal-hash candidate is checked against the actual pattern
qs.why: Hash equality alone is never accepted as proof of string equality.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.
qs.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: For P=25,T=1225,d=10,q=13, how many hash-equal candidates are examined before the first match?
qs.why: Windows 12 and 25 hash to12; window22 hashes to9.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.
qs.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: For that example, what is the number of character-verification comparisons?
qs.why: The spurious12 costs one mismatch check; the true25 costs two successful checks.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.
qs.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: For n=4,m=2, how many rolling updates follow the initial complete-window hash in a full scan?
qs.why: There are three windows, requiring two transitions after initialization.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.
qs.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: If h equal-hash candidates are verified, what general word-operation bound includes preprocessing and scan?
qs.why: Initial hashing and rolling cost linear-scale work; each candidate can add up to m checks.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.
qs.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: If h=0 after hashing/preprocessing, what scan-level character-verification work occurs?
qs.why: Different hashes reject all windows without direct comparisons; hashing still costs work.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.
qs.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: Why does a single complete window not make preprocessing disappear?
qs.correct: Reading and hashing a length-m pattern/window can still cost Θ(m)
options: Reading and hashing a length-m pattern/window can still cost Θ(m)
qs.why: A small n−m+1 does not erase the initial pattern-length work.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.
qs.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: What can create O(nm)-scale worst-case verification work?
qs.correct: Many hash-equal windows that disagree only after long prefixes
options: Many hash-equal windows that disagree only after long prefixes
A zero-length text with positive pattern length
qs.why: Many expensive candidates can erase the filter savings; actual candidate costs matter.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.
qs.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: What is needed to claim expected near-linear performance?
qs.correct: Suitable input or hashing assumptions controlling candidate work
options: Suitable input or hashing assumptions controlling candidate work
qs.why: An expectation requires a distribution/model; a fixed finite modulus alone supplies no universal guarantee.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.
qs.context: Exact first-match Rabin–Karp. Worked decimal example T=1225,P=25,d=10,q=13. Count hash decisions, rolling updates and direct character checks separately; h counts verified equal-hash candidates.

qs.stem: A first-match Rabin–Karp scan has n=12,m=5. Its hash-equal candidates occur at starts0,2,5,7 and cost respectively1,5,4,5 direct comparisons;only the final candidate is a true match. Other starts have different hashes. Give hash decisions,rolling updates,and actual verification work;compare actual verification with the bound h m.
qs.why: All n−m+1=8 windows through start7 are considered. The first hash is initialized,so only seven rolls follow. Verification costs1+5+4+5=15;h=4 yields upper bound h m=20,which need not be attained.
qs.source: String Matching pp15–19,25,56; study notes 07-string-matching §7.4.

qs.stem: What pattern occurrence determines charJump[c]=m−r?
qs.correct: The rightmost occurrence r of c

qs.why: The rightmost occurrence limits the safe displacement for that character.

qs.stem: For P=ABCA,m=4, what is charJump[A]?
qs.why: The rightmost A is at r=4, giving4−4=0.

qs.stem: For P=ABCA, what are charJump[B] and charJump[X] for absent X?

qs.stem: In that mismatch state, j advances 2→6. If the old alignment endpoint was4, how far does the pattern slide?

qs.stem: Why is a zero charJump entry not permission for a zero alignment shift?
qs.correct: The fallback m−k+1 forces positive endpoint progress
options: Zero means the character is absent
Every zero table entry is an error
The fallback m−k+1 forces positive endpoint progress

qs.stem: For one-based successful matching with k=0, why return j+1?

j always equals the pattern length
j remains at the right endpoint
qs.why: Each of m matches decrements both pointers; the final text pointer is immediately before the occurrence.

qs.stem: What preprocessing cost fits an alphabet table of size |Σ| and a length-m pattern?

qs.stem: Using one-based P=ABCA,T=AXCABCA,charJump[A]=0,B=2,C=1,absent=4,and mismatch increment max(charJump[T[j]],m−k+1),trace from j=k=4 through the first match. Give successive alignment endpoints,total character checks and returned start.

qs.stem: After a mismatch at one-based k in a length-m pattern, which suffix is already matched?
qs.why: Right-to-left successful comparisons have passed only the positions strictly to the right of k.

qs.stem: What is the length of that matched suffix?
qs.why: There are positions k+1 through m inclusive.

qs.context: Course one-based pattern positions. At mismatch k, suffix P[k+1..m] is matched. matchJump[k]=(m−k)+Slide[k]. Default table example WOWWOW,m=6, entries ordered k=1..6.

qs.stem: What condition qualifies an earlier full suffix occurrence in case1?
qs.correct: Its preceding pattern character differs from P[k]
options: Its preceding pattern character differs from P[k]
Its preceding character must equal P[k]
It must be to the right of the current suffix
qs.why: An equal predecessor would reproduce the already-known mismatch.

qs.context: Course one-based pattern positions. At mismatch k, suffix P[k+1..m] is matched. matchJump[k]=(m−k)+Slide[k]. Default table example WOWWOW,m=6, entries ordered k=1..6.

qs.stem: If neither a suitable full occurrence nor a prefix overlap exists, what pattern slide is used?

qs.context: Course one-based pattern positions. At mismatch k, suffix P[k+1..m] is matched. matchJump[k]=(m−k)+Slide[k]. Default table example WOWWOW,m=6, entries ordered k=1..6.

qs.stem: For RATSANDCATS,m=11,k=8, what matched suffix is used?
qs.why: Positions9,10,11 contain A,T,S.

qs.stem: For RATSANDCATS,m=11,k=8, the earlier ATS ends at position4. What is the pattern slide?

qs.stem: What mismatch-pointer increment corresponds to m=11,k=8 and slide7?

qs.stem: If no suitable full suffix occurrence exists, what does case2 seek?

qs.stem: For WOWWOW at k=4, why is the earlier full OW occurrence excluded?

topics.title: What makes a computational task hard?
topics.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2. Matching later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.
topics.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: What does a decision problem ask for?
qs.why: The output is membership/feasibility rather than a best value or all witnesses.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: Which is a TSP decision question?
qs.correct: Does a tour of cost at most K exist?
options: Does a tour of cost at most K exist?
qs.why: The threshold version has a yes/no answer.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: For standard three-peg Hanoi, may a larger disk rest on a smaller disk?
options: Only if disks have equal labels
qs.why: The size-order rule holds on every peg throughout the trace.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: Does one slow known algorithm prove every algorithm for the problem must be slow?
qs.why: An upper-bound implementation is not a lower bound over all algorithms.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: How many moves does the standard optimal three-disk Hanoi transfer need?
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: For M(1)=1 and M(n)=2M(n−1)+1, what exact solution follows?
qs.why: Substitution gives2(2^(n−1)−1)+1=2ⁿ−1 and the base fits.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: Why does explicitly listing all 2ⁿ binary strings of length n require exponential output work?
qs.correct: There are exponentially many output objects
options: No algorithm can generate any of them
There are exponentially many output objects
qs.why: Even one operation per output already costs Ω(2ⁿ), with writing all characters costing more.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: How can an exact optimisation solver answer its threshold decision version?
qs.correct: Compute the optimum and compare it with K
options: Compute the optimum and compare it with K
qs.why: For minimisation, optimum≤K exactly when a feasible solution meeting K exists, with infeasibility handled.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: Why must the task and representation be specified before discussing hardness?
qs.correct: Decision, optimisation and explicit enumeration can have different outputs and input measures
options: Decision, optimisation and explicit enumeration can have different outputs and input measures
qs.why: Complexity is measured against a defined input encoding and required output.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: Does an exponential-size explicit output imply its related yes/no decision problem needs exponential time?
options: Only if there are duplicate outputs
qs.why: The decision output is one bit; an enumeration output lower bound does not automatically transfer.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: Why does standard Hanoi force moving all n−1 smaller disks away before the largest disk first reaches the destination?
qs.correct: They must clear its source and cannot block its destination
options: They must clear its source and cannot block its destination
The largest disk can jump over them without constraints
qs.why: Under three pegs, this clearing requires transferring the smaller stack to the remaining peg, then restoring it on the destination.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: An exponential exhaustive search is shown for TSP. What conclusion is warranted?
qs.correct: That search has exponential cost; no universal lower bound follows from it alone
options: That search has exponential cost; no universal lower bound follows from it alone
No polynomial algorithm can exist by that fact alone
qs.why: A poor or exhaustive method does not prove optimal complexity over all possible algorithms.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

qs.stem: Define Hanoi H(n):if n=0 return;otherwise call H(n−1),emit one disk move,then call H(n−1). For n=5,count emitted moves and all invocations,including zero-base calls. What output lower-bound conclusion applies as n grows?
qs.correct: 31 moves;63 invocations;explicit move listing needs Ω(2ⁿ) output work
options: 15 moves;31 invocations;recursion alone proves universal hardness
31 moves;63 invocations;explicit move listing needs Ω(2ⁿ) output work
32 moves;63 invocations;every related decision problem is therefore exponential
31 moves;31 invocations;explicit listing needs only O(n) work
qs.why: Move counts satisfy M(0)=0,M(n)=2M(n−1)+1,giving2ⁿ−1=31. Invocation counts include the full binary tree through depth5,1+2+4+8+16+32=63. Exponentially many explicitly emitted moves require exponential output work;that does not automatically transfer to a different yes/no task.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp3–8; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.1–8.2.
qs.context: Distinguish decision, exact optimisation and explicit enumeration. Standard Hanoi uses three pegs, moves one disk at a time and never places a larger disk on a smaller one.

topics.title: What are P and NP, and what does verification mean?
topics.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5. Matching later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.
topics.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: What kind of problems are formally classified by P and NP here?
qs.why: The formal definitions concern yes/no membership languages.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: What does P require?
options: Only fast yes answers without no answers
A short program regardless of runtime
qs.why: A decider must correctly answer both yes and no within a polynomial input-length bound.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: What does NP verification require for yes instances?
qs.correct: A polynomial-length certificate checked by a polynomial-time verifier
options: A certificate for every no instance under the same definition
A polynomial-length certificate checked by a polynomial-time verifier
A random guess accepted without checking
qs.why: The witness length and checking time are both bounded polynomially in the encoded instance size.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: Which inclusion is known from the definitions?
qs.why: A polynomial decider can serve as a verifier that ignores the certificate.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: What does NP stand for?
qs.why: NP is not defined as the set of problems outside polynomial time.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: A TSP tour certificate lists a permutation of vertices. What must a verifier check beyond its cost?
qs.correct: Every vertex appears exactly once and the closing tour is valid
options: Only that all labels are integers
Every vertex appears exactly once and the closing tour is valid
qs.why: The certificate must meet the full feasibility predicate, including returning to the start.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: Why does rejecting one proposed certificate not prove an NP instance is no?
qs.why: Yes means there exists a valid witness; one failed candidate does not negate that existential claim.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: Does easy verification automatically give an easy deterministic search over all certificates?
qs.correct: No; the candidate space may be exponential
options: No; the candidate space may be exponential
Yes because the verifier ignores input
Yes; try every certificate in polynomial time
qs.why: Polynomial witness length permits exponentially many possible witnesses; checking one is different from finding one.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: A verifier accepts every input on certificate0. Why is it invalid for a nontrivial language with no instances?
qs.correct: It lacks soundness: no instances receive an accepted certificate
options: It lacks soundness: no instances receive an accepted certificate
qs.why: For a no instance, every certificate must be rejected.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: A verifier rejects all certificates for one actual yes instance. Which requirement fails?
qs.why: Every yes instance must have at least one accepted witness.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: If certificates of length polynomial in |x| are allowed but checking them can take 2^|x| time, is NP membership proved?
qs.correct: No; polynomial verification time is also required
options: No; polynomial verification time is also required
Yes if the verifier eventually halts
qs.why: Both bounds are required, measured against the encoded input size with a polynomially bounded witness.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: What would a proof that one language in NP is outside P establish?
options: Every NP problem is outside P
qs.why: Such a language would separate the classes, since P⊆NP.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: For an undirected four-vertex TSP instance let AB=BC=CD=1,DA=10,AC=BD=2 and threshold6. A verifier receives candidate tours A-B-C-A and A-B-D-C-A. Check the full tour predicate,not only cost. Which acceptance decisions and implication are correct?
qs.correct: Reject the first,accept the second;one rejected candidate does not prove no
options: Reject the first,accept the second;one rejected candidate does not prove no
Accept both because both costs are at most6
Accept the first only;shorter certificates are always preferred
Reject both because DA=10 must occur in every tour
qs.why: A-B-C-A costs1+1+2=4 but omits D,so it is not a Hamiltonian tour. A-B-D-C-A visits all vertices once and closes,costing1+2+1+2=6. That valid second witness establishes yes despite the first candidate failing.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

topics.title: Which direction does a polynomial reduction go?
topics.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6. Matching later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.
topics.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: What does A≤pB mean in the many-one model used here?
qs.correct: A instances map in polynomial time to equivalent B instances
options: A and B have identical inputs
A is faster on every measured input
A instances map in polynomial time to equivalent B instances
qs.why: There is one polynomial function f with x∈A iff f(x)∈B.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: Given A≤pB and a polynomial-time solver for B, what follows?
options: B must be harder than every language
qs.why: Compute f(x), run the B solver and return its yes/no answer.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: To prove a proposed target B hard using known-hard A, which direction is needed?
qs.why: An efficient B algorithm must then solve the known-hard source A.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: What logical relationship must a many-one reduction preserve?
qs.why: Both directions are necessary to preserve no instances as well.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: If A≤pB and B≤pC, what follows?
qs.why: Compose the polynomial transformations; output size is also polynomially bounded.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: If A≤pB and A is easy, does that prove B easy?
qs.why: An easy source may reduce to a much harder target; the solver implication goes from target to source.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: If A≤pB and B∈P, which result follows?
qs.why: Polynomial transformation followed by polynomial solving remains polynomial.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: If A≤pB and A∉P, what can be concluded about B?
options: A and B must have equal runtime
qs.why: Otherwise a polynomial B solver would yield a polynomial A solver, contradicting A∉P.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: A construction proves only x∈A⇒f(x)∈B. What is missing?
options: Prove the function has a shorter name
Prove every B instance is an output
qs.why: Without the reverse implication, no instances could map to yes instances and the answer would be unsound.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: Why must reduction runtime include the size of its constructed instance?
qs.correct: Writing the output must also fit polynomial time
options: Only the source certificate is measured
Writing the output must also fit polynomial time
A reduction may write infinitely many symbols
qs.why: A polynomial-time explicit construction cannot produce a superpolynomial-length output.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: Does an algorithm using several adaptive calls to B automatically constitute one many-one reduction A≤pB?
qs.correct: No; that is a different reduction model unless converted
options: No; that is a different reduction model unless converted
No reduction may use any solver conceptually
qs.why: A many-one proof needs a single transformed instance with an iff condition; an oracle-use illustration alone is insufficient.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: A known NP-complete problem A reduces to B, but B∈NP has not been proved. What is still missing before calling B NP-complete?
options: A proof that B has no algorithm
qs.why: Hardness and membership are separate obligations.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: A is NP-complete. A many-one map f reduces A to B in O(n²) time with output length O(n²);g reduces B to C in O(m³) time on m-bit inputs. Suppose C has a polynomial-time decider. Which composition bound and class consequence are justified?
qs.correct: g∘f takes O(n⁶) time;A and B are in P,and P=NP
options: The maps run in opposite directions,so no consequence follows
g∘f takes O(n⁶) time;A remains known outside P
g∘f takes O(n⁵) time;only C is in P
g∘f takes O(n⁶) time;A and B are in P,and P=NP
qs.why: The second map runs on an O(n²)-length output,so its cubic bound becomes O(n⁶),not the product of exponents written additively. A C solver solves B via g and A via both maps. A polynomial solver for NP-complete A then gives P=NP.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

topics.title: How does Hamiltonian path reduce to TSP?
topics.source: Introduction to NP pp22–23, physical p22 visually checked; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.7. Matching later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.
topics.context: HP→decision-TSP construction for a simple undirected n-vertex graph,n≥3: complete graph on the same vertices, original edges weight1, nonedges weight2, tour threshold n+1.

qs.stem: In the taught HP→TSP construction on n≥3 vertices, what weight is assigned to an original graph edge?
qs.why: Original adjacency is encoded by the cheaper complete-graph edge.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp22–23, physical p22 visually checked; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.7.

qs.stem: What weight is assigned to a pair that was not an edge in the original graph?
qs.why: The target is a complete graph with every pair assigned weight1 or2.

qs.stem: What decision threshold is used?
qs.why: An original Hamiltonian path uses n−1 cheap edges and can close using at most one weight-two edge.

qs.stem: How many edges are in a Hamiltonian cycle on n≥3 vertices?
qs.why: Each of n vertices contributes one edge to its successor in the cyclic order.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp22–23, physical p22 visually checked; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.7.

qs.stem: If the original Hamiltonian path has n−1 edges of weight1, what is the maximum constructed cost after closing it?
qs.why: The closing edge costs at most2, so(n−1)+2=n+1.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp22–23, physical p22 visually checked; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.7.
qs.context: HP→decision-TSP construction for a simple undirected n-vertex graph,n≥3: complete graph on the same vertices, original edges weight1, nonedges weight2, tour threshold n+1.

qs.stem: A target tour has r weight-two edges and n−r weight-one edges. What is its cost?
qs.why: Sum2r+(n−r)=n+r.

qs.stem: At threshold n+1, how many weight-two edges can an accepted tour contain?
qs.why: n+r≤n+1 implies r≤1.

qs.stem: If an accepted tour has exactly one weight-two edge, how is an original Hamiltonian path obtained?
options: Keep it and delete every weight-one edge
qs.why: The remaining n−1 edges are original weight-one adjacencies forming a spanning path.

qs.stem: If an accepted tour has zero weight-two edges, how is an original Hamiltonian path obtained?
qs.why: Breaking an all-original Hamiltonian cycle at any edge leaves a Hamiltonian path.

qs.stem: For n=5, can a constructed tour with two weight-two edges meet threshold6?
qs.why: Cost=n+r=5+2=7 exceeds n+1=6.

qs.context: HP→decision-TSP construction for a simple undirected n-vertex graph,n≥3: complete graph on the same vertices, original edges weight1, nonedges weight2, tour threshold n+1.

qs.stem: What construction time is sufficient using an adjacency matrix for n vertices?
qs.why: Assign weight1 or2 to each unordered vertex pair, a quadratic number of pairs.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp22–23, physical p22 visually checked; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.7.
qs.context: HP→decision-TSP construction for a simple undirected n-vertex graph,n≥3: complete graph on the same vertices, original edges weight1, nonedges weight2, tour threshold n+1.

qs.stem: Why does this prove an iff rather than only the forward implication?
qs.correct: Every accepted target tour can be broken into an original HP as well as every HP being closable
options: Only the forward path-to-tour step matters
Every accepted target tour can be broken into an original HP as well as every HP being closable
Complete target graphs always imply original HP
qs.why: The n+r argument establishes the reverse direction; completion alone would be unsound.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp22–23, physical p22 visually checked; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.7.
qs.context: HP→decision-TSP construction for a simple undirected n-vertex graph,n≥3: complete graph on the same vertices, original edges weight1, nonedges weight2, tour threshold n+1.

qs.stem: Apply the taught HP→TSP construction to n=6. Candidate tour X has four weight-one and two weight-two edges;candidate Y has five weight-one and one weight-two edge. Classify them at the specified threshold,and explain the reverse construction for an accepted candidate.
qs.correct: Threshold7;X costs8 and fails,Y costs7 and passes;delete Y’s weight-two edge
options: Threshold7;X costs8 and fails,Y costs7 and passes;delete Y’s weight-two edge
Threshold6;both fail,so no original Hamiltonian path can exist
Threshold8;both pass;delete any edge even if a weight-two edge remains
Threshold7;X costs6 and passes,Y costs7 and fails
qs.why: A six-vertex cycle has six edges. Its cost is6 plus the number of weight-two edges. Thus X=8>7 and Y=7. Removing Y’s unique non-original edge leaves five original weight-one edges forming an original Hamiltonian path. Failure of X alone does not decide the instance.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp22–23, physical p22 visually checked; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.7.
qs.context: HP→decision-TSP construction for a simple undirected n-vertex graph,n≥3: complete graph on the same vertices, original edges weight1, nonedges weight2, tour threshold n+1.

topics.title: How do we prove NP-completeness?
topics.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson. Matching later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.
topics.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: What two obligations establish NP-completeness of a decision problem B?
qs.correct: B∈NP and every NP problem reduces to B
options: B∈NP and every NP problem reduces to B
B∈P and B has a slow implementation
B reduces to an easy problem only
B has a short name and a graph
qs.why: Membership supplies efficient verification; reductions supply hardness.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: Which proof direction uses a known NP-complete source A?
qs.why: An efficient target solver would then solve A.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: What is a SAT yes-certificate?
qs.why: Evaluate the formula under the proposed assignment and accept exactly if it satisfies all requirements.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: Does one failed truth assignment prove a formula unsatisfiable?
options: Only if the assignment is all false
Only when it has three variables
qs.why: UNSAT requires every assignment to fail, not just the candidate tested.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: Why does reducing one known NP-complete A suffice for hardness once A≤pB is proved?
qs.correct: Every NP language reduces to A, and composition gives a reduction to B
options: The runtime of A is copied into B
Every NP language reduces to A, and composition gives a reduction to B
qs.why: Transitivity carries the universal hardness property from A to B.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: If B has a polynomial verifier but no hardness reduction has been supplied, what has been established?
qs.why: NP membership by itself includes easy problems and does not establish completeness.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: If an NP-complete problem has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, what follows?
options: Only that one instance is easy
qs.why: Every NP language reduces to that problem, yielding a polynomial decider for each.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: Why must the target be phrased as a decision problem for this definition?
qs.correct: P/NP completeness here classifies yes/no languages
options: P/NP completeness here classifies yes/no languages
Thresholds always simplify the answer to yes
qs.why: One can discuss related optimisation hardness, but the formal membership proof concerns a specified decision language.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: A proposed reduction maps all instances to one fixed satisfiable formula. Why does it fail for a source with no instances?
qs.correct: It maps no to yes and violates iff preservation
options: It maps no to yes and violates iff preservation
qs.why: A constant yes output cannot preserve source no answers.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: What distinguishes verifying a supplied satisfying assignment from solving SAT by enumeration?
qs.correct: Verification checks one candidate; enumeration searches many candidates
options: Verification checks one candidate; enumeration searches many candidates
qs.why: A polynomial check does not bound the number of candidates tried by a search.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: A correct reduction A≤pB is exponential-time to construct. Is NP-hardness via polynomial reductions established?
qs.correct: No; the construction must be polynomial
options: No; the construction must be polynomial
qs.why: Runtime is a defining requirement of the reduction, separate from logical correctness.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: If B∈NP and known NP-complete A≤pB, what conclusion is justified?
qs.why: These are the two required obligations; separation from P would additionally require resolving P versus NP.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

qs.stem: A is known NP-complete. A proof first supplies a polynomial verifier for B and only B≤pA. Later it also supplies A≤pB with output length O(n²). If B then has an O(m⁴) decider and that forward map takes O(n²),which combined assessment is correct?
qs.correct: The first proof lacks hardness;the added forward map completes NP-completeness;the hypothetical A solver is O(n⁸),implying P=NP
options: The added map proves B outside NP;the solver is exponential
A verifier alone proves P=NP;the maps are irrelevant
The first proof already establishes completeness;the solver is O(n⁶)
The first proof lacks hardness;the added forward map completes NP-completeness;the hypothetical A solver is O(n⁸),implying P=NP
qs.why: NP membership plus the wrong-way map does not show B hard. A≤pB supplies the needed hardness. Running B’s quartic solver on O(n²) output costs O(n⁸),yielding a polynomial solver for NP-complete A and hence P=NP.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp24–28; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.8–8.9. Verifier-to-circuit construction and p36 formal NP-hard extension are excluded from this lesson.
qs.context: Consider formal NP-completeness for decision languages with polynomial many-one reductions. A and B are language names; any stated NP-completeness of A is a given premise.

options: Cheapest edge from the current vertex to an unvisited vertex
Globally cheapest edge anywhere regardless of path

An edge to a new unlisted vertex

To prevent revisiting vertices before final closure

A specific approximation theorem for all metric instances

qs.stem: How does shortest-link order candidate edges?
options: By distance from the current endpoint only

qs.stem: Which degree limit applies before final closure?
qs.correct: No vertex degree may exceed two
options: No vertex degree may exceed two
Every vertex must immediately have degree two
No vertex degree may exceed one
qs.why: A Hamiltonian cycle gives each vertex exactly two incident selected edges.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp32–33; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.12. Fresh five-vertex trace; implementation cost derivation is an explanatory addition.

qs.stem: Which cycles must be rejected during construction?

options: Every cycle including the final closure
Cycles formed before all vertices belong to the final tour
qs.why: A premature closed subtour cannot later absorb remaining vertices without violating degree constraints.

qs.stem: What distinguishes Kruskal’s objective?

qs.stem: With sorted weights AB1,BC2,AC3,BD4,CD5,DE6,AE7,BE8,AD9,CE10, which first two edges are accepted?

qs.stem: Run both shortest-link TSP and Kruskal on the default five-vertex weighted graph in the supplied edge order. Give each final accepted edge set and total cost;explain why the two algorithms differ at BD.
